³ Covered by a stay of 3 s or more (cover_by="entries", min_stay=3). An ego accelerating from a stop to 60 km/h passes through every bucket below 60 without driving at any of those speeds. Holding a bucket for 3 s means driving at roughly that speed, not passing through it. The buckets are centred on the multiples of 10 km/h, where speed limits are, so an ego cruising at 50 km/h stays in [45, 55) instead of flickering between two buckets whose edge is at 50.

⁴ Covered by a stay of 1 s or more (min_stay=1): a gap the ego only closes through is not covered.

⁵ The item of a measure past its first definition is named for its version (@v2), so it is never merged with the same attribute measured the old way (Measure versions).

A reading the simulator does not support returns nothing. The item then has no samples, the report says so, and the run is not affected. Examples are the weather on a CARLA build without weather, and the Lanelet2 tags in a run without a Lanelet2 map.

A bucket an ODD's module rules out (nonurban, when the ODD is urban roads only) is outside the ODD. It is listed, and its hits are shown, but it is not a coverage target: the grade counts only the buckets inside the ODD.

CARLA's weather values are 0-100 intensities, not physical quantities such as mm/h of rain. The rain and fog buckets are therefore named levels.

Because ODD items are sampled every tick, their hits count ticks. The report also counts, per bucket, how many runs hit it. A bucket held for many ticks in a single run is still only one situation.

docs.title: Coverage criteria: cover_by and min_stay
docs.text:
By default a bucket is covered after target hits, one by default: a single tick is enough. That lets an ego that clips a three-lane section for one frame while merging cover lane_count=3. Two parameters say what covering means instead:

  • cover_by picks the measure target counts: "hits" (the default), "seconds" spent in the bucket, "meters" the ego drove in it, or "entries" into it (see exposure, below).
  • min_stay (seconds) leaves out stays shorter than it: their hits, seconds, metres and the entry itself do not count towards target.
self.register_cover(
    "gap", ego_gap, buckets=[0, 5, 10, 30], event=SamplingEvent.TICK,
    cover_by="meters", target=50, min_stay=1.0,   # 50 m per bucket, stays of 1 s or more
)

"seconds", "meters" and min_stay need an item sampled on SamplingEvent.TICK: a one-shot sample has no duration or distance. "entries" works on any event. ODD attributes take the same three parameters (OddAttribute(..., cover_by="meters", target=200, min_stay=2), or the same keys in a binding file). Crosses take them too.

The coverage file keeps the raw measures and, with min_stay, the counted ones under counted. The report grades on the counted measure and shows a hole's progress ((hole: 120/200 m)). Items whose criteria differ between runs are reported apart, like items whose buckets differ.

docs.title: Exposure: seconds, meters, entries
docs.text:
Ticks are a poor measure of how much of a situation a run saw: a stopped ego keeps adding them. So every item sampled on TICK (every ODD item, and any scenario item or cross with event=SamplingEvent.TICK) also records, per bucket:

Measure Meaning seconds simulated time spent in the bucket meters distance the ego drove while the item was in the bucket entries how many times the item entered the bucket; a run of consecutive ticks in it counts once

A tick stands for the step since the previous tick: its duration, and the ego's displacement over it. A tick with no sample (a missing value, an ignored one) ends the stay, so the next sample in the same bucket is a new entry. A step faster than 100 m/s is a respawn or a teleport, not driving, and adds no distance; without an ego, no distance is measured. A one-shot item (START, END, a condition) has no duration: each hit is an entry, and its seconds and meters stay 0.

docs.title: Situation coverage
docs.text: ODD modules covered as situations (docs/odd.md, Situations) report in a group of their own between ODD and scenario coverage. Each is an item odd.situation.<module> with one bucket, holds, sampled every tick from the module's verdict, and graded with its target, cover_by and min_stay. Ticks where the verdict rested on missing values are listed as unknown, outside the bucket.

docs.title: The report
docs.text:
# Every *_coverage.json under outputs/ and multirun/
scenario-coverage outputs/ multirun/

# Also write the merged report as JSON, and the Markdown to a file
scenario-coverage outputs/ --json coverage.json --markdown coverage.md

For each ODD the runs were measured against, the Markdown report first says how long they spent inside it, inside only because values were missing, and outside it. It then lists the modules that ruled ticks out, and the runs that left the ODD, with when. After that comes a summary table per group: item, event, grade, covered buckets (of those inside the ODD) and holes. Below it, each item gets its buckets with hits and runs, and an item sampled every tick its seconds, meters and entries too. Exposure sums over runs; a coverage file written before it was recorded makes the item's sums unknown (? in Markdown, null in JSON) rather than short. Runs merge per item: two coverage files describe the same item when the name, event and buckets agree. An item whose definition changed between runs is reported once per definition (name#2, ...), because adding up hits of different buckets would mean nothing.

docs.title: The ODD matrix
docs.text:
scenario-coverage outputs/ multirun/ --html coverage.html

writes a standalone page with openodd's coverage matrix (its CoverageView, docs/coverage_view.md): two ODD attributes, one per axis, and in each cell the runs that spent time in it, coloured by what they did -- flaky where they both passed and failed, fails where every one failed, passes where every one passed, and not sampled or outside the ODD where none could be. A cell with too few runs to judge has a dashed outline. Clicking a cell lays out the next two attributes inside it, keeping only the time spent there (--html-depth levels deep, 2 by default); each axis has a picker for any other attribute.

A sweep drawn from the ODD with flaky (Finding flaky cases) is what fills the yellow cells in: run the rounds one after another, each reading the earlier ones' outputs, and render the page over all of them.

docs.title: Exporting the observed conditions as an OpenODD COD
docs.text:
Besides the aggregates, the coverage file keeps every tick's ODD values (odd.samples): the elapsed time, the ego's latitude and longitude (from the map's OpenDRIVE geoReference), and each attribute's value, null when it was missing. odd.started_at is the run's start time in UTC. A run still writes one file; ten minutes at 20 Hz add about 1 MB.

OpenODD's exchange format for what was observed is the current operational domain (COD) table (ASAM OpenODD 1.0, section 8.3). Write one per run with:

scenario-coverage outputs/ --export-cod cod/

Each run gives three files:

File Contents <run>_cod.csv TEMPORAL_EXTENT (start time + elapsed, "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS.mmm"), SPATIAL_EXTENT ("lat lon"), then one column per attribute: name;unit for numbers, the literal for categoricals, true/false for booleans, empty when missing (OpenODD reads it as unknown) <run>_cod_manifest.csv The manifest (8.3.4): which column is which taxonomy concept, in which unit <run>_taxonomy.yml An OpenODD YAML taxonomy of the attributes, which a COD has to travel with (6.1.4.5)

A tick without an ego position is left out, since SPATIAL_EXTENT may not be empty. OpenODD wants every number to carry a unit: give numeric attributes a unit, or their column has none. A name such as env.rain.duration beside an attribute env.rain is written as OpenODD writes a measure of an element: the key rain.duration under env. Times are UTC. Coverage files written before samples were recorded are skipped with a warning. Scenario cover items are not taxonomy concepts and stay in the coverage file only.

docs.title: Coverage file format
docs.text:
{
  "schema": "openodd.coverage/1",
  "generator": {"openodd": "0.4.0", "framework": "autoware-carla-scenario==10.0.13"},
  "scenario": "CutInScenario",
  "items": [
    {
      "name": "gap_at_cut_in",
      "group": "scenario",
      "text": "",
      "unit": "m",
      "event": "condition:cut_in_started",
      "kind": "numeric",
      "buckets": ["[0, 5)", "[5, 15)", "[15, 40]"],
      "outside_odd": [],
      "target": 1,
      "cover_by": "hits",
      "min_stay": null,
      "amount": "hits",
      "samples": 1,
      "ignored": 0,
      "hits": {"[0, 5)": 0, "[5, 15)": 1, "[15, 40]": 0},
      "seconds": {"[0, 5)": 0.0, "[5, 15)": 0.0, "[15, 40]": 0.0},
      "meters": {"[0, 5)": 0.0, "[5, 15)": 0.0, "[15, 40]": 0.0},
      "entries": {"[0, 5)": 0, "[5, 15)": 1, "[15, 40]": 0},
      "out_of_range": {}
    }
  ],
  "crosses": [
    {
      "name": "speed_x_gap",
      "group": "scenario",
      "text": "",
      "event": "condition:cut_in_started",
      "items": ["speed_at_cut_in", "gap_at_cut_in"],
      "target": 1,
      "buckets": ["[0, 10) / [0, 5)", "..."],
      "outside_odd": [],
      "hits": {"[0, 10) / [0, 5)": 0, "...": 0},
      "seconds": {"...": 0.0},
      "meters": {"...": 0.0},
      "entries": {"...": 0}
    }
  ],
  "odd": {
    "name": "urban",
    "text": "Urban roads up to 60 km/h",
    "roots": ["root"],
    "modules": [{"name": "roads", "include_and": ["scenery.location in [urban]"], "...": "..."}],
    "unmeasured": [],
    "structure": "c591ab74...",
    "revision": "3a5ba08a...",
    "version": "2.1.0",
    "ticks": {"inside": 512, "assumed": 8, "outside": 40},
    "seconds": {"inside": 25.6, "assumed": 0.4, "outside": 2.0},
    "module_ticks": {"roads": {"failed_ticks": 40, "missing_ticks": 8}},
    "out_intervals": [[12.3, 14.3]],
    "started_at": "2026-10-12T09:00:00.000+00:00",
    "samples": {"attributes": [{"name": "scenery.speed_limit", "unit": "km/h", "values": null}, "..."],
                "rows": [[0.05, 35.6812345, 139.7671234, 50, "..."], "..."]},
    "cells": {
      "attributes": ["scenery.speed_limit", "environment.rain"],
      "rows": [[["[50, 60)", "none"], 512, 25.6, 301.2], [["[40, 50)", "<missing>"], 40, 2.0, 18.5]]
    }
  }
}
  • generator says what wrote the file: openodd's version and this framework's (null when one cannot be told), so files from different versions can be told apart when they are merged or traced.
  • amount is the measure a bucket's coverage is read from: cover_by, or with a min_stay the stays long enough to count (counted.<cover_by>). An ODD attribute's item also names its attribute (the name without odd.).
  • odd.cells counts every tick in its cell: one bucket of each attribute that has buckets (attributes, in order), bucketed by openodd exactly as the items are. Each row is the cell's labels, its ticks, seconds and the metres the ego drove in it, most ticks first. A missing value is <missing>, a number outside the buckets <below> / <above>. A reader can slice the run by any attributes from it (how a run with heavy rain spent its time across speed limits, say) without the per-tick samples, which stay for the COD export.

The ODD's structure, revision (an ODD read from files) and version (what its root modules declare) say which ODD the run was measured against; see Versions of an ODD. The format, the collector that writes it, the merge and the COD export are openodd's; files written before the collector moved there (autoware_carla_scenario.coverage/1) still merge.

docs.title: Not yet supported
docs.text:
• record(). KPIs such as minimum TTC are not collected.
  • sample(). There is no value captured at one event and reported at another. Sample on the event itself instead.

docs.title: Development Guide
docs.text: This guide is for developers who want to contribute to the autoware-carla-scenario project.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.10
  • uv (version 0.9.7+)
  • Git
  • CARLA Simulator 0.10.0+

docs.title: Setting Up Your Environment
docs.text:
1. Fork and clone the repository: 

    git clone https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/autoware_carla_scenario.git
cd autoware_carla_scenario

  2. Create a virtual environment and install dependencies: 

    uv venv
source .venv/bin/activate
uv sync

  3. Install pre-commit hooks: 

    pre-commit install

docs.title: Project Structure
docs.text:
autoware_carla_scenario/
├── src/
│   ├── autoware_carla_scenario/      # Main package
│   │   ├── actions/                  # Trigger-driven side effects (turn, lane change, traffic signal, attach camera)
│   │   ├── conditions/               # Pass/fail condition evaluators
│   │   │   └── composition/          # Composed conditions (lane position, area, speed, waypoint, ...)
│   │   ├── coordinate/               # Lanelet2 / OpenDRIVE / CARLA-world transforms, MapManager, snap
│   │   ├── entity/                   # VehicleEntity, EgoVehicle, the externally driven egos, spawn helpers
│   │   ├── examples/                 # Built-in scenarios + Hydra config tree (conf/)
│   │   ├── kinematics/               # Frame-tagged Vector3, velocity, acceleration
│   │   ├── sensor/                   # CameraSensorBase + CARLA RGB camera
│   │   ├── sweeper/                  # Lanelet-constraint sweeper logic
│   │   ├── tools/                    # detect-no-3d-model CLI
│   │   ├── ui/                       # Result viewer (FastAPI + scanner + runner + sweep resolver)
│   │   ├── utils/                    # Stop-line / traffic-light helpers
│   │   ├── constants.py, entity_role.py
│   │   ├── pytest_fixtures.py        # CarlaScenarioFixture
│   │   ├── scenario_base.py          # BaseScenario, EgoConfig
│   │   ├── scenario_queue.py         # ScenarioQueue (batch / retry / cooldown)
│   │   ├── scenario_runner.py        # Single-scenario execution
│   │   └── server.py                 # CarlaServerManager
│   └── hydra_plugins/
│       └── autoware_scenario_sweeper/ # Hydra-discoverable sweeper plugin shim
├── test/                              # Tests (use `-m "not integration"` to skip CARLA-dependent tests)
├── docs/                              # Documentation source (this site)
├── pyproject.toml                     # Project configuration
└── mkdocs.yml                         # Documentation config

docs.title: Running Tests
docs.text:
# Run unit tests only (skip the `integration` marker)
uv run pytest -v -m "not integration" autoware_carla_scenario/test/

# Run integration tests too (requires a running CARLA server, or one to launch: `scenario-setup` or CARLA_EXECUTABLE)
uv run pytest -v autoware_carla_scenario/test/

The workspace pyproject.toml defines these custom pytest markers:

  • integration — tests that need a live CARLA server; they skip themselves without one.
  • slow — tests that export a package and build a wheelhouse over the network. CI runs them in jobs of their own (-m slow).
  • codon — tests that compile with Codon, some 1,240 of them. A pull request runs them in one leg per architecture, split into two shards (AUTOWARE_CARLA_SCENARIO_TEST_SHARD=K/N runs the K-th of N shards of a selection; the conftest hashes each test's node id into one).
  • codon_selftest — the codon tests of the checker itself, on code of their own. A pull request runs them only when it changes something they read (the checker, the locked dependencies, the tests, CI; the list is in .github/actions/codon-selftests/action.yml); the nightly run and every other event run them. The compile checks of the package's own code (the library check, the built-in scenarios, the template) run on every pull request.

Local verification is the same command CI runs — no container involved:

# Full pytest suite (matches CI's `test` job)
uv run pytest -n auto

# Pre-commit (matches CI's `lint-and-format` job)
uv run pre-commit run --all-files

docs.title: Code Style and Quality
docs.text:
This project follows the same coding standards as the parent repository:

  • Type Hints: All functions and methods must include type annotations
  • Docstrings: Use Google-style docstrings
  • Code Formatting: Enforced by Ruff formatter via pre-commit hooks
  • Linting: Ruff linter with auto-fix enabled
  • Type checking: mypy --ignore-missing-imports over both src/ and test/

The full pre-commit configuration lives in .pre-commit-config.yaml at the repository root and runs the following hooks:

  • trailing-whitespace, end-of-file-fixer, check-yaml, check-toml, check-added-large-files, check-merge-conflict, debug-statements, mixed-line-ending
  • ruff (with --fix) and ruff-format (astral-sh/ruff-pre-commit)
  • mypy (local hook over src/ and test/, run when a commit touches Python or the project configuration)

pre-commit runs no tests: the fast suite runs some 1,240 Codon compiles, which took minutes on every commit. Run uv run pytest yourself; CI runs it on every pull request.

docs.title: Building Documentation Locally
docs.text:
# Serve documentation locally
uv run mkdocs serve --config-file autoware_carla_scenario/mkdocs.yml

# Build documentation
uv run mkdocs build --config-file autoware_carla_scenario/mkdocs.yml

Visit http://127.0.0.1:8000 to view the documentation.

docs.title: Contribution Guidelines
docs.text:
1. Create an issue first to discuss your proposed changes
  2. Fork the repository and create a feature branch
  3. Write tests for your changes
  4. Ensure all tests pass and code is properly formatted
  5. Submit a pull request with a clear description

docs.title: Commit Message Convention
docs.text:
Follow conventional commit format:

  • feat: - New features
  • fix: - Bug fixes
  • docs: - Documentation changes
  • test: - Test additions or changes
  • refactor: - Code refactoring
  • chore: - Maintenance tasks

docs.title: Packing a scenario package into a container image
docs.text:
A scenario package created with scenario-new is a normal Python distribution, so it can be shipped as a container image that carries the framework, the scenario, its configs, and its CARLA client -- typesafe_carla, whose released wheel carries its CPython package prebuilt, so nothing is compiled at build time or in a container.

The image is built by the pack-scenario-image composite action. Everything it needs lives in the action's own directory, so it is meant to be referenced from other repositories:

- uses: hakuturu583/autoware_carla_scenario/.github/actions/pack-scenario-image@master

The ref is both the action version and the framework version that ends up in the image — the runner checks the whole repository out alongside the action, and the framework packages are built from that copy. Pin a release tag instead of main for reproducible framework versions. Your own repository does not have to contain this framework, or even be checked out.

docs.title: What the image contains
docs.text:
Only installed code:

Present Absent /opt/venv — the framework, the scenario package, their dependencies (typesafe-carla, with its prebuilt CPython package, and its Codon toolchain among them) Source trees, pyproject.toml, tests, docs, git history uv, wheels, build caches, a C compiler, any apt package at all

The entry point is the scenario CLI and the working directory is /work, where Hydra writes its run directory.

/opt/venv arrives as four layers, not one, so a client that already holds another image built the same way pulls only what actually differs.

docs.title: Stage layout
docs.text:
.github/actions/pack-scenario-image/Dockerfile runs three stages, each handing the next strictly less than it was given:

flowchart LR
    A["wheelhouse<br/>(Alpine + uv)<br/>framework/ + scenario/ → wheels"]
    B["venv<br/>(Debian slim)<br/>four installs → /export/<layer>,<br/>then slimmed"]
    C["runtime<br/>(Debian slim)<br/>four COPY --link layers,<br/>no apt layer"]
    A -- "*.whl + requirements.txt" --> B
    B -- "/export/* only" --> C

wheelhouse is Alpine because everything it touches is pure Python — uv build emits py3-none-any wheels for all three packages — so the stage needs neither glibc nor a compiler, and nothing but the wheels survives it.

The runtime is not Alpine, and cannot be. typesafe-carla and its Codon toolchain, opencv-python-headless and simple-lanelet2 publish manylinux wheels only. There is no musllinux wheel to fall back to, so a musl runtime cannot install them at all. Debian slim is the smallest base that runs the code.

Neither the venv stage nor the runtime compiles anything, and neither installs a C compiler: the typesafe-carla wheel on PyPI carries typesafe_carla's CPython package prebuilt (typesafe_carla/carla/_prebuilt, one build for every Python 3.10+), so installing the wheel is all the client needs. typesafe_carla falls back to compiling that package on its first import (15-50 minutes, ~14 GB of memory, cc) only where no matching prebuilt one exists -- a typesafe-carla installed from source, or a typesafe-carla-toolchain other than the one the wheel was built with -- and the image rules that out: the build imports the client from the finished virtualenv with TYPESAFE_CARLA_PYCARLA_BUILD=0, and the runtime sets the same variable, so a prebuilt package that does not apply is an ImportError, at build time or on the first run, rather than a half-hour compile inside a container.

docs.title: Layer layout
docs.text:
An image is pulled as a stack of layers, and a client downloads only the ones it does not already have. A virtualenv shipped as a single COPY is a single layer, so changing one line of a scenario means pulling all ~400 MB of it again. The Dockerfile therefore installs /opt/venv in four steps and ships each step as its own layer, ordered from the input that changes least often to the one that changes on every commit:

# Layer Holds Rebuilt when 1 client The virtualenv, typesafe-carla with its prebuilt CPython package (import typesafe_carla.carla as carla) and its Codon toolchain (typesafe-carla-toolchain), at the versions uv.lock pins uv.lock moves typesafe-carla or its toolchain, or python-version or the base image changes 2 deps The rest of the framework's third-party dependency closure — OpenCV, scipy, numpy, the matplotlib stack, … uv.lock, python-version or the base image changes 3 framework autoware-carla-scenario Framework code changes 4 scenario The scenario wheel, plus any dependency it adds of its own The scenario package changes

(Before the move to typesafe_carla the dependency layer was ~400 MB and the two framework and scenario layers ~2 MB and ~80 kB; the client layer, with the Codon toolchain in it, has not been measured in an image yet.)

The client comes first because it depends on nothing else: layer 1 installs typesafe-carla alone, constrained to the lock's versions, so its content is a function of the typesafe-carla and typesafe-carla-toolchain versions and the base image and nothing more. Two images built for the same client share that layer whatever else they contain, and a lock change that leaves the client alone moves only the dependency layer behind it.

So editing a scenario and rebuilding transfers the fourth layer. Bumping the framework transfers the third and fourth. A lock change moves the dependency layer, and the client layer only when it moves typesafe-carla or its toolchain. The push is incremental for the same reason: a registry that already holds a blob is sent the new layer and nothing else.

docs.title: What makes it hold
docs.text:
Layer reuse is by digest, and a digest covers file metadata as well as content, so two things could quietly defeat the split:

  • Install timestamps. The same wheel installed twice produces the same bytes at different times, and that alone is a different layer. venv-layer.sh therefore stamps every exported file with one fixed timestamp (LAYER_MTIME, 2020-01-01 by default) as it captures it, and re-stamps afterwards whatever the slim pass rewrote. A rebuild from a cold cache reproduces all four layers byte for byte: every one of them, the client included, is installed from wheels, and nothing in the image is compiled.
  • The layers underneath. A layer can only be reused together with its whole parent chain, so anything that varies has to sit behind the virtualenv rather than in front of it. The runtime stage therefore copies the four layers first and only then creates the user: useradd writes the current date into /etc/shadow, which would otherwise put a fresh digest on every layer behind it. The copies use COPY --link, so each layer is built against an empty base and stays the same blob wherever it lands.

slim-venv.py runs once per layer rather than once over the virtualenv, so stripping a shared object rewrites it inside the layer that installed it instead of duplicating a stripped copy into a later one. The build then reassembles the four trees exactly as the runtime stage stacks them and imports the native extension modules from the result, so a file lost or shadowed by the split fails the build rather than the container.

docs.title: Sharing the build cache
docs.text:
Layers are about the pull; cache-scope is the same idea for the build. It defaults to one scope per image, but images that share a lock and framework are the same build up to their scenario layer, so pointing several of them at one scope lets the later ones restore the client and dependency stages instead of resolving and installing them again. The action reports the scope it used, so a second build in the same workflow can just name the first's:

- uses: ./.github/actions/pack-scenario-image
  id: first
  with:
    scenario-package-path: packages/first_scenario
    image: ghcr.io/my-org/first-scenario

- uses: ./.github/actions/pack-scenario-image
  with:
    scenario-package-path: packages/second_scenario
    image: ghcr.io/my-org/second-scenario
    cache-scope: ${{ steps.first.outputs.cache-scope }}

docs.title: Keeping the image small
docs.text:
Two things do the work, measured on a scaffolded package with the official CARLA 0.10.0 client (before the move to typesafe_carla, whose Codon toolchain adds to these totals):

virtualenv Naive install 565 MB opencv-python-headless instead of opencv-python 512 MB …plus the slim pass 413 MB
  • Headless OpenCV. The framework's only OpenCV calls are imencode and pointPolygonTest; there is no imshow or namedWindow anywhere, so the GUI build's GTK/GStreamer payload is dead weight. Dropping it also removes the last external shared-library dependency: every .so in the venv now needs nothing beyond glibc, libgcc_s, libstdc++ and libz, all of which the base image already has. The runtime therefore installs no apt packages and carries no apt layer (the with-ffmpeg input went with the video in 15.0.0).

  • The slim pass (on by default, slim: "false" to disable) drops byte-code caches, vendored test suites, C headers, Cython sources and type stubs (29 MB), then runs strip --strip-unneeded over every bundled shared object (64 MB) — the manylinux wheels for scipy, numpy and OpenCV ship unstripped. Stripping leaves the dynamic symbol table intact.

    GNU binutils up to 2.40 — the version in Debian bookworm — rewrites some objects into a layout the kernel's ELF loader rejects with "ELF load command address/offset not page-aligned"; scipy's bundled OpenBLAS is one. So slim-venv.py re-reads every object it strips and restores the original unless each PT_LOAD segment still satisfies the loader's congruence rule. A newer binutils strips everything and restores nothing; on bookworm the one restored file costs about 2 MB. The build then imports the native extension modules and fails right there if anything did break. - Stage separation. Wheels are built in a throwaway Alpine stage and the virtualenv in a throwaway Debian stage, so no source tree, wheel, build cache or copy of uv reaches the final image.

The layer layout does not change any of these totals — the same bytes are simply split across four layers instead of one, so that a rebuild transfers only the layers that changed.

What is left is dominated by dependencies with no smaller variant: OpenCV, scipy, numpy, and the matplotlib stack that pyxodr requires.

docs.title: Pinning the CARLA client — and everything else
docs.text:
The client is the typesafe-carla that uv.lock pins (CARLA UE5: the wheel's LibCarla is built from a CARLA ref, which the build prints), with the CPython package that wheel carries prebuilt, loaded before the image is finished. Nothing in the image can change it afterwards. The default tags are :latest and the commit (:<sha>); to see which client an image carries:

docker run --rm --entrypoint python ghcr.io/tier4/my-scenario:latest -c \
  "from importlib.metadata import version; from typesafe_carla import paths; print(version('typesafe-carla'), paths.native_info()['carla_git_ref'])"

The whole dependency tree is pinned, so the same ref rebuilt months apart gives the same image: the build context carries uv.lock, the wheelhouse stage exports it as a requirements file with uv export --frozen, and that file is what constrains the client install, what the dependency layer installs, and what constrains the two installs after it. This buys reproducibility rather than size — and, with the timestamps normalised, it is what lets an unchanged dependency layer keep its digest across rebuilds. Constraints only bound what is resolved, so a scenario package that brings dependencies of its own still installs — they are the one part that floats, and they land in the scenario layer.

docs.title: In a workflow
docs.text:
jobs:
  pack:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Log in to GHCR
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Pack the scenario package
        uses: ./.github/actions/pack-scenario-image
        with:
          scenario-package-path: packages/my_scenario_package
          image: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/my-scenario
          push: "true"

The scenario package does not have to live in this repository — check it out anywhere on the runner and point scenario-package-path at it.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
action.yml carries the full list with defaults; these are the ones worth explaining further:

Input Meaning scenario-package-path The generated package — the directory with its pyproject.toml. Required, and may sit outside this repository. framework-path uv workspace root supplying the framework. Defaults to the action's own checkout, which is what makes the pinned ref the framework version. Its members are read from [tool.uv.workspace] members, globs included. slim Strips the virtualenv (see above). On by default. platforms Target platforms. Empty (the default) builds for the runner's own: linux/amd64 on an x86_64 runner, linux/arm64 on an arm64 one such as ubuntu-24.04-arm — see Architectures. cache-scope Cache key namespace. Defaults to one scope per image and platform, so images built in the same workflow do not evict each other — give two images the same scope to share it instead. A given scope is used as is, so give each platform its own.

Outputs: image-ref, tags, digest (pushed images only), cache-scope.

docs.title: Architectures
docs.text:
typesafe-carla and its Codon toolchain ship wheels for Linux x86_64 and aarch64, and so does every other native dependency of the image, so the action packs for either. Run it on an arm64 runner to get an arm64 image:

jobs:
  pack:
    strategy:
      matrix:
        include:
          - { runner: ubuntu-latest, arch: amd64 }
          - { runner: ubuntu-24.04-arm, arch: arm64 }
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.runner }}
    steps:
      # ...
      - uses: ./.github/actions/pack-scenario-image
        with:
          scenario-package-path: packages/my_scenario_package
          image: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/my-scenario
          # One tag per architecture: the default tags are the same on both
          # legs, so whichever pushed last would win.
          tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/my-scenario:${{ github.sha }}-${{ matrix.arch }}
          push: "true"

Each leg builds, loads and smoke-tests its own image natively. To publish one multi-architecture tag, join the per-architecture tags in a later job with docker buildx imagetools create. Cross-building on one runner (platforms: linux/amd64,linux/arm64 after docker/setup-qemu-action) also works, but emulated, and a multi-platform build cannot be loaded, so it needs load: "false" and smoke-test: "false".

docs.title: The smoke test
docs.text:
With smoke-test: "true" the action runs its smoke-test.py inside the freshly built image and checks that

  1. typesafe_carla's prebuilt CPython package loads without compiling anything (TYPESAFE_CARLA_PYCARLA_BUILD=0), and the official carla package is not installed,
  2. the scenario package's autoware_carla_scenario.scenarios entry point loads and registers at least one scenario,
  3. Hydra discovers AutowareScenarioSearchPathPlugin, so the package's conf/ directory reaches the config search path, and
  4. scenario --help composes a config without a CARLA server.

Check 3 is worth its keep: hydra_plugins is a namespace package that an editable install resolves via src/, so losing it from the wheel breaks every scenario=<name>/… override in the image while leaving development untouched.

docs.title: Building by hand
docs.text:
ACTION=.github/actions/pack-scenario-image

# 1. Assemble a minimal build context (framework + scenario, nothing else).
"$ACTION/assemble-context.sh" \
  --scenario ../my_scenario_package \
  --out /tmp/scenario-ctx

# 2. Build. Nothing is compiled: the CARLA client's CPython package comes
#    prebuilt in the typesafe-carla wheel.
docker build \
  --file "$ACTION/Dockerfile" \
  --tag my-scenario:latest \
  /tmp/scenario-ctx

# 3. Verify.
docker run --rm -i --entrypoint python \
  my-scenario:latest - < "$ACTION/smoke-test.py"

docs.title: Running a scenario
docs.text:
The image holds the client, not the simulator, so point it at a CARLA server and give it the map files:

docker run --rm \
  --network host \
  --volume "$PWD/maps:/maps:ro" \
  --volume "$PWD/outputs:/work/outputs" \
  --env NISHISHINJUKU_XODR_PATH=/maps/nishishinjuku_carla.xodr \
  --env NISHISHINJUKU_LANELET2_PATH=/maps/nishishinjuku.osm \
  my-scenario:latest \
  scenario=my_scenario/default map=nishishinjuku

Without --network host, pass the server address explicitly with server.host=<address> server.port=2000. Hydra writes under the working directory, so /work needs a volume for the results to outlive the container — the image runs as UID 1000, which must be able to write to it.

docs.title: External Driver Interface
docs.text:
The ego vehicle in a scenario is normally driven by CARLA's TrafficManager. This page describes the alternative: handing the ego to an external driving policy that plans over gRPC, so a scenario becomes a test of that policy rather than of TrafficManager.

The wire contract is alpasim's egodriver.EgodriverService. Its policy side is carla-driver-interface (2.x), a light package (grpcio, protobuf, numpy, Pillow; Python 3.10+) a policy depends on without pulling in the scenario framework. It is versioned on its own: the framework accepts any carla-driver-interface>=2.1,<3, so a policy and a scenario package can share an environment whenever their majors agree.

A policy run as a separate process may be on another major. Each side declares the contract revision it speaks (carla-driver-interface's major) in gRPC metadata, and the framework declares its cameras in the policy's revision:

Policy on rig_to_camera the framework declares carla-driver-interface 2.x (revision 2) the camera's optical frame in the rig (x right, y down, z along the optical axis), as alpasim declares it carla-driver-interface 1.x (declares no revision) the camera body in the rig (x along the optical axis, y left, z up), as 1.x reads it

Either way the pose is in the rig, whose origin is the rear axle (see Coordinate frames below), while a camera's position_* mount is relative to the CARLA actor origin, the vehicle's centre, where CARLA attaches it: the declared pose is the mount moved by the rear-axle offset, as the LiDAR's sweeps and a T4 dataset's camera calibration are. The default camera at position_x: 1.5 on a car whose rear axle is 1.4 m behind its centre is declared at x = 2.9 in the rig.

A 2.x policy is handed the optical frame either way, also by autoware_carla_scenario 4.x, whose cameras its server translates. A revision the framework does not know fails start_session with ContractError, before the scenario starts.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
The scenario framework plays the runtime role: it owns the world, ticks the simulation, renders observations, and asks the policy what to do. The policy is a separate process serving egodriver.EgodriverService.

flowchart LR
    subgraph scenario["Scenario process (Python 3.10-3.14)"]
        SR["ScenarioRunner<br/>owns the world and the tick loop"]
        CDE["CarlaDriverEntity"]
        CAM["CarlaCameraSensor(s)"]
        TF["TrajectoryFollower<br/>pure pursuit + yaw-rate trim<br/>Autoware's PID longitudinal controller<br/>through the powertrain model"]
        SR -->|on_tick| CDE
        CAM -->|frames| CDE
        CDE --> TF
        TF -->|VehicleControl| SR
    end

    subgraph policy["Policy process"]
        P["egodriver.EgodriverService<br/>e.g. carla-driver-interface serve"]
    end

    CDE -->|"observations + drive()"| P
    P -->|"planned trajectory"| CDE

Each simulation tick, CarlaDriverEntity tracks the most recent plan and applies a control. Every driver.policy_timestep_s it also submits fresh observations — camera frames, the ego's pose and dynamic state at every tick since the previous step (the egomotion history the upstream runtime sends), and a route window rolled forward from the ego's current position — and asks the policy to re-plan. Between policy steps the cached plan keeps being tracked, which is how a policy slower than the simulation stays usable.

docs.title: Running a scenario against a policy
docs.text:
The scenario can serve the policy itself, in its own process, so one command runs everything. Name the policy in driver.policy (a reference policy, or package.module:Class for your own BaseDriver):

uv run scenario ego.entity=carla_driver driver.policy=route_follower

The policy is built once per run and served on a free local port; driver.address is not used. Every scenario of a batch opens its own session on it, so a model is loaded once. Over the wire nothing changes: by default the scenario still dials it over gRPC, exactly as it dials a policy in another process, and with driver.transport=direct it exchanges the same messages without a socket (below).

To run the policy as a process of its own (another environment, a GPU host, an alpasim driver), leave driver.policy unset and start the policy first. It is a server, and the scenario is the client:

# In the policy's own environment
uv run carla-driver-interface serve --policy route_follower --port 50051

Then run any scenario with the carla_driver ego entity:

uv run scenario ego.entity=carla_driver driver.address=localhost:50051

docs.title: How the run reaches the policy: driver.transport
docs.text:
driver.transport driver.policy set (the run serves it) driver.policy unset (another process) tcp (default) served on a free local port and dialled there dials driver.address (host:port) unix served on a Unix socket in a directory of the run's own (0700, under $TMPDIR, or /tmp) dials driver.address, which must name a socket (unix:///run/policy.sock) direct no socket: the run calls the policy's servicer through carla_driver_interface.inprocess refused: a policy in another process has to be dialled 
uv run scenario ego.entity=carla_driver driver.policy=route_follower driver.transport=direct
# a policy in its own process, on a socket
uv run carla-driver-interface serve --policy route_follower --host unix:///run/policy.sock
uv run scenario ego.entity=carla_driver driver.transport=unix driver.address=unix:///run/policy.sock

Whichever it is, the policy sees the same alpasim egodriver messages: direct still serializes every request and response to the bytes the wire would carry and parses them on the other side, and its servicer is the one a server runs, with a context that behaves as gRPC's (an abort is a grpc.RpcError with the same code and details, the contract revision is negotiated through the same metadata). A policy that is an alpasim driver therefore drives the same whether it is dialled over TCP or called in-process; only the transport's cost goes (a sweep's megabytes are not copied through the loopback twice per step). The one difference is a deadline (driver.timeout_s): the policy runs on the run's own thread, so an overrun is reported when its call returns rather than cut short.

unix with driver.policy and direct need carla-driver-interface 2.2 or later; with an older one the run stops as it sets up, naming the installed version, and tcp keeps working. Under the SLURM launcher every task serves its own policy, so neither uses a port of its slot (slurm.md).

ScenarioRunner logs Autopilot skipped for ego (id=…) — external control expected when the policy has taken over. Pass and fail conditions, recording, the trajectory log, and sweeps all behave exactly as they do for a TrafficManager-driven ego.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The driver config group (conf/driver/default.yaml) holds the settings:

driver:
  address: localhost:50051
  policy: null               # e.g. route_follower: served by the run itself
  transport: tcp             # tcp | unix | direct; see "How the run reaches the policy"
  timeout_s: 60.0
  policy_timestep_s: 0.1     # a positive multiple of the 0.05 s tick; others are refused
  image_quality: 90
  warmup_s: 0.0              # run-up onto the spawn pose; see "Warming up a policy"
  route_horizon_m: 80.0
  route_resolution_m: 2.0
  rear_axle_offset_m: null   # null derives it from the wheel physics
  send_ground_truth: false
  send_renderer_data: true       # CARLA ground truth: lights, traffic, speed limit
  send_actor_ground_truth: true
  traffic_light_sight_distance_m: 60.0
  actor_horizon_m: 150.0
  random_seed: null           # null: the run's seed (`seed`)
  cameras:
    - logical_id: camera_front_wide_120fov
      image_width: 960
      image_height: 604
      fov: 120.0
      position_x: 1.5
      position_z: 1.6
  control:
    lookahead_gain_s: 0.6
    wheelbase_m: 2.8
    max_steer_angle_deg: 56.0   # CARLA 0.10: angle = 56 deg * steer**2
    steer_exponent: 2.0
    yaw_rate_ki: 3.0            # integral trim on the measured yaw rate
    longitudinal_controller: pid  # Autoware's autoware_pid_longitudinal_controller
    delay_compensation_time: 0.17 # ... and any of its parameters, by name
    throttle_deadband: 0.3      # vehicle interface: least throttle to pull away

docs.title: A camera with a lens of its own: driver.cameras[].lens
docs.text:
A camera's frames are CARLA's pinhole of its fov unless it says otherwise. A carla_canvas renderer may draw a camera through another lens: the Cosmos3 world model (cosmos3-canvas) draws only its Hyperion 8 cameras, each through its F-theta fisheye lens. Such a camera carries its lens, so the policy and a T4 dataset are told what the frames are:

driver:
  cameras:
    # python -m cosmos3_canvas.camera camera_front_wide_120fov
    - logical_id: camera_front_wide_120fov
      image_width: 832
      image_height: 480
      fov: 120.0
      lens:
        model: ftheta
        principal_point: [412.641208, 242.790324]
        pixeldist_to_angle_poly: [0.0, 0.00243165382, -4.05625414e-08, 6.10818843e-10, -9.93181484e-13, 8.73787714e-16]
        angle_to_pixeldist_poly: [0.0, 411.286296, 2.40299018, -16.2530848, 10.3586782, -3.39986006]
        max_angle: 1.226783919
        linear_cde: [1.00234926, 0.0, 0.0]
Field Meaning model ftheta, NVIDIA's F-theta model: the only one principal_point [x, y] in pixels (the centre of the top-left pixel is (0, 0)) pixeldist_to_angle_poly Radius from the principal point (pixels) to the angle from the optical axis (radians); coefficients from the constant term up angle_to_pixeldist_poly Its inverse, the angle to the radius max_angle The largest angle the lens sees (radians) linear_cde [c, d, e]: [[c, d], [e, 1]] maps the radial offset to pixels reference_poly Which polynomial defines the lens: pixeldist_to_angle (default) or angle_to_pixeldist

The policy is sent the lens as alpasim's FthetaCameraParam, in place of the pinhole. The CARLA camera is still made with image_width, image_height and fov: what the renderer reads to know which of its cameras it is.

docs.title: How the plan is tracked
docs.text:
TrajectoryFollower (driver/control.py) does what Autoware's control stack does behind an end-to-end planner:

  • Speeds on the plan. A plan is poses and times. The speeds Autoware's controller reads off a trajectory are put on it as autoware_tensorrt_e2e puts them on its own (autoware_diffusion_planner's get_trajectory_from_poses): each point's speed is its distance from the previous point -- the first point's from where the ego was as the plan arrived -- over the plan's time step; then a forward moving average over velocity_smoothing_window (8) points, the tail keeping the last average. While the ego moves, the first average to fall below stopping_threshold (0.3 m/s) stops the plan there. Each point's acceleration is the change of speed to the next.
  • Longitudinal. A port of autoware_pid_longitudinal_controller with the defaults of its param.yaml, under its parameter names. The plan is read spatially: the stop distance is the arc length from the ego to the plan's first zero-speed point (or its end). STOPPED departs once that is over drive_state_stop_dist (0.5 m), DRIVE stops through STOPPING (smooth stop) once it is under stopping_state_stop_dist, STOPPED holds stopped_acc, and an overshoot of emergency_state_overshoot_stop_dist brakes at emergency_acc (EMERGENCY). DRIVE follows the speed at the point the ego will be at after delay_compensation_time, with Autoware's velocity lookahead feedback (or, with enable_velocity_lookahead_feedback: false, its PID and feedforward), within the acceleration and jerk limits.
  • Lateral. Pure pursuit on the plan's points, with an integral trim on the measured yaw rate.
  • Vehicle interface. The asked acceleration becomes pedals through the ego's powertrain model, read from its CARLA physics control, as Autoware's raw_vehicle_cmd_converter does with its accel and brake maps. The model lets a standing car move at any throttle while CARLA 0.10's MKZ stays put below 0.25. A plan pulling away at a crawl asks a standing car for a throttle near 0.23, so throttle_deadband (0.3) floors the throttle of a standing car asked to speed up: it moves as a real car would creep.

What differs from Autoware, because CARLA or the plan has no counterpart:

  • The plan carries no pitch, so there is no slope compensation; CARLA's towns are flat where the scenarios drive.
  • The follower has no steering angle feedback: the steering counts as converged, so enable_keep_stopped_until_steer_convergence holds only the first tick of a departure, as Autoware's first check does.
  • The ego is always under Autoware's control (AUTONOMOUS), and always in drive: the manual-driving transitions and reverse gear are left out.
  • The ego's acceleration is estimated from its speed with autoware_twist2accel's low-pass gain (accel_lowpass_gain, 0.9).
  • The filters run per control step, at the simulation's 20 Hz rather than Autoware's 33 Hz.
  • A plan's times come from its timestamps rather than the node's fixed 0.1 s, and the smoothing window is capped at one less than the plan's points; a 0.1 s plan gets Autoware's numbers. carla-driver-interface leads each plan with the ego's pose at the planning time; that anchor is the base the first speed is measured from (the node's ego position), not a point of the tracked trajectory. A plan without one is measured from where the ego is as it arrives. Either is latched with the plan.
  • A plan of fewer than two points is ignored and the last one tracked on, as Autoware's setTrajectory does.
  • So is a plan that is not all finite (a NaN or an infinity in a pose, or in a ROS 2 trajectory's speeds or accelerations), with a warning, the first time and then once in a hundred; with no plan before it, the ego is held. A non-finite yaw rate is not fed back, and a non-finite speed or ego pose, or a command that comes out non-finite gives no throttle and the stop brake, the steering held. No controller state is updated with a non-finite value, so one bad inference cannot latch in it.
  • A follower taken over on a moving ego (the warm-up's hand-off, a spawn at speed, a new ROS 2 command source) starts in DRIVE rather than STOPPED, which would brake for a tick.
  • The smooth stop fits the speed history of the delay's control steps: 3 at 0.05 s, where Autoware keeps 5.

A ROS 2 autoware_planning_msgs/Trajectory is tracked on its own longitudinal_velocity_mps and acceleration_mps2, every point kept (a stop included) even when its time_from_start is not set.

A plan that dwells on the ego's spot -- the first eight speeds averaging to zero -- stops at its first point, and the ego stays STOPPED until a plan's stop point is more than 0.5 m away, as Autoware's would. longitudinal_controller: time_indexed selects the tracker this framework had before: the plan read on its own clock, a PI on the speed it has the ego at now and a pull towards where it has it (speed_kp, speed_ki, integral_limit, position_gain, max_position_correction_mps, speed_preview_s, stop_distance_m); RoutingAction in follow mode drives timed trajectories with it. Those keys are ignored, with a warning, for pid.

docs.title: Warming up a policy
docs.text:
A policy that reads a history -- past LiDAR maps, the ego's past poses -- has none at the first step and plans as if the ego had stood still: an ego spawned moving brakes on those first plans. driver.warmup_s gives it a run-up instead: the warmup_s before the scenario's first frame are played by rule, so that everything arrives at its first-frame pose at its initial speed.

  • Every vehicle with an initial speed, the ego among them, is put back along its lane by its initial speed times warmup_s, keeping its offset from the lane centre and its heading relative to the lane, and driven onto its pose. One with no initial speed stands on its pose.
  • Every pedestrian with an initial speed is moved in a straight line along its heading; one with none stands where it starts.
  • The traffic lights are frozen, so the run-up spends none of their phases, and thawed on arrival. A light the scenario (a TrafficSignalAction in register_init, say) or a signal controller already froze stays frozen and is not thawed on arrival.

The policy gets every observation and plans all the way, but does not drive; the scenario's clock starts, and the policy takes over, on arrival. Set warmup_s to the history the policy reads (3 s for ResWorld's ego past).

ego.entity selects the entity and accepts four values:

Value Behaviour autopilot (default) CARLA's TrafficManager drives the ego. autoware Nothing drives the ego; the actor is left for an external stack. carla_driver An external policy drives the ego over the contract described here. ros2 ROS 2 nodes drive the ego over DDS (ROS 2 over DDS).

A policy is usually built for one rig, so a preset can choose the vehicle and cameras along with the rest of the group. driver=vision_pilot is VisionPilot's: a Lincoln MKZ with one 1920×1280, 50° front camera at 10 Hz (its own CARLA rig), and it hands the ego to the policy (ego.entity: carla_driver):

uv run vision-pilot-driver --model-dir <weights> --port 50051   # in vision_pilot
uv run scenario driver=vision_pilot

A preset extends driver/default (defaults: [default, _self_]) and may set ego.*, since the driver group is composed after ego.

logical_id is the name the policy looks a camera up by, so it must match what the policy expects. carla-driver-interface's reference policies use camera_front_wide_120fov.

docs.title: A stack serving the policy's world (driver.bridge)
docs.text:
A policy can drive in a world something else serves it -- splatsim rendering what its cameras see, say -- that has to come up before the policy can drive, and has to know where the run goes. driver.bridge gives the ego the same AutowareBridge handshake an ego.entity=autoware run uses: the framework hosts the bridge, the stack's interface node dials it, pulls the scenario's mission (initial pose, goal, waypoints, at its base_link) and reports when it is ready.

driver:
  bridge:
    address: 0.0.0.0:50052     # AutowareBridgeConfig's fields
    ready_timeout_ticks: 1200

With a bridge the scenario needs a goal (ego.goal_lanelet_id, or one the scenario derives), handed over when the scenario starts. Until the stack reports ready the policy is not queried and the scenario's clock does not start; the policy then starts -- its warm-up first, when warmup_s is set -- on the tick the stack turns ready. A stack that is not ready within ready_timeout_ticks, or exits, ends the run. null (the default) runs the policy alone, from the first tick.

From Python the same is CarlaDriverEntity(config, bridge=..., bridge_config=..., launcher=...); a launcher starts and stops the stack per scenario, as it does for Autoware.

docs.title: Using it from Python
docs.text:
Scenarios that build their ego themselves can attach the entity directly:

from autoware_carla_scenario import CarlaDriverEntity, DriverClientConfig

scenario.ego_entity = CarlaDriverEntity(
    DriverClientConfig(address="localhost:50051", policy_timestep_s=0.1)
)

ScenarioRunner calls BaseScenario.create_ego(), which returns ego_entity when one is set and otherwise instantiates ego_type. Assigning ego_entity is the supported way to supply an entity that needs constructor arguments.

To test against a fake policy, pass a BaseEgoDriverClient implementation:

CarlaDriverEntity(config, client=MyFakeDriverClient(config))

docs.title: CARLA ground truth
docs.text:
The alpasim contract has no field for a traffic light and none for other vehicles. Both ride inside DriveRequest.renderer_data, an upstream-sanctioned bytes extension point, as a serialized carla_driver.v0.CarlaRendererData:

Field Contents ego_traffic_light State of the light governing the ego lane ego_traffic_light_distance_m Distance to its stop line along the ego's heading; negative once crossed or when no line applies speed_limit_mps Posted limit for the ego lane, 0 when unknown actors[] Other vehicles: pose, bounding box, and velocity, all in the local frame weather, map_name, frame_id Scene context lidar[] One sweep per driver.lidars entry, packed [N, 4] float32 (x, y, z, intensity) in the rig frame map_id, traffic_lights[] With driver.map_dir: which map file set describes the world, and every light with its state and stop points

Turning this off is not a no-op

A policy reads the payload defensively — a missing one means "no light applies" and "no other vehicles" rather than an error. So send_renderer_data: false does not fail loudly. It silently disables every rule that depends on the world outside the ego. For a specification-driven policy such as stl_driver, that is stop_on_red, collision_free and safe_headway — the car keeps driving and the rules simply stop applying.

docs.title: Finding the light that governs us
docs.text:
CARLA's is_at_traffic_light() answers a different question: whether the ego is inside the light's trigger volume, which is about a metre thick along the road. A policy asking CARLA therefore learns of a red light at the moment it arrives at it, when stopping from any ordinary speed is already impossible.

So the lane graph is walked forward instead — up to traffic_light_sight_distance_m — and any light whose stop line lies on one of those lanes governs us. Inside a junction nothing governs us: having crossed the line, the thing to do is clear the box.

The point reported is not the stop waypoint itself but the mouth of the junction it governs, reached by walking forward from the waypoint. Upstream measured stop waypoints a median of 5.5 m short of their junction on Town10HD_Opt; a policy told to stop there hesitates most of a car-and-a-half before the line a driver aims at.

This logic is ported from carla_driver_interface's reference runtime (runtime/carla_world.py at af1dcd3) so that a policy tuned against that runtime sees the same numbers here.

docs.title: LiDAR
docs.text:
The contract has no LiDAR submission RPC, so sweeps ride in renderer_data too. Each driver.lidars entry mounts a sensor.lidar.ray_cast (mount in CARLA's convention, like a camera) spinning one full revolution per simulation tick, and each policy step sends that tick's sweep, already converted into the rig frame. A sweep that does not arrive within a second is left out rather than replaced by an older one.

A policy does not see that transport: the servicer records each sweep before drive as a LidarFrame in session.frame_history, beside the camera frames, and announces it through on_frame -- the one path every sensor takes. frame_history_length applies to both, and session.latest_frame("lidar_top").as_array() unpacks the [N, 4] points as latest_frame("camera_front").as_array() decodes an image.

driver:
  lidars:
    - {logical_id: lidar_top, channels: 64, range_m: 100.0, position_z: 2.0}

CARLA's ray-cast LiDAR ignores the weather, so the sweep sent has the world's rain (precipitation) and fog (fog_density, beyond fog_distance) put on it, read when the sweep is taken -- the ODD's rain and fog knobs (environment.rain, environment.fog_density) and an EnvironmentAction mid-run set it alike (sensor/lidar_weather.py):

  • attenuation: a return at range r keeps exp(-2 alpha r) of its intensity and survives with that probability, so far returns thin out first;
  • range noise: a normal error along the ray, growing with the distance travelled through the weather;
  • early returns: a few beams come back off a drop or the fog a few metres out, at low intensity.

Each grows with its intensity (0-100). Clear weather leaves a sweep as CARLA cast it.

Field Default weather_noise 1.0 Scale of the weather noise: 0 off, 1 as tuned, more exaggerates it noise_seed null Seed of the noise (the run's seed when null); with the sweep's frame, it repeats a run's sweeps fog_density_scale server.fog_density_scale, else 0.001 The server's carla.Weather.FogDensityScale; normally left to server

How thick a fog_density looks is the server's carla.Weather.FogDensityScale, and the LiDAR's fog follows it so that it matches the cameras': the model is tuned at 0.01, the scale that draws fog a camera sees, and CARLA's default 0.001 gives a tenth of its fog. server.fog_density_scale sets both: a server the run starts is started with -ExecCmds="carla.Weather.FogDensityScale <scale>", and every LiDAR that sets no scale of its own takes it. A server already running keeps the scale it was started with (the run warns), so start it with the same one. Built without the runner, pass fog_density_scale_args(scale) (autoware_carla_scenario.server) as the server's extra_args and the same scale to each LiDAR.

driver:
  lidars:
    - {logical_id: lidar_top, weather_noise: 1.5}
environment:
  rain: 80        # heavy rain: sparser, noisier sweeps
server:
  fog_density_scale: 0.01   # fog the cameras and the LiDARs both see

docs.title: The map, as files
docs.text:
alpasim's services read a scene's map from its artifact, never off the wire; this is the CARLA counterpart. With driver.map_dir set (and the map extra installed), the world's OpenDRIVE is converted by roadgen at scenario start and written to <map_dir>/<map_id>/, in the formats driver.map_formats names (Lanelet2 by default), beside the OpenDRIVE source, roadgen's IR and its traces. map_id is <map name>-<first 12 hex digits of the OpenDRIVE's SHA-256>, so a set is written once per map and a changed map gets a new id.

Each step then carries only what changes: every light's state, named by its OpenDRIVE signal id, with its stop points on OpenDRIVE lanes. A policy that sets map_dir (its own copy of the directory) gets the set opened as ctx.map, and ctx.stop_lines() resolves the lights through roadgen's traces into its format's own elements -- for Lanelet2, the approach lanelet, the traffic-light regulatory element and the light's line strings:

class MyPolicy(BaseDriver):
    map_dir = "/shared/maps"   # the runtime's driver.map_dir, as this process sees it

    def drive(self, ctx):
        for stop in ctx.stop_lines():
            stop.state, stop.lane_ids, stop.position_local

To hand the policy a Lanelet2 map of your own instead of roadgen's conversion, name it with driver.lanelet2_path:

driver:
  map_dir: /shared/maps
  lanelet2_path: /path/to/lanelet2_map.osm

The file is copied into the set as lanelet2_map.osm, as it is (with the map_projector_info.yaml beside it, if any), and its content is part of map_id, so another file gets another set. roadgen is not needed unless driver.map_formats names other formats too. The file carries no roadgen trace (the manifest marks the format "provided": true, its trace empty), so ctx.stop_lines() finds each light on the map instead (carla-driver-interface 2.3 and later):

  • lane_ids are the lanelets the stop point lies on;
  • rule_ids are the traffic-light regulatory elements of the first lanelets on or ahead of it that carry one, up to 50 m past its own lanelet, so a map may hang its lights off the approach or off the junction lanes past the line;
  • light_ids are the line strings those elements refer to.

The map's local_x / local_y must be the local frame (CARLA's world with y mirrored, as carla-ue5-maps' are). Nothing checks that the file and the world's OpenDRIVE describe the same roads in the same frame.

docs.title: Diagnostics coming back
docs.text: DriveResponse.debug_info.unstructured_debug_info is decoded as carla_driver.v0.CarlaDriveDebugInfo when it parses as one, surfacing the policy's name, its inference time, and whatever scalars it chose to publish. They are logged every ten policy steps. Anything that does not parse is left as raw bytes — the field is deliberately unstructured, and a policy is free to use its own encoding.

docs.title: Turn indicators
docs.text:
A policy commands the ego's turn indicators as well as its plan (DriveResult.turn_indicator on the policy side, carla-driver-interface 2.1+). The egodriver contract carries only the plan, so the command does not ride in the response: after each drive the client asks for it with carla_driver.v0.CarlaVehicleService's get_vehicle_command, which the policy's server serves on the same port. A server that predates it answers UNIMPLEMENTED, and the policy is then taken to command nothing.

The entity lights the ego's LeftBlinker / RightBlinker with the command, leaving its other lights as they are, and holds them until the policy asks for others: DISABLE turns both off, and NO_COMMAND -- the default, and what a policy that never sets it sends -- changes nothing. The numbers are Autoware's TurnIndicatorsCommand ones, so a planner that classifies Autoware's recorded signal (DISABLE / LEFT / RIGHT) passes its class plus one. CarlaDriverEntity.turn_indicator is what is lit now; a value the runtime does not know is logged and ignored.

Because the indicators are the CARLA vehicle's own lights, a scenario checks them with TurnIndicatorCondition -- the policy signals left before it turns, say -- and sets another vehicle's with TurnIndicatorAction (a car ahead signalling that it pulls out). An action aimed at the policy's ego holds only until the policy's next command.

from autoware_carla_scenario import (
    EntityRole,
    TurnIndicatorAction,
    TurnIndicatorCondition,
    TurnIndicatorState,
)

signals_left = TurnIndicatorCondition(
    EntityRole.ego(), TurnIndicatorState.LEFT, label="ego_signals_left"
)
npc_signals_right = TurnIndicatorAction(EntityRole.npc(1), TurnIndicatorState.RIGHT)

docs.title: Coordinate frames
docs.text:
Two conversions sit between CARLA and the contract, both handled in autoware_carla_scenario.driver.observation:

  • Handedness. CARLA's world is left-handed (x=East, y=South, z=Up, yaw clockwise); the contract is right-handed (x forward, y left, z up). Positions flip y, yaw is negated, and angular velocity — a pseudovector — picks up an extra sign flip.
  • Rig origin. alpasim puts the rig origin at the rear-axle centre projected to the ground, while a CARLA actor's origin is at the vehicle centre. The offset is derived from the vehicle's wheel physics and logged at session start. Sensor mounts (driver.cameras, driver.lidars) are relative to the actor origin; the cameras' rig_to_camera and the LiDAR sweeps are moved by the offset into the rig.

Rear-axle offset on CARLA 0.9.x

CARLA 0.9.x reports wheel positions in world coordinates and centimetres, so the derived offset can land far outside a plausible range. When that happens the value falls back to half the bounding-box length and a warning is logged. Set driver.rear_axle_offset_m (e.g. -1.4) to pin it explicitly.

Observations are submitted with the ego pose in the local frame and velocities in the rig frame; the route is submitted in the rig frame. The plan comes back in the local frame and is converted to the rig frame before the controller tracks it.

docs.title: Early termination
docs.text: A policy can set terminate_session on its response. The entity records it, and ScenarioRunner ends the tick loop — but only after evaluating the scenario's own pass and fail conditions, so a condition firing on the same tick still decides the outcome. On its own, an early stop is reported as a failure with the message Ego entity requested session termination: The driver policy requested session termination, because the scenario never satisfied its pass condition.

docs.title: Writing a policy
docs.text:
A policy subclasses BaseDriver and returns a plan in the rig frame (x forward, y left, origin on the ground below the rear axle); the servicer handles sessions, frame retention, ego history and the rig/local conversion:

from carla_driver_interface.driver import BaseDriver, DriveContext, DriveResult
from carla_driver_interface.server import run_server


class MyPolicy(BaseDriver):
    name = "my_policy"

    def drive(self, ctx: DriveContext) -> DriveResult:
        ...


run_server(MyPolicy(), port=50051)

Without CARLA, carla_driver_interface.testing.FakeLoop drives a policy server over real gRPC on a straight road, rendering each declared pinhole camera, which is what a policy's CI runs (carla-driver-interface demo --driver localhost:50051 from the command line). The scenario framework is then the CARLA-backed runtime for the same server.

docs.title: Protobuf definitions
docs.text:
The protobuf definitions are vendored, not installed, in carla_driver_interface. alpasim's published alpasim-grpc requires Python ≥ 3.11, while this workspace supports 3.10 onwards -- Autoware's own environment is 3.10 -- so depending on it would drop 3.10 support. Instead the .proto files are copied verbatim from two upstreams (both Apache-2.0) and compiled locally:

Proto Source Carries alpasim_grpc/v0/* NVlabs/alpasim@6870924 The egodriver service and its messages carla_driver/v0/* hakuturu583/carla_driver_interface@af1dcd3 The CARLA extension payloads

Field numbers, package names, and import paths are preserved exactly, which is what keeps the messages wire compatible.

Regenerate the committed modules after updating the vendored protos:

uv run python autoware_carla_scenario/scripts/compile_protos.py

test_proto_generated.py fails if the committed output drifts from the .proto files. See carla_driver_interface/proto/README.md for the full provenance.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Only RGB cameras and ray-cast LiDARs are streamed.
  • CARLA has no recorded drive, so with send_ground_truth: true the reference sent through submit_recording_ground_truth is the route itself: its waypoints, headed along the path and spaced policy_timestep_s apart. This is the recorded trajectory channel, unrelated to the CARLA ground truth in renderer_data.
  • The route is a lane-following walk of CARLA's road graph, taking the first continuation at each fork. It is a rolling window, re-sent on every policy step so the horizon stays ahead of the vehicle, but it is not a global plan: the ego will not turn toward a goal. Scenarios needing a specific route should submit their own waypoints through the client.
  • Actor reporting covers vehicles only — pedestrians are not included.
  • Actor dynamic_state carries linear velocity; angular velocity and acceleration are left zero, matching the reference runtime.

docs.title: HILS: ECUs in the Loop
docs.text:
scenario-hils is a hardware-in-the-loop bridge. It is a resident process on the HILS PC wired to the ECUs under test, independent of the scenario runner. It follows the ego of a scenario run in CARLA and sends the ECUs what their real sensors and buses would deliver: CAN frames, a GNSS receiver's output, a LiDAR's UDP packets, camera frames. It initializes and finalizes the ECUs around each scenario, and hands what they command back to the run, which drives the ego with it. The ECU traffic goes through hilspy (a Rust core with a thin Python layer).

flowchart LR
    subgraph sim["Simulation host"]
        runner["scenario runner<br/>ego.entity=hils<br/>(ticks the world)"]
        carla[("CARLA server")]
        runner -- typesafe_carla --> carla
    end
    subgraph hils["HILS PC: scenario-hils (resident)"]
        bridge["HilsBridge<br/>(a second CARLA client, never ticks)"]
        canvas["carla_canvas renderer<br/>(optional)"]
        hilspy["hilspy channels"]
        bridge -- "sensors (listen)" --> canvas
        bridge <--> hilspy
    end
    carla -- "ticks, ego state, sensor data" --> bridge
    runner <-- "TCP :7700<br/>start / ready / command / disconnect / reconnect / end / ended" --> bridge
    hilspy <-- "can:// dbc<br/>(inputs: ECU commands)" --> ecu1["ECU: vehicle CAN"]
    hilspy -- "tcp:// sbf, serial:// nmea" --> ecu2["ECU: GNSS input"]
    hilspy -- "udp:// lidar:MODEL" --> ecu3["ECU: LiDAR driver"]
    hilspy -- "v4l2://" --> ecu4["ECU: camera input"]

The bridge is a CARLA client of its own: it waits for the runner's ticks (World.wait_for_tick), so it works with the runner's synchronous mode, and it never ticks the world itself. One scenario-hils serves scenario after scenario, a whole batch, for as long as it runs.

A scenario's life, with ego.entity=hils:

  1. The runner spawns the ego and connects to the bridge (hils.host, hils.port): start, with the ego's actor id.
  2. The bridge starts the devices' periodic messages, runs the scenario_start steps (wake the ECUs, wait until they say they are ready) and then attaches its sensors to the ego, so the ECUs get no sensor data measured before the scenario is live. The runner ticks the world meanwhile, holding every vehicle still, until the bridge answers ready -- or fails the run when a step fails or nothing comes within hils.ready_timeout_s.
  3. Every tick the ego's state goes to the ECUs; whenever an ECU sends a command message (inputs), the bridge forwards the command and the runner applies it to the ego.
  4. When the scenario ends the runner sends end; the bridge runs the scenario_end steps, stops the periodic messages, removes its sensors and answers ended. A run that goes away mid-scenario ends it as well.

Without a run connected (any other ego.entity), the bridge streams the ego to the ECUs all the same, and the ego appearing and disappearing start and end the scenario; the ECUs' commands then go nowhere. The ego of a run that went away -- it failed, or ended -- can stay in the world a while; it does not start a scenario, but an ego spawned after it does.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
The bridge is the hils extra. With uv, one command installs it in a cached environment and runs it:

# Write a commented example configuration and edit it.
uvx --from 'autoware-carla-scenario[hils]' scenario-hils --example > hils.yaml

# Check it: what each device sends, nothing opened.
uvx --from 'autoware-carla-scenario[hils]' scenario-hils hils.yaml --check

# Run it, until Ctrl-C or SIGTERM.
uvx --from 'autoware-carla-scenario[hils]' scenario-hils hils.yaml

# Sensors rendered by carla_canvas (`canvas:` in hils.yaml).
uvx --from 'autoware-carla-scenario[hils]' --with 'carla-canvas[client]>=0.2' \
    scenario-hils hils.yaml

--host, --port, --role-name and --listen override the file's CARLA address, ego and run link. In a checkout, uv sync --dev installs hilspy and uv run scenario-hils hils.yaml runs it.

Then run scenarios with the ego driven by the ECUs, on the same CARLA server:

uv run scenario ego.entity=hils hils.host=hils-pc
hils. setting Default host, port localhost, 7700 the bridge's runner.listen connect_timeout_s 10.0 reaching the bridge ready_timeout_s 60.0 its scenario_start steps (wall clock) end_timeout_s 30.0 its scenario_end steps (wall clock) stale_s 0.5 a command older than this (wall clock) is stale on_stale brake brake, or hold the last command, once stale; before any command the ego brakes

docs.title: Keeping it resident
docs.text:
The bridge waits for a CARLA server that is not up yet, and for runs, for as long as it runs; Ctrl-C or SIGTERM end a running scenario (its scenario_end steps), run the shutdown steps and close the devices. A systemd unit keeps it up across reboots:

# /etc/systemd/system/scenario-hils.service
[Unit]
Description=scenario-hils (HILS bridge)
After=network-online.target

[Service]
User=hils
ExecStart=/home/hils/.local/bin/uvx --from 'autoware-carla-scenario[hils]' scenario-hils /etc/scenario-hils/hils.yaml
Restart=on-failure
KillSignal=SIGTERM
TimeoutStopSec=60

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

A failing startup step stops the bridge with status 1 (systemd restarts it).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
One YAML file describes everything. Relative paths in it (the canvas file, a codec's file, a profiles option) are relative to the file. Unknown keys are refused, so a typo fails at start-up instead of being ignored.

carla: {host: sim-host, port: 2000, timeout: 10.0}
ego: {role_name: Ego, wait: 120.0}
canvas: canvas.yaml        # optional
clock: simulation          # or wall
devices:
  vehicle_can: {...}
  lidar_top: {...}
Key Default carla.host, carla.port localhost, 2000 the CARLA server the scenario runs on; the port is a whole number from 1 to 65535 carla.timeout 10.0 seconds (positive), for RPCs and for each tick ego.role_name Ego the runner's ego ego.wait 120.0 seconds (not negative) without an ego before a warning (it keeps waiting) canvas none a carla_canvas configuration: see carla_canvas clock simulation the devices' time: see Time runner.listen 0.0.0.0:7700 where runs with ego.entity=hils reach the bridge; null: no run link commands.mode control how the ECUs' command drives the ego: see ECU to simulation devices one entry per device, by name lifecycle none steps around the bridge and each scenario: see Lifecycle

Names, addresses and raw bytes are text. YAML 1.1, which the bridge reads, turns some unquoted values into something else: 0102 is the octal number 66, 1:30 is 90, and on, off, yes and no are booleans. What was written is then lost, so the bridge refuses these forms anywhere in the file, field values and codec options included, naming the line and the key (write true/false, a decimal or 0x number, or quote the text). 0x7DF, 1.5 and true mean what they say and are taken.

Where text is expected, a value YAML reads as a number or a boolean is also refused (carla.host: 10.0 is the number 10.0) and must be quoted. This covers device names, url, codec, field names (a DBC signal called On is written "On": 1), signal: and field:, carla.host, ego.role_name, runner.listen, canvas, clock, commands.mode and a raw frame's data. Message, input and step names also take a whole number, as its decimal text (RTCM's name: 1005). Field values and id are numbers and stay unquoted (id: 0x7DF).

The numbers the bridge itself uses are checked as well, naming the key: carla.port is a whole number from 1 to 65535 (2000.7 is refused, not truncated); every duration -- carla.timeout, ego.wait, a message's period, a step's sleep and a wait's timeout -- is finite (YAML's .inf and .nan are refused), ego.wait and sleep are not negative and the others are positive; and a field's scale and offset, a sensor's transform and its intensity_scale are finite.

A device is one hilspy channel: url (the transport), codec (raw when omitted) and options (codec options), exactly what hilspy.open(url, codec, **options) takes. It has messages (periodic messages filled from the ego's signals, sent while a scenario runs) and inputs (messages the ECU sends that carry its command), or a sensor (a CARLA sensor on the ego whose measurements it is sent). A device with neither still serves the lifecycle steps (a power supply on a serial port, say).

docs.title: Message devices
docs.text:
Each message is sent periodically through the codec, and its fields are updated from the ego on every tick:

vehicle_can:
  url: can://vcan0
  codec: dbc:vehicle.dbc
  options: {ecu: VCU}          # send only what the VCU transmits
  messages:
    - name: VehicleSpeed
      period: 0.01             # seconds; omitted: the DBC's GenMsgCycleTime
      fields:
        Speed: $speed_kmh
        YawRate: {signal: yaw_rate, scale: 1.0, offset: 0.0}
        Gear: D

A field is

  • a constant (D, 4, true),
  • $name: a signal (below), or
  • {signal: name, scale: k, offset: c}: signal * k + c.

$$ starts a constant that begins with $. scenario-hils --signals lists the signals:

Signal Unit time, frame s, - the world's elapsed seconds and frame x, y, z m world position (CARLA's frame) roll, pitch, yaw deg CARLA rotation heading deg clockwise from north, [0, 360) latitude, longitude, altitude deg, deg, m from the map's geo-reference latitude_rad, longitude_rad rad as SBF's PVTGeodetic takes them velocity_north, velocity_east, velocity_up m/s course deg course over ground, clockwise from north speed, speed_kmh m/s, km/h magnitude of the velocity longitudinal_velocity, lateral_velocity, vertical_velocity m/s vehicle frame: x forward, y left, z up longitudinal_acceleration, lateral_acceleration, vertical_acceleration m/s² vehicle frame roll_rate, pitch_rate, yaw_rate deg/s right-handed: yaw_rate positive turning left yaw_rate_rad rad/s throttle, brake, steer - the control last applied (steer positive right, as CARLA) hand_brake, reverse, gear - 0 or 1, 0 or 1, CARLA's gear

Any codec hilspy encodes with works. A GNSS receiver over TCP, as a Septentrio receiver streams SBF:

gnss:
  url: tcp://0.0.0.0:28784?listen
  codec: sbf
  messages:
    - name: PVTGeodetic
      period: 0.1
      fields: {mode: 4, latitude: $latitude_rad, longitude: $longitude_rad,
               height: $altitude, vn: $velocity_north, ve: $velocity_east,
               vu: $velocity_up}
    - name: AttEuler
      period: 0.1
      fields: {heading: $heading, pitch: $pitch, roll: $roll}

or NMEA on a serial port:

gps:
  url: serial:///dev/ttyUSB0?baud=115200
  codec: nmea
  options: {talker: GN}
  messages:
    - name: GGA
      period: 0.1
