      fields: {latitude: $latitude, longitude: $longitude, altitude: $altitude,
               fix_type: Rtk, fix_satellites: 14}
    - name: RMC
      period: 0.1
      fields: {lat: $latitude, lon: $longitude, speed_over_ground: {signal: speed, scale: 1.943844},
               true_course: $course, status_of_fix: Autonomous}

hilspy's README lists the codecs and their message fields (DBC and FIBEX networks, SOME/IP, SBF, NMEA, UBX, RTCM).

docs.title: Sensor devices
docs.text:
The bridge spawns the sensor on the ego (its role_name is the device's name), listens to it, and sends each measurement:

lidar_top:
  url: udp://192.168.1.201:2368          # the ECU's LiDAR driver
  codec: lidar:pandar_xt32
  sensor:
    blueprint: sensor.lidar.ray_cast
    transform: {x: 0.0, y: 0.0, z: 2.0, roll: 0.0, pitch: 0.0, yaw: 0.0}
    attributes: {channels: 32, range: 120, points_per_second: 640000,
                 rotation_frequency: 10, upper_fov: 15, lower_fov: -16}
    intensity_scale: 255                  # CARLA's 0-1 intensity -> a byte

front_camera:
  url: v4l2:///dev/video10?format=BGRA&width=1280&height=720&fps=20
  sensor:
    blueprint: sensor.camera.rgb
    transform: {x: 1.5, z: 1.6}
    attributes: {image_size_x: 1280, image_size_y: 720, fov: 90}
    encoding: bgra
  • LiDAR (sensor.lidar.ray_cast, with a lidar:MODEL codec: Hesai Pandar and Velodyne models). CARLA measures the arc a LiDAR sweeps in one tick; the bridge gathers the arcs into whole revolutions (by rotation_frequency and the time between measurements) and hilspy encodes each revolution into the model's UDP packets, paced over the revolution as the sensor streams them. Points go from CARLA's sensor frame (y right) to the sensor's (y left). Match channels, the field of view and rotation_frequency to the model.
  • Cameras (sensor.camera.*, codec raw). Each image is one frame, in encoding: bgra (CARLA's raw image), bgr, rgb, jpeg or png. v4l2:// makes it a V4L2 camera any client on the PC sees (hilspy built with its v4l2 feature, and v4l2loopback: hilspy's README, "Cameras"); udp:// or tcp:// send the bytes.

docs.title: ECU to simulation
docs.text:
A device's inputs name the messages an ECU sends that carry the command driving the ego, and which message field fills which command field:

commands:
  mode: control                  # or ackermann
devices:
  vehicle_can:
    url: can://can0
    codec: dbc:vehicle.dbc
    inputs:
      - name: ControlCmd         # as the codec decodes it
        command:
          throttle: {field: AccelPedal, scale: 0.01}   # % -> [0, 1]
          brake: {field: BrakePedal, scale: 0.01}
          steer: {field: SteeringCmd, scale: -1.0}     # left-positive -> CARLA's right
      - name: GearCmd
        command: {reverse: {field: Reverse}}

A command field is a message field (AccelPedal), a scaled one ({field: ..., scale: k, offset: c}), or a constant. Several messages can each fill part of the command; the bridge merges the newest values into one command and forwards it to the run whenever an input arrives. The fields:

commands.mode Fields CARLA control throttle, brake (0-1), steer (-1-1, positive right), hand_brake, reverse, manual_gear_shift (0/1), gear VehicleControl ackermann steer (rad, positive right), steer_speed (rad/s), speed (m/s), acceleration (m/s²), jerk (m/s³) VehicleAckermannControl

A value that is not finite (NaN or an infinity: a decoded IEEE-float signal, a scale that overflows), or larger in magnitude than a 32-bit float holds (CARLA's controls would make it an infinity), is dropped with a warning, as a missing field is: the command keeps the field's previous value. The run drops one it receives too, and the field takes its default. A constant, scale or offset must be finite. The run clamps gear to a 32-bit integer.

The run applies the newest command every tick. One older than hils.stale_s (the ECUs stopped sending) is stale: the ego brakes, or with hils.on_stale=hold keeps the last command.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
lifecycle lists steps for four moments:

Phase When If a step fails startup once, when the bridge starts (devices just opened, before CARLA is reached) the bridge stops (status 1) scenario_start a scenario starts (the run's start, or the ego appearing); the periodic messages are already running, and the run waits for the steps; the sensors are attached after them (even when one fails), so no sensor data measured during the steps is sent the run fails, with the step's error scenario_end the scenario ends (the run's end, the run going away, or the ego disappearing); then the periodic messages stop and the sensors go logged; the other steps still run shutdown once, when the bridge stops (Ctrl-C, SIGTERM) logged; the other steps still run 
lifecycle:
  startup:
    - send: vehicle_can                    # a message through the codec
      name: PowerMode
      fields: {Ignition: 0}
  scenario_start:
    - send: vehicle_can
      name: PowerMode
      fields: {Ignition: 1, Odometer: $x}  # signals are the ego's, at the start
    - wait: vehicle_can                    # for an ECU's message with these fields
      name: EcuStatus
      fields: {Ready: 1}
      timeout: 10.0
  scenario_end:
    - send: diag_can                       # a raw frame: id and hex bytes
      id: 0x7DF
      data: "02 11 01"
    - sleep: 0.5
  shutdown:
    - send: power
      data: "4F 55 54 30 0A"

A raw frame's data is a quoted string of hex bytes, with or without spaces (data: "0102" or data: "01 02"), or a list of byte values (data: [0x01, 0x02]). Unquoted, YAML reads a hex string as a number (0102 is octal 66, 0x10 is 16), so the bridge refuses it rather than send other bytes.

A wait is satisfied by a matching message received since its phase began, so an ECU that answers a send at once is not missed. While steps run the bridge does not follow the world, and with clock: simulation its clock follows the wall clock instead, so periodic messages keep flowing to an ECU that is being waited on. startup and shutdown steps have no ego, so their fields are constants.

docs.title: Communication loss
docs.text:
CommunicationLossAction reproduces a break in the communication path to an ECU: the data it names -- a CAN frame, a LiDAR's or a camera's packets, a GNSS receiver's stream -- stops, for as long as the action runs. The run asks the bridge (disconnect on the link) when the action fires and asks it to carry the data again (reconnect) when the action ends; the bridge stops it in the device's hilspy channel (Channel.disconnect). The bus or socket stays open and the device's other traffic carries on.

from autoware_carla_scenario import CommunicationLossAction, ElapsedTimeCondition

# VehicleSpeed stops reaching the ECU for 2 s, 10 s into the scenario.
self.register_pre_tick(
    CommunicationLossAction(
        "vehicle_can",
        messages=["VehicleSpeed"],
        direction="to_ecu",
        duration=2.0,
        condition=ElapsedTimeCondition(10.0, label="at_10s"),
    )
)
# The top LiDAR's packets stop from 20 s until 25 s.
self.register_pre_tick(
    CommunicationLossAction(
        "lidar_top",
        condition=ElapsedTimeCondition(20.0, label="at_20s"),
        until=ElapsedTimeCondition(25.0, label="at_25s"),
    )
)
Argument Default device None the configuration's device; None for every device messages None the messages to stop, by the names the device's codec gives them (VehicleSpeed of a DBC, scan of a LiDAR); a list or one comma-separated string. None stops everything the device carries (camera frames, which have no name, included) direction both to_ecu (what the bridge sends the ECU), from_ecu (what the ECU sends back), or both duration None scenario seconds the action runs until None a condition that ends the action entity_name Ego the HILS ego

The action runs from its trigger until until fires or duration has passed, whichever comes first; with neither, until the scenario ends. Several actions add up: a device stops what any running action names. While data is stopped, the periodic messages are still encoded and only their frames are dropped, so an E2E counter or a sequence number moves on as an ECU's would on a cut bus. Stopping an ECU's command messages (from_ecu) makes the run's command go stale after hils.stale_s, and the ego brakes or holds it (hils.on_stale). The bridge carries everything again when the scenario ends, before its scenario_end steps, so they reach the ECUs. A device the bridge does not have ends the run with an error; on any ego but ego.entity=hils the action only logs a warning, so one scenario serves HILS and simulation runs alike.

docs.title: Time
docs.text:
With clock: simulation (the default) every device runs on simulated time: a hilspy.Clock that the world's ticks advance by the simulated time that passed. Periodic messages go out as the clock passes their periods and a LiDAR revolution's packets as it reaches their times, so the ECU sees the traffic the simulation implies even when CARLA runs slower or faster than real time; the clock starts at the wall-clock time the bridge starts, so GNSS time stamps are plausible.

With clock: wall the devices run on real time: periodic messages from hilspy's threads, sensor data sent from a thread per device as it arrives (the newest data wins when a device falls behind). Use it when the simulation runs in real time and the ECUs check timing against their own clocks.

docs.title: Sensors rendered by carla_canvas
docs.text: canvas: canvas.yaml has carla_canvas render the bridge's cameras and LiDARs (3D Gaussian splatting, or any renderer behind its gRPC protocol) instead of the CARLA server. The bridge points typesafe_carla's sensor plugin at carla_canvas before anything listens, as canvas.config does for a run (autoware_carla_scenario.canvas.use_canvas). Its sensors rules can select the bridge's sensors by role_name, which is the device's name. Keep carla_canvas's asynchronous rendering (renderer.async, its default): the bridge does not tick the world, and the asynchronous path renders each frame the runner ticks. carla_canvas's client is installed with --with 'carla-canvas[client]>=0.2'.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• One run at a time: a second run that connects while one is served waits for it (and fails its own hils.connect_timeout_s meanwhile).
  • One ego. Run one scenario-hils per ego role (and runner.listen port) for more.
  • Sensors are the ray-cast LiDAR and the cameras; GNSS and IMU are signals of the ego's state, without CARLA's sensor noise.
  • A sensor's data reaches the devices on the tick after the one it was measured on when it arrives after that tick; an ECU command reaches the ego on the run's next tick after it arrives.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: This guide will help you install the autoware-carla-scenario package.

docs.title: Operating System
docs.text:
• Linux x86_64 or aarch64 (Ubuntu 22.04 is the reference; CI runs on ubuntu-latest and ubuntu-24.04-arm). Every runtime dependency resolves to a wheel on both, the CARLA client's CPython package included (see CARLA client), so nothing is compiled on install.
  • On aarch64 the framework, its CARLA client and the static check all run, but CARLA itself does not: its server is built for x86_64 only. Run the server on an x86_64 host and point the runner at it with server.host=<address> (a server already listening is used rather than launched); scenario-setup refuses to download the nightly there.

docs.title: Python Version
docs.text:
• Python 3.10 – 3.14 — pyproject.toml declares requires-python = ">=3.10,<3.15": the interpreters CI tests. No dependency caps it any more; it is raised together with CI's interpreter matrix. Check your version with python --version.
  • Hydra on Python 3.14 — Hydra 1.3 gives --shell-completion a help object that Python 3.14's argparse refuses ("badly formed help string"), so a @hydra.main command would fail before it parses anything (#692). autoware_carla_scenario.hydra_compat works around it: the scenario entry point and the lanelet sweeper import it, and it has Hydra build its parser with an ArgumentParser subclass that skips argparse's check for help that is not a string (argparse itself is left as it is, and --hydra-help still shows the completion instructions). On Python 3.10 to 3.13 importing it changes nothing. A @hydra.main app of your own that runs on 3.14 imports it before calling the decorated function: import autoware_carla_scenario.hydra_compat # noqa: F401.

docs.title: CARLA Simulator
docs.text: The framework targets CARLA UE5 (0.10.0 and ue5-dev). CARLA 0.9.x (UE4) is not supported. uv run scenario-setup downloads CARLA's nightly Linux build into ~/.autoware_carla_scenario/bin/carla, and the runner launches it from there (see the Quick Start). A CARLA installed any other way is used through CARLA_EXECUTABLE.

docs.title: CARLA client
docs.text:
The Python client is typesafe_carla, a plain dependency of the package (typesafe-carla>=0.8.1,<0.9, from PyPI, Linux x86_64 and aarch64), imported as import typesafe_carla.carla as carla. It also provides the Codon library the static check compiles scenarios against, and pulls in typesafe-carla-toolchain, the pinned Codon compiler. The official carla wheels are not used, and no extra has to be requested.

The released wheel on PyPI carries its CPython package prebuilt (typesafe_carla/carla/_prebuilt), one build that serves every Python 3.10+, so uv sync (or pip install) is the whole installation: nothing is compiled, no C compiler is needed, and nothing is fetched beyond the install itself.

Only where no matching prebuilt package exists -- typesafe_carla installed from a source checkout or an sdist, edited Codon sources, or a typesafe-carla-toolchain release other than the one the wheel was built with -- does the first import typesafe_carla.carla build it instead. That build takes 15 to 50 minutes and about 14 GB of RAM, needs a C compiler (cc), and lands in ~/.cache/typesafe_carla/pycarla.

uv run typesafe-codon pycarla

runs it ahead of time, and reports that there is nothing to build when the prebuilt package applies. Set TYPESAFE_CARLA_PYCARLA_DIR to put the build elsewhere (a directory set this way is used in preference to the prebuilt package), and TYPESAFE_CARLA_PYCARLA_BUILD=0 to make a missing build an ImportError instead of starting one.

docs.title: Package Manager
docs.text: • uv (version 0.9.7+) — modern Python package manager, used as both the build backend and the workflow runner.

docs.title: Installing uv
docs.text:
If you don't have uv installed yet:

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

For more options, see the official uv documentation.

docs.title: Installing the Package
docs.text: The framework does not depend on autoware_lanelet2_to_opendrive, the converter that typically produces its OpenDRIVE maps: a Lanelet2 map and an OpenDRIVE map are loaded as two independent coordinate systems. Install the converter separately when you need to generate a map.

docs.title: For Developers (Editable Installation)
docs.text:
1. Clone the repository:

    git clone https://github.com/hakuturu583/autoware_carla_scenario.git
cd autoware_carla_scenario

  2. Sync dependencies from the lock file:

    uv sync

    The CARLA client arrives with its CPython package prebuilt; nothing more to build (see CARLA client).

Note

The Lanelet2 binding comes from simple-lanelet2 as a prebuilt wheel, so uv sync needs no apt packages and no C++ toolchain on any host, and the CARLA client's prebuilt CPython package means no cc either.

docs.title: Environment Configuration
docs.text:
Configure your environment by exporting the variables consumed by the package, or by loading a .env file (the package depends on python-dotenv). The most common variables:

Variable Required Description CARLA_EXECUTABLE optional Path to CarlaUnreal.sh, for a CARLA that scenario-setup did not install. Unset, the installed one is launched; pytest's CARLA tests skip when there is neither. AUTOWARE_CARLA_SCENARIO_HOME optional Moves ~/.autoware_carla_scenario, where scenario-setup installs CARLA (bin/carla). NISHISHINJUKU_MAP_PATH when overwriting the built-in .xodr Path inside the CARLA install where the original .xodr lives. NISHISHINJUKU_XODR_PATH optional Override the default OpenDRIVE file resolved in conf/map/nishishinjuku.yaml. NISHISHINJUKU_LANELET2_PATH optional Override the default Lanelet2 .osm path. VIEWER_BASE_PATH, VIEWER_HOST, VIEWER_PORT, VIEWER_CACHE_DIR, VIEWER_RERUN_WEB_VIEWER, VIEWER_RERUN_MAP_DIR optional viewer web-app overrides (viewer --help for the flags that win over them).

See the Usage Guide and Architecture for the full list.

docs.title: Verifying Installation
docs.text:
python -c "import autoware_carla_scenario; print('Installation successful!')"

This works without CARLA — running an actual scenario additionally requires a CARLA server: a live one, or one to launch (scenario-setup, or CARLA_EXECUTABLE).

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
The package's runtime dependencies (declared in pyproject.toml):

  • typesafe-carla>=0.8.1,<0.9 (Linux x86_64 and aarch64) — the CARLA client and its Codon library; pulls in typesafe-carla-toolchain
  • pyxodr>=0.1.0 — OpenDRIVE parser used by MapManager / to_opendrive
  • opencv-python-headless>=4.8 — frame processing for the camera recorder (headless: the package makes no GUI calls)
  • numpy>=1.21
  • pytest>=9.0.1
  • python-dotenv>=1.2.2
  • simple-lanelet2>=1.2.3 — the Lanelet2 binding, plus the Autoware regulatory-element extensions, as a single wheel
  • tqdm>=4.67.1
  • hydra-core>=1.3.2, omegaconf>=2.3.0
  • fastapi>=0.115.0, uvicorn[standard]>=0.34.0, jinja2>=3.1.0 — result viewer
  • pyyaml>=6.0, pydantic>=2.0.0

docs.title: Import Errors
docs.text:
Ensure that:

  1. You're using a supported Python (see Python Version).
  2. The package was installed in your active environment (uv sync from the repository root, or a fresh uv venv followed by uv sync).
  3. If you see ImportError: ... lanelet2 ..., a lanelet2 distribution from PyPI may be shadowing the one simple-lanelet2 provides. Reset the environment with rm -rf .venv && uv sync --dev.

docs.title: CARLA Connection Issues
docs.text:
If you cannot connect to the CARLA simulator:

  1. Ensure the CARLA server is running.
  2. Check that your overrides match: server.host, server.port, traffic_manager.port.
  3. Verify network connectivity to the CARLA server.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text: Once installed, see the Usage Guide to run scenarios.

docs.title: Logical Scenarios from Routes
docs.text:
A concrete scenario names lanelets: the ego spawns on lanelet 242, an NPC follows vertices in one map's coordinates. It runs on that map only.

A logical scenario describes the ego's drive as a route pattern -- "30 to 60 m of road with an oncoming lane, a signalised left turn with traffic coming from the opposite approach, then up to 40 m out of it" -- and places every other road user relative to that route. Any map with such a road can run it: the route search finds every matching route of the map, and each match is one concrete scenario.

This is the shape a recorded drive (a T4 scene) is transpiled into by scene_to_scenario_transpiler: the ego's drive becomes the route pattern, each NPC becomes a hidden entity that appears when the ego has progressed to the point it was first seen, and then drives in FOLLOW mode along waypoints that advance on the ego's progress.

flowchart LR
    doc["document.yaml<br/>route: segments..."] --> search["route search<br/>(on the run's map)"]
    search -->|match 0..N| exp["scenario-expand<br/>one case per match"]
    exp --> run["DeclarativeScenario<br/>ego on the match,<br/>route poses + route_progress"]

docs.title: The document
docs.text:
Everything is in the Scenario IR (ScenarioDocument). A full example, using every feature this page describes:

version: 1
id: logical_left_turn
title: Left turn with an oncoming car and a pedestrian
timeout_seconds: 60

# --- The ego's drive, as a pattern of road ------------------------------------
route:
  segments:                       # in driving order
    - kind: lane
      length: {min: 30, max: 60}  # m along the route; either bound optional
      lanes_left: {max: 0}        # same-direction lanes to the left (count range)
      lanes_right: {}             # {} = any
      opposite_lane: "yes"        # any | yes | no (bare YAML yes/no accepted)
      shape: straight             # any | straight | curved_left | curved_right
      stop_line: any              # at the segment's end (its last lanelet)
      traffic_light_stop_line: any
    - kind: junction
      turn: left                  # any | left | right | straight
      traffic_light: "yes"
      crossing_from_left: any
      crossing_from_right: any
      crossing_from_opposite: "yes"
      crosswalk_entry: any
      crosswalk_exit: "yes"
    - kind: lane
      length: {max: 40}
  ego_spawn_s: 5.0                # ego spawns 5 m along the route
  ego_goal: true                  # ego's goal = route end ...
  ego_goal_margin: 2.0            # ... less 2 m
  match_index: 0                  # which match an unexpanded run takes
  max_matches: 64                 # 1..1000
  seed: null                      # null: sorted order; int: shuffled with it

entities:
  - {id: ego, kind: ego, driven_by: autoware}   # no spawn/goal needed: the route gives them
  - id: oncoming
    kind: vehicle
    vehicle_type: vehicle.tesla.model3
    spawn: {hidden: true}         # parked out of the world; no lanelet needed
  - id: walker
    kind: pedestrian
    spawn: {hidden: true}

actions:
  # The oncoming car: brought in when the ego is 40 m short of the junction,
  # at 8 m/s (a Spawn card; with no place of its own it enters where it was
  # declared -- give lanelet_id/s for a place, shift_max to take a clear one
  # further on); then its Set Goal card, triggered on the Spawn card
  # completing, drives it FOLLOW mode from 30 m before the junction on the
  # opposite approach and waits at the junction entry until the ego is 5 m
  # from it.
  - id: oncoming_enters
    type: spawn
    actor: oncoming
    trigger:
      type: route_progress
      params: {value: -40.0, anchor: "junction:0:entry"}     # entity: ego (default)
    params:
      speed_ms: 8.0               # its speed as it enters
  - id: oncoming_drive
    type: routing
    actor: oncoming
    trigger:
      type: action_state
      params: {action: oncoming_enters, state: completeState}
    params:
      path_source: route
      mode: follow
      time_domain: none
      speed_ms: 8.0               # its pace
      route_vertices:
        - {kind: crossing, junction: 0, approach: opposite, turn: straight, distance: -30.0}
        - {kind: crossing, junction: 0, approach: opposite, turn: straight, distance: 0.0}
        - {kind: crossing, junction: 0, approach: opposite, turn: straight, distance: 25.0}
    advance_conditions:
      - vertex: 2                 # counted from 1
        condition:
          type: route_progress
          params: {value: -5.0, anchor: "junction:0:entry", rule: greater_than_or_equal}

  # A pedestrian: brought in when the ego enters the junction, and walks
  # across the exit crosswalk from its right end.
  - id: walker_enters
    type: spawn
    actor: walker
    trigger:
      type: route_progress
      params: {value: 0.0, anchor: "junction:0:entry"}
    params:
      speed_ms: 1.3
  - id: walker_cross
    type: routing
    actor: walker
    trigger:
      type: action_state
      params: {action: walker_enters, state: completeState}
    params:
      path_source: route
      mode: follow
      time_domain: none
      speed_ms: 1.3
      route_vertices: |          # the editor's text form is accepted too
        crosswalk junction=0 leg=exit side=right along=-1.5
        crosswalk junction=0 leg=exit side=right along=6

  # The other route vertex kinds, for reference (an entity "lead" not shown):
  #   - {kind: lane, ds: 15.0, d_lane: -1, offset: 0.0, yaw: null, anchor: null}
  #   - {kind: opposite, ds: 10.0, lane: 1, offset: 0.0, yaw: null, anchor: "segment:0:start"}
  #   - {kind: roadside, ds: 20.0, side: left, kerb_distance: 1.0, yaw: null, anchor: start}

assertions:
  pass:
    - type: route_progress
      params: {value: -2.0, anchor: end}
  fail:
    - type: timeout
      params: {timeout_seconds: 60}

docs.title: route -- the route search
docs.text:
Key Type Default Meaning segments list -- (required, >= 1) The pattern, in driving order. Each item is a lane or a junction segment, told apart by kind. ego_spawn_s float >= 0 0.0 The ego spawns this far along the route (route s). Must lie on the route. ego_goal bool true The ego's goal is the route's end (less ego_goal_margin). With true the ego must not name a goal of its own (validation error); set false to keep the ego's own goal. ego_goal_margin float >= 0 0.0 How far before the route's end the goal is. The goal must be ahead of the spawn. match_index int >= 0 0 Which match a run that was not expanded takes. Must be below max_matches (validation error). max_matches int 1..1000 64 How many matches the search returns at most. seed int or null null null keeps matches sorted (by lanelet ids, then start); an int shuffles the full list with random.Random(seed) before max_matches cuts it -- a deterministic sample spread over the map.

Lane segment (kind: lane) -- a stretch of road between junctions (no lanelet with a turn_direction tag):

Key Values Meaning length {min, max} metres Its length along the route. No max: grown to at most 300 m. lanes_left, lanes_right {min, max} counts How many same-direction lanes lie on that side (routing-graph neighbours, lane-changeable or not, counted outwards), on every lanelet of the segment. {min: 1} reads "at least one". opposite_lane any / yes / no Whether an opposite-direction lane runs beside the road, on every lanelet of the segment (yes) or on none (no). shape any / straight / curved_left / curved_right By the net heading change from the segment's start point to its end point: within +-15 deg is straight, above +15 deg (anticlockwise) curved_left, below -15 deg curved_right. An S-bend with no net change reads straight. stop_line any / yes / no Whether its last lanelet owns a stop line (any of the three patterns has_stop_line uses). traffic_light_stop_line any / yes / no Whether its last lanelet's stop line is a traffic light's.

Junction segment (kind: junction) -- the ego's way through a junction: one to four consecutive lanelets carrying turn_direction:

Key Values Meaning turn any / left / right / straight The lanelets' turn_direction: straight when all are straight, else the one non-straight tag (lanelets turning both ways match only any). traffic_light any / yes / no A traffic-light regulatory element on one of its lanelets or on the lanelet entering it. crossing_from_left / _right / _opposite any / yes / no Whether a lanelet of the same junction, entering it from that approach, conflicts with the ego's way (see Junctions below). crosswalk_entry / crosswalk_exit any / yes / no Whether a crosswalk crosses the ego's path on the way in / out (see Crosswalks below). length {min, max} (m) The length of the ego's way through the junction (its junction lanelets' centrelines); open by default. paths list of {approach, turn, before, after, path} (default none) Other paths through the junction it must have: a member entering from approach (same, left, right, opposite) whose path turns turn (left, right, straight). It need not conflict with the ego's way. before / after (ranges, m, open by default) bound the road the path runs on before the junction and after it (see Junctions below). What a crossing pose with that approach and turn needs. With path (from 1) the junction has at least that many such paths, and before / after bound the path-th from the left: what a crossing pose naming that path needs.

Unknown keys are refused (extra="forbid"), so a typo is an error, not a silently ignored constraint. A junction segment does not take lane keys and vice versa.

docs.title: Route vertices (path_source: route)
docs.text:
A Set Goal card with path_source: route lists its vertices in route_vertices: a list of mappings, each with a kind, or the editor's text form, one vertex per line, kind key=value ... (commas allowed between pairs; blank lines and # comments skipped and not counted). Unstated keys take their defaults. At least two vertices.

kind Keys (default) Python class lane ds (0), offset (0), d_lane (0), yaw (null), anchor (null) RouteLanePose opposite ds (0), lane (1), offset (0), yaw (null), anchor (null) RouteOppositePose crossing junction (0), approach (left), distance (0), turn (null), offset (0), yaw (null), d_lane (0), path (null) RouteCrossingPose crosswalk junction (0), leg (entry), side (right), along (0), yaw (null) RouteCrosswalkPose roadside ds (0), side (left), kerb_distance (0.5), yaw (null), anchor (null) RouteRoadsidePose

All are resolved when the action starts (and again at every new run of it), against the scenario's route match; an unanchored ds counts from the ego's position projected onto the route at that moment. yaw (radians, anticlockwise positive) is relative to the direction named in each row; null faces along the trajectory. junction counts the route's junction segments from 0.

  • lane -- route s base + ds, then d_lane same-direction lanes across (+1 left, -1 right, through routing-graph neighbours, lane-changeable or not; the lane change is made abreast, not at equal s), offset metres from that lane's centreline (positive left). Before the route's start or past its end the lane is followed on (the straightest predecessor / successor).
  • opposite -- the lane running the other way abreast of route s base + ds, on whichever side the opposite road is (left- and right-hand traffic alike); lane counts from the centre line outwards (1 = next to it). The pose is on that lane's lanelet abreast of the route point, at the point's projection onto it -- also where the two directions are split into lanelets at different places. Faces that lane's own direction.
  • crossing -- a lanelet of junction junction entering from approach (same, left, right or opposite, seen from the ego; same is the ego's own approach: its lane turning another way, or a lane beside it), whose path through the junction turns turn if given, d_lane lanes across from that path's own lane (positive to its left: another lane of the road it is on); of several, one whose path conflicts with the ego's way wins, then the lowest id -- or, given path (from 1), that one of them counted from the left as they enter the junction (by where their first junction lanelets start, across the way they come in): two lanes turning the same way, say. distance is metres along that path from where it enters the junction (its first junction lanelet's start): negative is back on its approach road (straightest predecessors), positive through the junction and beyond.
  • crosswalk -- the crosswalk across the leg (entry/exit) of junction junction (of several, the one nearest the junction). side picks its end on the ego's left or right; along is metres from that end towards the other (negative: behind the end, on the pavement). Faces across.
  • roadside -- abreast of route s base + ds, beyond the road's edge on side -- past every same-direction lane and, when the opposite road is on that side, past it too, taking each lane's lanelet abreast of the route point -- kerb_distance metres out (negative: onto the road). Faces along the route.

A pose the map cannot give -- no opposite lane there, no crosswalk on that leg, no lanelet from that approach, a ds running off the map -- raises when the action starts, naming the vertex and what is missing. The validator checks what it can without the map: the rows' shape, at least two vertices, and that every anchor and junction index exists in the pattern.

docs.title: Anchors
docs.text:
An anchor names a point of the route by its role, so a distance means the same thing on every map:

Anchor Route s start 0 end the route's length segment:K:start, segment:K:end where segment K (from 0, all segments) starts / ends junction:K:entry, junction:K:exit where junction segment K (from 0, junction segments only) starts / ends

docs.title: route_progress condition
docs.text:
type: route_progress
params:
  entity: null                 # null: the ego
  rule: greater_than_or_equal  # less_than | less_than_or_equal | greater_than | greater_than_or_equal | equal_to
  value: -15.0                 # metres past the anchor; negative is before it
  anchor: "junction:0:entry"   # default start

Holds when the entity's route s -- its position projected onto the route's reference line (the route lanelets' centrelines end to end) -- compares with anchor_s + value by rule. Projection makes it robust to lane changes onto parallel lanes: a vehicle on the lane beside the route is at the route s it is abreast of. Successive checks look within 40 m of the last answer, so a route that passes the same place twice is followed pass by pass; when the entity is more than 12 m from the route within that window (it was teleported -- an appearing entity --, or the condition was not checked for a while) the whole route is searched instead and the nearer answer kept. The result is clamped to [0, length]. An entity 50 m or more below the route where it projects (spawned hidden, parked under the map) or not in the world has no progress: the condition does not hold, and progress is None. Usable anywhere a condition is: a trigger, an assertion, inside all/any/not, and as a waypoint condition (advance_conditions) -- a vertex departs when the ego has progressed to the recorded point.

docs.title: Traffic lights: the traffic_signal card on a route junction
docs.text:
A Set Traffic Signal card with target: route sets the lights of a path through a junction of the route, not lights named by their Lanelet2 ids: the paths through junction route_junction (from 0) that enter it from route_approach (same -- the ego's own approach --, left, right, opposite) and turn route_turn (any, left, right, straight). Their lights are the traffic light regulatory elements on each such path's first junction lanelet and on the lanelet entering it (for same, on the ego's own way through the junction and the lanelet it enters on too, when it turns so), found on the map the run is on when the card fires. A junction the route search does not have is a validation error; a path with no light there is said and changes nothing. freeze (default on) keeps CARLA's own cycle off those lights.

- id: ego_light_red        # no trigger: on the first tick
  type: traffic_signal
  params: {state: Red, target: route, route_junction: 0, route_approach: same,
           route_turn: any, freeze: true}

docs.title: Bringing an entity in: the spawn card
docs.text: An entity spawned hidden is brought into the scene by a Spawn card (SpawnAction, the counterpart of despawn; appear_on_start until 1.0): set on its place (lanelet_id, s, t, heading; or route_pose, one route vertex as route_vertices takes them, placed on the scenario's route -- what keeps a logical scenario map-independent; none: where it was declared to spawn), physics on, facing its heading, moving at speed_ms. Its Set Goal card is triggered on the Spawn card completing (action_state completeState) and routes it from where it stands. To wait until its place is clear, put a place_clear condition on the same place (route_pose too) in the Spawn card's trigger -- with a give-up, e.g. all(<progress>, any(place_clear, persistent(sticky(<progress>), 20))); with shift_max it then takes the nearest clear place that far on along its lane if its own is still taken (a route pose shifts when it is on a lane -- lane, opposite, crossing -- and counted from an anchor). An entity a Spawn card brings in that is not spawned hidden draws a warning (it would stand at its spawn until then). To bring one in when the ego comes near its place, whatever its progress, trigger the Spawn card on a distance condition (Distance to a place) from the ego to the same route_pose, e.g. distance < 60; a despawn card on entity_distance from the ego takes it out again once the ego is far enough away.

docs.title: Entities in a logical scenario
docs.text:
• The ego needs no spawn lanelet and, with ego_goal: true, no goal: the route gives both. An Autoware ego is valid without its own goal then.
  • A hidden entity needs no spawn lanelet either: it is parked out of the world -- 500 m under the ego's spawn, 10 m apart -- until an action brings it in.
  • A visible entity on a fixed lanelet draws a warning: that lanelet exists on one map only.
  • A route search and a lanelet constraint search cannot both drive the expansion (validation error).
  • A vehicle other than the ego with vehicle_type: auto and a size ({length, width}, m -- a recorded box, say) is the vehicle of the running CARLA whose bounding box is nearest that size, chosen when it is spawned: each candidate (a car, van, truck or bus; no emergency vehicle) is spawned once out of sight to read its box, so the choice follows the server's version and assets rather than a table written for one (entity.fit). With none fitting, it is the kind's default. auto on a pedestrian, or without a size, is a validation error, and so is a size on an entity that names its blueprint: nothing would read it.

docs.title: Matching semantics
docs.text:
A match is a sequence of lanelets, each following the one before in the routing graph (vehicle participant, German traffic rules -- the same graph the constraint sweeper builds; no lane changes, no lanelet twice), cut into the pattern's segments in order:

  • lane segments cover non-junction lanelets, junction segments junction lanelets (turn_direction tagged), so a lane segment always ends where the next junction begins;
  • segments meet at lanelet boundaries, except that a first lane segment may start part-way into its first lanelet and a last lane segment may end part-way into its last -- which is how their length is kept within range.

The part of the road a match covers is fixed, so one road is found once:

  • a first lane segment is grown backwards from where it ends to its maximum length and cut there; if the road runs out first (a junction, or nothing precedes), it starts where the road does;
  • a last lane segment is grown forwards to its maximum, and ends earlier only at a junction or where the road ends;
  • a lone lane segment (the whole pattern) starts where its road starts;
  • every interior lane segment covers whole lanelets; its length is their sum and must lie in its range;
  • a first junction segment starts where the junction does (its first lanelet has no junction predecessor); a last one ends where it does.

At a fork every branch is tried, and where two adjacent lane segments may meet at more than one lanelet boundary, each split is its own match. Matches are deduplicated by (lanelet ids, start, end, lanelets per segment) and sorted by the same; RouteMatch.index is the position in the returned list.

Route s runs along the route lanelets' centrelines, 0 at the match's start (start_s metres into its first lanelet) to its length (end_s metres into its last).

docs.title: Junctions
docs.text:
The ego's entry heading is its way's heading where it enters (the start of its first junction lanelet). The junction's members are the junction lanelets reachable from the ego's through the routing graph's conflicting relation (transitively), starting within 60 m of the centroid of the ego's way. Each is walked back through junction predecessors (the straightest one, at most 4) to the first junction lanelet of its path: a member is that path, named by its first lanelet, with the path's turn (straight, or its one non-straight turn_direction); paths are deduplicated by (first lanelet, turn). A member's approach is the angle from the ego's entry heading to its first lanelet's heading where it enters:

Angle Approach within +-45 deg same: the ego's own (another way out of its lane, or another lane of its road) -45 to -135 deg (clockwise: it drives towards the ego's right) left +45 to +135 deg right beyond +-135 deg opposite

crossing_from_X: yes needs a member from approach X with a lanelet that directly conflicts with one of the ego's junction lanelets (X is never same). A paths entry {approach: A, turn: T} needs a member from approach A whose path turns T, conflicting or not; with path: K, at least K of them, and its before / after then bound the K-th from the left. Its before and after bound the reach of the one a crossing pose takes (conflicting first, then the lowest id): before is the road before its first junction lanelet, walked back through the straightest predecessor to the junction before it (or a dead end); after the road after its junction lanelets, walked on through the straightest successor to the next junction (or a dead end); each walked no further than 500 m. A crossing pose at distance -D (before the junction) or T + D (past its junction lanelets, T long) lies D m into that road. A crossing pose takes any member from that approach, of that turn if it names one (conflicting ones first, then the lowest id), or the path-th of them from the left; a match with fewer such members leaves a pose naming a later one unresolved.

docs.title: Crosswalks
docs.text: A crosswalk is a lanelet of subtype crosswalk. Along the ego's local path -- the last 10 m of the lanelet it enters on, its junction lanelets, the first 10 m of the lanelet it leaves on -- with u = 0 at the junction entry and J the length of its way through, a crosswalk whose centreline crosses the path at u is on the entry leg for -10 m <= u <= J/2 and on the exit leg for J/2 < u <= J + 10 m. For a junction at the end of the route, the lanelet it leaves on is the straightest successor (and for one at the start, the straightest predecessor is the one it enters on).

docs.title: Opposite lanes
docs.text: The opposite lane abreast of a point is a road lanelet whose heading differs by at least 150 deg, beside the outermost same-direction lane on either side there: one sharing that lane's outer bound, else one within 4 m beyond it (probed 1 m past the bound's nearest point). Both lanes are followed along (forwards and backwards through the routing graph, not across a junction) to the lanelet whose centreline is nearest the point, so it is the lanelet actually abreast. Both sides are looked at, so a left-hand-traffic map (opposite road on the right) answers the same way as a right-hand one. For the search's opposite_lane, a lanelet "has" an opposite lane when one is abreast of its middle.

docs.title: Caps and performance
docs.text:
Cap Value Lane segment without length.max grown to 300 m Lanelets per lane segment 50 Lanelets per junction segment 4 DFS steps per search 200 000 (then the matches found so far are returned and a warning is logged) max_matches default 64, at most 1000

The search is a depth-first walk from every lanelet that may start the first segment, in id order. Unshuffled (seed: null) it stops once it has max_matches matches, since later starting lanelets sort later. Measured on the nishishinjuku fixture map (884 road lanelets): a lane / junction / lane pattern with the default max_matches: 64 takes about 0.2 s; one that has to walk the whole map -- max_matches: 200, or a five-segment pattern with no match -- takes about 3.5-4 s. Properties are cached per lanelet.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
Expansion. scenario-expand (and the lanelet_constraint Hydra sweeper) read the document's sweep.route and emit, per match:

ego.spawn_lanelet_id=101 ego.spawn_s=45.0
ego.goal_lanelet_id=301 ego.goal_s=38.0                 # with ego_goal
scenario.route.index=0
scenario.route.lanelet_ids=[101,102,602,301]
scenario.route.start_s=40.0 scenario.route.end_s=40.0
scenario.route.segment_kinds=[lane,junction,lane]
scenario.route.segment_ends=[60.0,78.5,118.5]           # route s where each segment ends
scenario.route.segment_lanelet_counts=[2,1,1]
scenario.route.junction_turns=[left]

A match the ego cannot be placed on (spawn past the end, goal not ahead of the spawn) is skipped and logged. The exported Hydra config declares every scenario.route.* key, empty, so struct mode accepts them.

A run. DeclarativeScenario takes the match it was given; with none (an unexpanded run) it searches the loaded map and takes match_index, spawning the ego ego_spawn_s along it and sending it to the end. Either way the match becomes the scenario's route (autoware_carla_scenario.route.set_scenario_route), and the ego is sent along it:

  • the route's lanelets between the ego's spawn and goal lanelets become its waypoints (unless waypoints were configured), which the ego's RoutingAction hands it with the goal: an Autoware ego plans the matched route rather than the shortest one, and an ego the TrafficManager drives is handed the whole route as one path, a point every 5 m along the lanelets' centrelines (BackendDriven.route_to, which the TrafficManager follows through set_path), so it chooses no junction of its own;
  • with no goal (ego_goal: false) nothing is handed over, and an ego the TrafficManager drives gets a TurnAction per junction segment instead, in the junction's actual turn_direction, triggered when it is 100 m short of the junction (or past the previous one).

docs.title: Python API
docs.text:
from autoware_carla_scenario import (
    RouteLanePose, RouteOppositePose, RouteCrossingPose, RouteCrosswalkPose,
    RouteRoadsidePose, RouteProgressCondition, RoutingAction, RoutingMode,
)
from autoware_carla_scenario.route import (
    parse_route_search, RouteMatch, set_scenario_route, scenario_route,
)
from autoware_carla_scenario.route.search import find_route_matches
from autoware_carla_scenario.route.frame import RouteFrame, ego_placement
from autoware_carla_scenario.route.positions import resolve_route_pose

spec = parse_route_search({"segments": [...]})
matches = find_route_matches(spec, lanelet_map, routing_graph)
set_scenario_route(matches[0])          # laid on the loaded map when first used

Every name imported from the top-level package is mirrored in the Codon model, so a hand-written scenario using them passes the static check.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• One route per scenario, the ego's. Route poses are always measured on it. The route is process-wide; the runner clears it before every scenario's setup, and a scenario with a route search sets it there.
  • Lane properties hold on every lanelet of a segment; a road whose lane count changes mid-way needs two lane segments (whose boundary is then a lanelet boundary).
  • shape is the net heading change; it does not see an S-bend.
  • Junction membership relies on the map's lanelets overlapping (conflicting); a junction whose crossing lanelets never overlap the ego's has no members.
  • A crosswalk is recognised only as a lanelet of subtype crosswalk crossing the ego's local path.
  • Without a time reference a FOLLOW entity drives every segment at speed_ms; recorded speed changes between vertices are expressed by waypoint conditions only.
  • A Spawn card does not take the entity out again: a despawn card does (triggered on its Set Goal card completing, say).

docs.title: HD Maps from a Git Repository
docs.text:
An HD map is not a file that belongs next to a scenario. It is published, it is versioned, and several scenarios share it. So a scenario names its map with a source URI pointing at a git repository, and the framework fetches it, caches it, and reads it from there:

map:
  name: Town10HD_Opt
  source: git+https://huggingface.co/datasets/AutowareFoundation/carla-ue5-maps@dea2cfeab0e00238c3bdbefc48621cefb3dc04a2#autoware_maps/Town10HD_Opt

Everything below is available two ways, because a scenario is written two ways: in the Scenario Editor, and in the library that runs one.

docs.title: The URI
docs.text:
git+https://huggingface.co/datasets/OWNER/NAME@REF#PATH
\________________ repository ______________/ \_ref_/ \_path_/

Only the repository is required. @REF selects a branch, tag or commit and defaults to the repository's own default branch; #PATH selects the directory holding the map and defaults to the repository root.

How the string is split:

  1. A leading git+ is dropped.
  2. #PATH is everything after the first #.
  3. @REF is everything after the last @ of the repository path. The repository path starts after the host part — after scheme://host/ for a URL, after user@host: for an scp-like URL — so an @ in the host part is the user name, never a ref. A ref may therefore contain /:
URI Repository Ref Path git+https://github.com/o/r@feature/x#maps https://github.com/o/r feature/x maps https://user@example.com/o/r@v1 https://user@example.com/o/r v1 git@github.com:o/r.git@release/1.0#maps/T git@github.com:o/r.git release/1.0 maps/T git@example.com:maps.git@v1 git@example.com:maps.git v1 file:///srv/maps@main#T file:///srv/maps main T

Because the last @ decides, a ref may not contain an @, and neither may the path of a remote repository (write one as %40: https://example.com/o/a%40b@v1).

A local repository — a plain absolute path or a file:// URL — may have an @ in a directory name (a Nix store path, a user@domain home directory), so there the filesystem decides:

  1. a path that is an existing directory as a whole has no ref: /srv/maps@2/repo is the repository /srv/maps@2/repo;
  2. otherwise the ref follows the last @ whose left-hand side is an existing directory: /srv/maps@2/repo@feature/x is the repository /srv/maps@2/repo at feature/x;
  3. if no such @ exists on this machine, the last @ decides, as above.

To take the filesystem out of it, write the @ of a directory name as %40 in a file:// URL (file:///srv/maps%402/repo@main); git decodes it.

The URL you actually have is the one in your browser's address bar, and that is accepted as-is and normalised — GitHub's /tree/<ref>/<path> and HuggingFace's /tree/, /resolve/ and /raw/ forms all parse. Paste the page you are looking at.

Any git server works: HuggingFace, GitHub, GitLab, an internal host, a file:// path on a shared filesystem.

docs.title: What a map directory holds
docs.text:
A map is any directory containing a Lanelet2 .osm. This is the layout Autoware publishes, and the one the editor's Map library looks for:

autoware_maps/Town10HD_Opt
├── lanelet2_map.osm          # the map
├── map_projector_info.yaml   # the projection it is read with
└── pointcloud_map.pcd        # not read by this framework, and not downloaded

Only the files this framework reads are pulled out of git-lfs — the .osm, the .xodr if there is one, and the YAML beside them. The point cloud stays a pointer file of a few hundred bytes, which is what keeps fetching a 2 MB map from costing 22 MB.

A repository can carry symlinks, so each file is checked for where it really is. The .osm, the .xodr and map_projector_info.yaml are used only when they resolve to a regular file inside the map directory: a link within the directory is followed, but one that leads out of it, dangles, or names a directory is ignored, as if the file were absent. An OpenDRIVE read back from CARLA is held to the same rule inside its derived directory. A #path that is itself a link out of the checkout, or that contains .., is refused. Local directories (map.directory) go through the same file checks.

docs.title: How a map is read
docs.text:
map_projector_info.yaml names the projection the map's lat/lon is read with, and every loader in this framework -- the run's MapManager, the sweeper, the editor's preview, the ODD route check -- reads it the same way, and the way Autoware does:

projector_type Read with MGRS mgrs (MGRSProjector) LocalCartesianUTM utm (UtmProjector at map_origin) LocalCartesian local_cartesian (LocalCartesianProjector at map_origin) TransverseMercator transverse_mercator (TransverseMercatorProjector at map_origin) Local local_xy (each node's local tags; see below)

LocalCartesianUTM is read through UTM, not a local tangent plane, despite its name: the two place a city-sized map tens of metres apart.

The projector is anchored at the whole map_origin -- latitude, longitude and altitude -- as Autoware's get_lanelet2_projector() anchors it. Only LocalCartesian uses the altitude: it measures every z from it, so near an origin at 40 m a node's z, and the map-frame poses sent to Autoware, are its ele less 40 m. The other projections ignore it.

A projector_type: Local map stores its map frame in each node's local_x and local_y tags (and local_z, when it has one), which is what Autoware's own loader reads. So does this framework: such a map is read with the local_xy projection, which takes each node from its local tags and falls back to its lat/lon (through UTM at the map origin) for a node without them. Set map.projector_type: utm to read every node from its lat/lon instead.

The two agree only where the lat/lon were themselves derived from the local tags with UTM, as on the official CARLA towns. A map converted by another tool can differ by about 0.1 % -- 9 cm over 89 m, growing with distance from the origin -- so the log says which reading was used, and a disagreement beyond 1 cm is logged as a warning.

docs.title: Where maps are cached
docs.text:
~/autoware_data/maps, overridable with AUTOWARE_DATA_DIR (whose maps subdirectory is used) or AUTOWARE_CARLA_SCENARIO_MAP_CACHE (used as-is).

That default is the same directory Autoware's own demo_artifacts ansible role downloads map datasets into, unpacked at their repository-relative paths. So on a machine that has run the Autoware setup, the map is already there:

~/autoware_data/maps/autoware_maps/Town10HD_Opt/lanelet2_map.osm

and a source naming that path resolves to it in about a millisecond, cloning nothing. A map this framework did fetch itself lands under .repos/ in the same root, so the two never collide and the copy Autoware provisioned always wins.

Nothing re-reads a map's contents over the network once it is cached; refresh is the only way to make it fetch again.

One entry under .repos/ holds one repository at one commit, and every map in that repository shares it. Its sparse checkout only grows: resolving #autoware_maps/TownB after #autoware_maps/TownA adds TownB beside TownA rather than replacing it, so a map resolved earlier -- held by the editor, a running case or a sweep over both -- keeps its files. The repository root (a source with no #path) checks the whole tree out. The entry's meta.json lists every directory checked out in it under materialised.

One question is asked, though, and it is asked before anything is fetched: when the ref is a branch, a single git ls-remote resolves it to the commit it points at right now, and everything after that runs as if the source had been pinned to that commit. So a branch tracks, which is what it reads like -- and, just as importantly, the cache entry is named after a commit, so a map that moves lands at a new path rather than replacing the bytes under an old one. Anything holding a parsed map keyed on its path therefore notices.

A machine that cannot reach the remote falls back to the commit that ref last resolved to, so an offline run still works exactly as it did before.

docs.title: Pinning, and why it matters
docs.text:
A source naming a branch means "whatever is on that branch today" -- and, since the branch is re-resolved on every fetch, it means it literally. Two runs of the same scenario a month apart are then two runs against two different maps, and the result of one says nothing about the other.

A source naming a full commit hash is pinned: the same URI names the same bytes forever.

from autoware_carla_scenario.maps import pin_source

pin_source("https://huggingface.co/datasets/OWNER/NAME/tree/main/maps/T")
# 'git+https://huggingface.co/datasets/OWNER/NAME@<40-hex commit>#maps/T'

In the editor this is the Pin to commit button in the Scenario inspector, which also tells you when a source is still unpinned.

One consequence is worth stating plainly: an already-unpacked map directory records no revision, so a pinned source never uses one. It always resolves through git, where the commit is checked rather than assumed. Pinning would be worthless otherwise.

docs.title: OpenDRIVE comes from CARLA
docs.text:
An Autoware map published for a CARLA town ships no .xodr, and should not: the roads belong to the CARLA asset. So the OpenDRIVE is read back out of CARLA, in the order that costs least:

  1. one the repository ships, or one already cached;
  2. the asset inside a local CARLA installation, named by the same <MAP_NAME>_PATH environment variable the rest of the framework uses (TOWN10_HD_OPT_PATH, and see .env.example);
  3. a running server, over the CARLA Python API.

Whatever it comes from is cached under .derived/ beside the map, so it is fetched once.

You do not need it to write a scenario. A scenario is written against Lanelet2 — a spawn, a goal and a constraint search all name lanelets — so the editor's preview and a constraint sweep work with no OpenDRIVE and no CARLA anywhere. A run needs it, and a run has CARLA: ScenarioQueue writes the loaded world's OpenDRIVE into the cache the first time a scenario runs on it.

To fetch it ahead of time, use Fetch OpenDRIVE in the Scenario inspector, or:

from autoware_carla_scenario.maps import ensure_xodr, resolve_map

ensure_xodr(resolve_map(uri), host="localhost", port=2000)

docs.title: Selecting a published map
docs.text:
uv run scenario scenario=cut_in/default map=town10hd_opt

conf/map/town10hd_opt.yaml is a normal map group whose map.source names the published map at a pinned commit. Override it like any other key:

uv run scenario map=town10hd_opt \
  map.source='git+https://huggingface.co/datasets/OWNER/NAME@REF#maps/T'

map.xodr_path and map.lanelet2_path still win where they are set, so a single file can be overridden without abandoning the source.

docs.title: From Python
docs.text:
from autoware_carla_scenario.maps import list_maps, resolve_map

for entry in list_maps("https://huggingface.co/datasets/AutowareFoundation/carla-ue5-maps@main"):
    print(entry.name, entry.uri)

hd_map = resolve_map(
    "git+https://huggingface.co/datasets/AutowareFoundation/carla-ue5-maps"
    "@main#autoware_maps/Town10HD_Opt"
)
hd_map.lanelet2_path   # -> Path to the .osm, downloaded if it was not there
hd_map.commit          # -> the revision it is at

autoware_carla_scenario.maps imports neither CARLA nor Lanelet2, so it is safe to use from any process.

docs.title: From a local directory
docs.text:
A map that is on this machine but in no repository -- a copy handed over on a USB stick, a map still being edited -- is named by its directory:

uv run scenario map=town10hd_opt map.directory=/path/to/autoware_maps/Town10HD_Opt

The directory is read exactly as a map directory in a repository is: its .osm (lanelet2_map.osm when there are several), map_projector_info.yaml, and any .xodr it ships. It may name the .osm itself to pick one out of several. Nothing is cloned and no revision is recorded, so such a map cannot be pinned.

map.directory wins over map.source, which is what lets a run be pointed at a local copy without first clearing the source its map group selects. map.xodr_path and map.lanelet2_path still win over both.

An OpenDRIVE taken from CARLA for it is cached under .derived/local/<name>-<hash> in the map root rather than written into the directory, which may well be read-only.

from autoware_carla_scenario.maps import resolve_directory

hd_map = resolve_directory("~/maps/Town10HD_Opt")
hd_map.lanelet2_path   # -> ~/maps/Town10HD_Opt/lanelet2_map.osm
hd_map.local           # -> True

docs.title: In the editor
docs.text:
Map library in the header browses a repository and lists every map in it. Each one either starts a new scenario or, when you arrived from a draft, becomes that scenario's map.

The Scenario inspector carries the same thing per scenario: the source, whether it is downloaded and whether it is pinned, and buttons to download, refresh, pin and fetch OpenDRIVE.

Its Map directory field is map.directory. Setting one clears the Lanelet2 and OpenDRIVE file fields unless they were edited in the same change, and takes the CARLA map name from the directory. The editor only serves a map from inside SCENARIO_EDITOR_MAP_ROOTS (the working directory unless set), so a directory elsewhere has to be added there to be previewed.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause git is not installed The cache clones with git; install it. A map resolves but the .osm is a few hundred bytes git-lfs did not pull it. Install git-lfs, then Refresh. does not name a directory in the repository The #path is wrong for that ref. Browse the repository in the Map library. names a directory outside the repository / names a link to a directory outside the repository The #path contains .., or is a symlink leading out of the checkout. Point it at the real directory. A map's .xodr or map_projector_info.yaml is ignored It is a symlink to a file outside the map directory, a dangling link, or a link to a directory. A pinned source re-clones on a machine that has the map Expected: a pinned source never trusts an unpacked directory, because it records no revision.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
A run reads two kinds of quantity off the world while it drives, under keys the framework fixes:

Reads Example An ODD maps onto it Watched by Measure (Scenario measures) A condition the ego drives in: what the scenario sets up vehicle_ahead_gap_m Yes (measure: in a binding file) Coverage; a sweep draws a scenario's parameters from it Metric (this page) How the ego drives: an outcome collision_at_fault No MetricCondition

An ODD describes the conditions a system is built to operate in, whatever it then does there. A metric reads what it did, so it has no place in one: were an ODD to map onto offroad, the ego's own driving would decide whether a run is inside the domain it is tested in, and an ODD excluding offroad would report a run that left the road as outside the ODD rather than as failed. scenario_measure("offroad"), measure: offroad in a binding file and register_measure("offroad", ...) are all refused.

docs.title: The built-in metrics
docs.text:
They are the per-timestep driving-quality metrics of NVIDIA's AlpaSim (src/eval/src/eval/scorers), under AlpaSim's own names so results read the same in both, computed from CARLA's actors and map (autoware_carla_scenario.metrics, BUILT_IN_METRICS). An event reads 1 while it holds and 0 while it does not; every metric reads nothing without an ego, and those of the road nothing without a map. A metric reads one frame; AlpaSim folds a run's frames into one value with the aggregation in the last column (Metric.aggregation).

Key Unit Reads AlpaSim folds with collision_any The ego's bounding box overlaps another vehicle's or a pedestrian's max collision_front ... and the other overlaps the ego's front edge max collision_rear ... its rear edge, and not its front max collision_lateral ... neither edge: a side swipe max collision_at_fault A front or a lateral collision max offroad A corner of the ego's box is on no driving lane max offroad_or_collision Off the road, or any collision max offroad_or_collision_at_fault Off the road, or a collision at fault max wrong_lane The ego heads more than 120 degrees away from the driving lane under its centre; nothing off the road max min_distance_to_obstacle_m m Box to box, to the nearest other vehicle or pedestrian; 0 touching, nothing when the ego is alone min min_distance_to_lane_boundary_m m From the ego's box to the edge of the driving lanes around it (lanes beside its own count while their near edge is within 6 m of its centre); 0 off the road min importance_sampling_weight ratio Not AlpaSim's: the run's importance-sampling weight so far, the product of NADE's p/q and (1-p)/(1-q) (AdversarialTrafficAction); 1 without NADE. Weight a batch of runs by its last value to estimate the naturalistic rate of what they count last lateral_reversals count Not AlpaSim's: how many times so far the ego's drift across its lane turned back by more than 0.1 m (Weaving) last lateral_wobble_m m Not AlpaSim's: how far the ego strayed across its lane about its course over the last 4 s, RMS (Weaving) max steering_reversals count Not AlpaSim's: how many times so far the steering applied to the ego turned back by more than 0.05 of full lock (Weaving) last turn_indicator_changes count Not AlpaSim's: how many times so far the ego's turn indicators changed, between off, left, right and hazard (Weaving) last

Where AlpaSim's geometry is not CARLA's, the reading follows CARLA: AlpaSim asks whether the union of the lane polygons around the ego covers its box, CARLA whether a point is on a driving lane, so offroad asks it of the box's corners; the lane boundary takes the lanes beside the ego's as parallel strips as wide as CARLA says they are there, an approximation through a junction. Boxes are those of vehicles (vehicle.*) and pedestrians (walker.*); props are not road users. collision_* reads the boxes, not CARLA's collision sensor (CollisionCondition): it sees a collision as AlpaSim does, and tells the front from the rear.

docs.title: Weaving
docs.text:
Three metrics read how the ego weaves from side to side, and a fourth how often its turn indicators changed. Unlike the others they read the run so far, not one frame: the runner hands the ego's motion to autoware_carla_scenario.metrics every tick (track_ego_motion), and they read what it has gathered.

The ego's drift is how far it has moved across its lanes since the run began: its velocity across the lane under its centre, summed over time. The lane's heading is taken anew every frame, so following a bend is not a drift, and moving to the next lane is a drift of a lane's width with no jump at the lane line. Off the driving lanes the drift holds until the ego is back on one.

  • lateral_reversals counts the times the drift turned back by more than 0.1 m: it went right, then came back left by 0.1 m or more. This is the reversal count of driver-workload studies (Markkula and Engström, 2006). A lane change is one drift, however long, and adds nothing; a weave adds two a cycle. Under 0.1 m it is the noise of holding a lane.
  • lateral_wobble_m is how far the drift strayed about its course over the last 4 s: the RMS about the straight line that fits it best there. A weave of 0.25 Hz or faster turns back within the window and reads nearly in full (about 92% at 0.5 Hz); a lane change, slower, is mostly the course, and adds about a tenth of the lane's width while it lasts. It reads nothing before the third frame.
  • In a junction, whose lanes overlap, the drift holds, as it does off the driving lanes; a lane the other way is crossed the ego's way.
  • steering_reversals counts the times the steering applied to the ego (get_control().steer, 1 the vehicle's full lock) turned back by more than 0.05, about 3.5 degrees at the wheels of a car that locks at 70. It sees the controller's weaving before the vehicle shows it. Closed loop, a driver policy's controller moves its steer by a few hundredths while it holds a lane or a bend, which the gap leaves out; sawing through a turn is a tenth or more.

turn_indicator_changes counts the changes of the indicators the ego shows (its CARLA light state: off, left, right, hazard), from the first frame on: a turn signalled and cancelled is two. It is counted apart from the steering, so an indicator that flickers through a turn and a steering that saws there each read on their own count. A vehicle's light state holds while an indicator is commanded, so its blinking is not a change.

The counts are of the run so far, so a longer run reads more: compare runs of one scenario, or fail on a count, not on a rate:

self.register_fail_condition(
    MetricCondition(LATERAL_REVERSALS, ComparisonRule.GREATER_THAN, 6, label="weaving")
)
self.register_fail_condition(
    MetricCondition(LATERAL_WOBBLE_M, ComparisonRule.GREATER_THAN, 0.5, label="weaving")
)

AlpaSim's other metrics need more than the world, and are not metrics here:

AlpaSim metric Needs progress, progress_rel, dist_to_gt_trajectory, dist_to_gt_location, gt_dist_traveled_m The logged ground-truth trajectory of the ego min_ade@*, plan_deviation, open_loop_collision The driver's planned trajectories safety_monitor_triggered The driver's safety monitor img_is_black A camera image dist_traveled_m, duration_frac_20s, avg_dist_between_incidents The run, not a frame

docs.title: Watching a metric
docs.text:
MetricCondition(metric, rule, value, tolerance, *, label) holds while the metric satisfies the comparison. The rule defaults to GREATER_THAN_OR_EQUAL and the value to 1, so an event metric on its own reads "it happens". A frame the metric reads nothing in does not satisfy it. It is usually a fail condition:

from autoware_carla_scenario import ComparisonRule, MetricCondition
from autoware_carla_scenario.metrics import (
    COLLISION_AT_FAULT,
    MIN_DISTANCE_TO_OBSTACLE_M,
    OFFROAD,
)


class MyScenario(BaseScenario):
    def setup(self) -> None:
        ...
        self.register_fail_condition(
            MetricCondition(COLLISION_AT_FAULT, label="collision at fault")
        )
        self.register_fail_condition(MetricCondition(OFFROAD, label="off the road"))
        self.register_fail_condition(
            MetricCondition(
                MIN_DISTANCE_TO_OBSTACLE_M,
                ComparisonRule.LESS_THAN,
                0.5,
                label="closer than half a metre",
            )
        )

It composes like any other condition: PersistentCondition to require a metric to hold for a while (off the road for more than a second), NotCondition to pass only while it does not. In the Scenario Editor it is the Metric card, under World.

A run a metric condition fails is a failure of what the metric reads (Why a run failed): a collision metric collision, offroad and min_distance_to_lane_boundary_m lane_keeping, wrong_lane traffic_rule, min_distance_to_obstacle_m safety_margin, and the weaving metrics and turn_indicator_changes stability. offroad_or_collision and its at-fault twin read two things and say neither, nor does the importance-sampling weight: register a condition on them with its category.

To read a metric yourself -- in a probe, a test, a recorder -- read_metric(key, world) returns its value in the frame, or None.

docs.title: Off the road as a fail condition
docs.text:
offroad is a measurement, and a strict one: it reads 1 as soon as any one corner of the ego's box is on no driving lane. A corner over a gap between lanes at a junction entry, or a small offset between the OpenDRIVE lanes and where the vehicle drives, counts though the vehicle is in its lane, so MetricCondition(OFFROAD, ...) fails such runs. To judge a run by how much of the box is off instead, use OffRoadFractionCondition(fraction, entity_name, *, label), a condition rather than a metric:

from autoware_carla_scenario import OffRoadFractionCondition

self.register_fail_condition(OffRoadFractionCondition(0.3, label="offroad"))

Every tick it samples a 5 x 3 grid of points over the entity's bounding box (the ego's unless entity_name names another): 5 evenly spaced along its length and 3 across its width, the box's edges and corners included. A point is off when get_waypoint(point, project_to_road=False, lane_type=carla.LaneType.Driving) finds no lane there, asked at the height of the entity, so that where roads cross at different heights the lane is the one it is on. It fails once at least fraction (in (0, 1]) of the 15 points are off. The fraction is of points, not of area: one corner off is 1/15, the front edge 3/15, one long side 5/15. fraction=1/15 fails on any one point, the way the metric does on a corner; 0.3 fails at 5 points, so it tolerates a corner or the front edge over a lane gap and fails once a whole long side of the box is off. In the Scenario Editor it is the Off the road card, under Entity.

A scenario or a Python ODD may import any name of autoware_carla_scenario.metrics -- the keys, Metric, BUILT_IN_METRICS, is_metric() and read_metric() -- and is checked against them like any other (Static Check). A Metric is frozen: assigning to one of its fields fails the check, as it fails the run. A scenario may build its own (Metric("my_metric", read)); the check calls its read with a world and refuses one that returns anything but a float or an Optional[float].

docs.title: The viewer and the editor bind 127.0.0.1 by default
docs.text:
viewer and scenario-editor now take command-line options (--help, --host, --port, and the directories they serve; see usage and the editor's configuration). They used to ignore every argument and bind 0.0.0.0; both now bind 127.0.0.1, because neither has authentication and the viewer's API starts scenario runs and SLURM submissions.

To serve other machines as before, say so: uv run viewer --host 0.0.0.0, or VIEWER_HOST=0.0.0.0 / SCENARIO_EDITOR_HOST=0.0.0.0 in the environment, which still works (a flag wins over it). Either prints a warning on stderr.

docs.title: To 15.0.0: no video, the trajectory log instead
docs.text: 15.0.0 removes the video a run used to render ({Scenario}.mp4). After each run, the runner replayed the CARLA recording on the same server with an RGB camera and encoded the frames with ffmpeg. That took about as long as the run, and the next case waited for it. It also needed ffmpeg on every machine that ran scenarios. A run is now seen through its trajectory log, which every run already writes, from a Rerun recording made out of it.

docs.title: What is gone
docs.text:
Removed Instead {Scenario}.mp4 after each run {Scenario}.rrd, a Rerun recording of {Scenario}.trajectory.jsonl made as the run ends (rerun.enabled=true, the rerun extra), opened in the Rerun viewer (Seeing a run) video.width, video.height (and video.enabled, which never shipped in a release) Nothing to set. A run that sets one warns that it is ignored CameraRecorder, autoware_carla_scenario.camera_recorder, check_video_size, DEFAULT_IMAGE_WIDTH/HEIGHT — ScenarioRunner(video_width=, video_height=), ScenarioQueue(video_width=, video_height=), run_scenario_with_queue(video_size=) Drop the arguments ScenarioRunner._render_video_from_recording, DebugMarkerLog, DrivenPathDrawer, draw_debug_markers The trajectory log's markers records (the ego's plan) and its ticks (the path it drove) SpectatorCameraConfig, BaseScenario._spectator_camera_config (where the video's camera went) — : BaseScenario.follow_with_spectator() still moves CARLA's spectator, and takes the same arguments The viewer's video player and its /video/... route The scenario page shows the run in an embedded Rerun web viewer (/recording/...rrd): the recording rerun.enabled=true made as the run ended, else one the viewer makes on demand The ffmpeg-python dependency, and ffmpeg itself — with-ffmpeg of the pack-scenario-image action —

The CARLA recording ({Scenario}.log) is still written: CARLA's replayer (client.replay_file()) plays it back on a server running the same map. The ego's debug markers are still collected (EgoVehicle.debug_markers()), and are written into the trajectory log.

docs.title: What to change
docs.text:
• Command lines and configs that set video.*: drop it. It is accepted, so an old script still runs, and warned about.
  • Code that passes video_width/video_height/video_size, or imports CameraRecorder or the drawing helpers: remove that. These are gone, and passing them is a TypeError or an ImportError.
  • Seeing runs: install the converter and the viewer (pip install 'autoware-carla-scenario[rerun,viewer]') and run with rerun.enabled=true: each run's log is converted into X.rrd beside it as the run ends, the result (rerun_recording) names it, and the viewer's scenario page shows it. Open it with rerun X.rrd. Runs made without it convert afterwards with python -m autoware_carla_scenario.rerun outputs/... (a session, a sweep, or one X.trajectory.jsonl). The log carries the map it was recorded on (paths and SHA-256 of the Lanelet2 and OpenDRIVE files), the warm-up, the ego's plan, every condition's state and the verdict (Trajectory Log).
  • Container images built with with-ffmpeg: true: drop the input.

docs.title: ODD
docs.text:
An Operational Design Domain (ODD) states the conditions a system is built to drive in: urban roads, up to 60 km/h, no heavy rain, and so on. Every run is measured against one. The runner samples the ODD's attributes on every tick. Their buckets are the run's ODD coverage: which conditions it reached (see Coverage). The ODD's modules say which ticks were outside the ODD.

An ODD is written in one of two ways. Both build the same objects, so they are measured, judged and reported the same way:

  • Python: openodd's model (Writing an ODD in Python), with this framework's probes. It is checked with Codon before it is used, like a scenario (Static Check).
  • ASAM OpenODD 1.0 YAML (the standard's chapter 10). It is read into the same objects. A binding file next to it names the probes that measure its concepts.
 OpenODD YAML + binding file ──(load_odd_binding)──┐
                                                    ├──▶ OddDefinition ──▶ coverage + inside/outside per tick
 Python (checked by Codon) ─────────────────────────┘

OpenODD also maps its model to OpenSCENARIO DSL (chapter 9, model to DSL only) and to tables (chapter 8). Neither is read here.

The reading, judging, versioning, sampling and coverage are openodd (openodd-py, a Rust core with a Python API), which knows nothing of CARLA. This framework is its backend: autoware_carla_scenario.odd.backend.CarlaBackend, a subclass of openodd.Backend, gives the built-in probes a binding file names, measure: keys read from the running scenario, the knobs that set the weather and the sun, and where the ego is (for coverage). Importing autoware_carla_scenario.odd makes it openodd's default backend, so openodd.load_odd_binding() and autoware_carla_scenario.odd.load_odd_binding() read the same.

docs.title: Versions of an ODD
docs.text:
OpenODD 1.0 defines no version of an ODD; openodd builds one on what it does define (its versioning profile):

  • the revision is the SHA-256 of the files the ODD was read from -- the binding file, the OpenODD files it names and every file they IMPORT -- by name and content. The same files are the same revision on any machine and from any repository or commit; any change to any of them is a new one;
  • the version is what the root modules (those under ODD:) declare in their METADATA (version: 2.1.0);
  • the structure is the digest of the ODD as built (modules, buckets, the buckets outside it), for an ODD written in Python, which has no files.

All three are written to every coverage file (the ODD's revision, version, structure), so coverage can be told apart by the ODD it was measured against. OddDefinition.archive() packs the files into a deterministic .tar.gz that openodd.load_odd_archive() reads back exactly; a run writes it beside its coverage file ({ScenarioName}_odd.tar.gz).

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
The model and its semantics follow OpenODD 1.0 (chapters 6 and 7).

Concept What it is Attribute A taxonomy concept, measured on every tick: a probe reads it from the world, and its buckets make it a cover item. Condition A test on one attribute (speed_limit.between(0, 60)), a group of conditions (all_of, any_of), another module's verdict (module_holds), or a missing value (is_unknown).
