The walker is told to walk only the way it faces, at the motion's speed that way: CARLA turns a walker towards where it is told to go, and a motion's root drifts and steps aside. A step sideways or back therefore reads as standing in the walker's velocity, though the walker goes where the motion takes it (#957).
  4. Each time the motion it holds is about to run out, it asks for more, generated from the motion shown so far.

CARLA runs synchronously, so the simulation waits for each answer, and the same seed replays the same motion.

The action takes the pedestrian's movement and animation control domains for as long as it moves the walker. It runs for duration_s. Without that, it runs until its last waypoint's time, and without waypoints, until the scenario ends.

The generator and the action talk over proto/pedestrian_motion/v0/pedestrian_motion.proto, which uses a right-handed, z-up frame (CARLA's world with y negated). The generator receives joint positions, and the action turns them into bone directions (pedestrian.skeleton.directions_from_joints).

docs.title: Keyframes
docs.text:
A keyframes file lists full-body poses:

{
  "keyframes": [
    {
      "time_s": 3.0,
      "x": 104.0, "y": -12.5, "yaw_deg": 90.0,
      "joints": {"Hips": [0.0, 0.0, 0.95], "Head": [0.05, 0.0, 1.62], "...": [0, 0, 0]}
    }
  ]
}
  • time_s is the time into the motion.
  • x, y and yaw_deg place the pose in CARLA's world. Without them, the pose is placed where the motion began and faces the way it did then.
  • joints gives each joint the generator places (the joint_names it answers with; ARDY's SOMA model has 30) in metres. The axes are forward, left and up from the root's ground point, as the body faces.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Meaning entity_name The pedestrian prompt "" What it does, in words, from the start prompts () TimedPrompt(time_s, text): texts that take over later waypoints () WalkWaypoint(x, y): CARLA world points it passes speed_ms 1.3 Walking speed along the waypoints, m/s keyframes None A keyframes file (relative paths are taken from the working directory) duration_s None Stop after this long seed 0 The generator's draws overrides False Take over a domain another action holds, stopping it

The backend's own settings, including its image, GPU memory and Hugging Face cache, are backends.ardy of the config (Backends a Run Starts).

docs.title: Quick start: test a driving policy
docs.text:
From an empty directory to a scenario result, with no ROS 2 and no Autoware. The framework downloads CARLA, launches it, serves the driving policy in its own process and runs the scenario: after the setup it is one command.

You need Linux x86_64, uv, git, an NVIDIA GPU that runs CARLA UE5, and about 30 GB of free disk for the simulator. (The framework also runs on Linux aarch64, but CARLA's server does not: there, run CARLA on an x86_64 host and add server.host=<address> to the commands below; see installation.)

docs.title: 1. Add the framework to your project
docs.text:
The framework is a Python library on PyPI. Depend on it from your project's pyproject.toml:

[project]
name = "my-policy-tests"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.10,<3.15"
dependencies = ["autoware-carla-scenario>=5"]

uv sync

This also installs carla-driver-interface 1.x, the policy side of the gRPC contract (versioned on its own; a policy depending on any 1.x shares the environment), and the CARLA client, typesafe_carla. Its wheel carries a prebuilt CPython package. Where that package does not match the installed toolchain, the first run that imports the client builds it once instead (15-50 min, ~14 GB of memory, needs cc) into ~/.cache/typesafe_carla. uv run typesafe-codon pycarla does that ahead of time, and says "nothing to build" when the prebuilt package applies.

docs.title: 2. Download CARLA
docs.text:
uv run scenario-setup

This downloads CARLA's nightly Linux build (about 16 GB, with a progress bar) and unpacks it, while it downloads, into ~/.autoware_carla_scenario/bin/carla. That is where the scenario runner looks for CARLA when CARLA_EXECUTABLE is not set. Run it again at any time: an install that is still the current nightly is kept, a newer one replaces it. If the connection drops partway, the download picks up where it stopped (with an HTTP range request) instead of starting over; it gives up after several reconnections in a row that deliver nothing, and stops (the next run fetches it whole) if the nightly was replaced in the meantime.

Option Meaning --force Download again even if the install is current --url URL Install another CARLA Linux package (.tar.gz), e.g. a release: a URL, or a local path (~/Downloads/CARLA.tar.gz, ./CARLA.tar.gz) to install an archive already downloaded --dir DIR Unpack into DIR (new or empty) instead; then point CARLA_EXECUTABLE at the launcher it prints

AUTOWARE_CARLA_SCENARIO_HOME moves ~/.autoware_carla_scenario as a whole.

docs.title: 3. Run a scenario against a policy
docs.text:
uv run scenario scenario=cut_in/left map=town10hd_opt \
  ego.spawn_lanelet_id=324 scenario.npc_lanelet_id=446 \
  ego.entity=carla_driver driver.policy=route_follower

The single command does everything:

  1. It launches CARLA (CarlaUnreal.sh, on server.port). The first boot takes a minute or two. A CARLA already listening on that port is used instead.
  2. It fetches the Town10HD_Opt Lanelet2 map into ~/autoware_data/maps, the first time only.
  3. It serves route_follower, a reference policy, inside the scenario's own process.
  4. It runs the scenario, prints the pass/fail result, writes it under outputs/, and stops CARLA again. It does so even when the run is stopped with SIGTERM (it then exits 143) or killed: a CARLA the run launched does not outlive it. A CARLA that was already running is left running.

ego.entity=carla_driver hands the ego to a policy over alpasim's egodriver.EgodriverService contract. driver.policy names the policy the scenario serves itself.

The example scenarios name lanelets of the NishishinjukuMap by default, so on Town10HD_Opt a run gives its own. The two above are one of the cases the scenario's sweep matches. scenario-expand lists every case, each as the overrides to add to the command above, without running anything:

uv run scenario-expand scenario=cut_in/left map=town10hd_opt

docs.title: 4. Test your own policy
docs.text:
A policy implements BaseDriver.drive(). It gets the session's observations and returns a trajectory in the rig frame (x forward, y left):

# src/my_policy_tests/__init__.py
from carla_driver_interface.driver import BaseDriver, DriveContext, DriveResult
from carla_driver_interface.geometry import Pose, Trajectory


class MyPolicy(BaseDriver):
    name = "my_policy"

    def drive(self, ctx: DriveContext) -> DriveResult:
        plan = Trajectory.empty()
        for i in range(1, 41):  # 4 s ahead at 5 m/s
            plan.append(ctx.time_now_us + i * 100_000, Pose.from_xyz_yaw(0.5 * i, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0))
        return DriveResult(trajectory_in_rig=plan)

So that uv sync installs the module, give the project a build backend:

[build-system]
requires = ["uv_build>=0.9.7,<0.10.0"]
build-backend = "uv_build"

Then name the policy by its import path:

uv run scenario scenario=cut_in/left map=town10hd_opt \
  ego.spawn_lanelet_id=324 scenario.npc_lanelet_id=446 \
  ego.entity=carla_driver driver.policy=my_policy_tests:MyPolicy

See External Driver Interface for what a policy receives (cameras, LiDAR, the map, traffic lights). Other scenarios are listed in Example Scenarios.

docs.title: Running the policy as a separate process
docs.text:
A policy can also live in a process of its own, for example an alpasim driver or a model in another environment. Leave driver.policy unset and point driver.address at it:

# Terminal 1 -- the policy
uv run carla-driver-interface serve --policy my_policy_tests:MyPolicy --port 50051

# Terminal 2 -- the scenario
uv run scenario scenario=cut_in/left map=town10hd_opt \
  ego.spawn_lanelet_id=324 scenario.npc_lanelet_id=446 \
  ego.entity=carla_driver driver.address=localhost:50051

Both modes use the same gRPC contract and the same policy class. The only difference is which process serves the policy.

docs.title: ROS 2 over DDS
docs.text:
ego.entity=ros2 hands the ego to ROS 2 nodes directly over DDS. The framework joins the DDS domain itself, through Cyclone DDS's Python binding: no rclpy, no ROS 2 installation, no bridge node and no gRPC. It publishes the ego's state on ROS 2 topics, takes commands from them, and applies the one that drives.

It takes the place of the CARLA-to-ROS 2 bridge nodes a ROS 2 stack would otherwise run beside CARLA: the ego-state and speed publishers, and the arbiter that chooses between command sources.

flowchart LR
    subgraph scenario["Scenario process"]
        SR["ScenarioRunner<br/>ticks the world"]
        E["Ros2EgoEntity<br/>arbiter + controller"]
        SR -->|on_tick| E
        E -->|"VehicleControl /<br/>VehicleAckermannControl"| SR
    end
    subgraph ros["ROS 2 nodes (rmw_cyclonedds_cpp)"]
        P["planner / VisionPilot /<br/>safety island ..."]
    end
    CARLA["CARLA server<br/>(native ROS 2)"]
    E -->|"/localization/kinematic_state<br/>/vehicle/status/steering_status<br/>/vehicle/speed"| P
    P -->|"trajectory / control /<br/>steering + acceleration"| E
    CARLA -->|"camera, /clock<br/>(or the entity, for a server<br/>built without ROS 2)"| P

docs.title: Installing
docs.text:
The DDS binding is the ros2 extra:

pip install 'autoware-carla-scenario[ros2]'

In this repository the dev group installs it too (uv sync --dev).

cyclonedds ships wheels for Linux x86_64 on CPython 3.10-3.13 only, and the extra installs nothing elsewhere; ego.entity=ros2 then fails at scenario start, saying so.

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
uv run scenario ego.entity=ros2 server.max_tick_rate_hz=20

The ROS 2 nodes run with RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_cyclonedds_cpp on the same ros2.domain_id. Cyclone reads CYCLONEDDS_URI in the scenario process exactly as it does in a node, so the same configuration file (interfaces, peers, fragment size) applies to both.

docs.title: Timing
docs.text:
Nothing waits for a command. Every tick the entity publishes the ego's state, takes the commands that arrived since the previous tick, and applies the one that drives; the simulation goes at the pace server.max_tick_rate_hz sets, and a source that falls silent goes stale. Set server.max_tick_rate_hz=20 -- real time at the 0.05 s step -- when the nodes measure wall-clock deadlines: a lockstep that stopped the simulation to wait for them would starve exactly the timeouts they are there to check. This is how a ROS 2 bridge that relays to CARLA behaves (VisionPilot's runs the world in synchronous mode, paced to wall-clock 10 Hz, without waiting for a command).

ego.entity=ros2 without server.max_tick_rate_hz logs a warning: unpaced, the simulation outruns the nodes and their sources look stale.

Published stamps and the freshness of commands are both in simulation time, the time CARLA's /clock carries, which is what nodes with use_sim_time read.

docs.title: What the ego publishes
docs.text:
Setting Type Contents kinematic_state_topic (/localization/kinematic_state) nav_msgs/Odometry pose in frame_id, twist in child_frame_id steering_status_topic (/vehicle/status/steering_status) autoware_vehicle_msgs/SteeringReport front tyre angle, positive to the left speed_topic (/vehicle/speed) std_msgs/Float64 ground speed, m/s clock_topic (off) rosgraph_msgs/Clock for a CARLA server built without ROS 2 turn_indicators_report_topic (/vehicle/status/turn_indicators_status) autoware_vehicle_msgs/TurnIndicatorsReport the indicators the ego shows (hazard, both lit, reports as off, as the report has no hazard)

null leaves a topic unpublished. The pose is in the right-handed local frame -- CARLA's world with y flipped, as CARLA's own ROS 2 interface publishes it -- with its origin on the rear axle, Autoware's base_link (rear_axle_offset_m, derived from the wheel physics when null). The run's trajectory log (its rear_axle record) and T4 dataset put the ego's base_link there too.

Cameras and /clock are CARLA's to publish when the server is built with ROS 2. For a server built without it, the entity publishes them as well:

Setting Type Contents clock_topic rosgraph_msgs/Clock the simulation time, every tick cameras[].topic sensor_msgs/Image each frame of a camera on the ego, bgra8, stamped with the simulation time it was rendered at

A camera in cameras takes the rendering and mount fields of a driver camera (image_width, image_height, fov, fps, position_x/y/z, roll, pitch, yaw, in CARLA's convention), plus its topic and frame_id. Its frames go out from the sensor's own thread as they are rendered, the way CARLA's own interface publishes them, and under the names a node already subscribes to:

ros2:
  clock_topic: /clock
  cameras:
    - logical_id: main_cam
      topic: /carla/hero/main_cam/image
      frame_id: main_cam
      image_width: 1280
      image_height: 720
      fov: 60.0
      fps: 10.0
      position_x: 1.25
      position_z: 1.58

docs.title: Where commands come from
docs.text:
ros2.sources lists the publishers the ego takes commands from:

kind Topics Applied by trajectory topic: autoware_planning_msgs/Trajectory the framework's trajectory follower (pure pursuit + Autoware's PID longitudinal controller on the trajectory's own speeds, through the powertrain model), as for an external driver policy control topic: autoware_control_msgs/Control CARLA's Ackermann controller; Autoware's steering (positive left) is negated into CARLA's (positive right) steer_accel steering_topic, acceleration_topic: std_msgs/Float64 CARLA's Ackermann controller, as VisionPilot's carla_control_publisher hands it: target speed speed + acceleration * speed_horizon_s

The turn indicators are not a source: whichever source drives, the newest autoware_vehicle_msgs/TurnIndicatorsCommand on turn_indicators_command_topic (/control/command/turn_indicators_cmd; null turns it off) lights the ego's indicators, leaving its other lights as they are, until another changes them. NO_COMMAND changes nothing.

A steer_accel command pairs the steering and the acceleration of one publisher cycle, and each value is used once, so a node that publishes one of each per cycle drives once per cycle. The halves are matched by the DDS source timestamp of each sample (when the publisher wrote it), not by when a tick happens to read it, so a tick that reads two cycles at once, or one half of a cycle before the tick and the other after it, still pairs every cycle with itself.

Two halves pair only if they were written at most a window apart. By default the window is half the publisher's cycle, measured from the timestamps themselves (the median of the last few write intervals), so no rate or timing is assumed: any publisher that writes a cycle's two halves closer to each other than to the next cycle's pairs every cycle, whether it writes them back to back (VisionPilot does) or from two timers 40 ms apart at 10 Hz. A half with no partner in the window is dropped, never paired with another cycle's: a lost steering or acceleration message costs that one cycle instead of shifting every later command by a cycle. An unmatched half is held only until the next sample of either topic shows it has no partner (a newer half of its own topic, or a half of the other topic written further than the window away).

Dropped halves are logged as a warning (at most every 10 s, with the count and the window). An occasional drop is a lost message; a steady stream of them means the window does not fit the publisher. Set pair_window_s on the source to fix the window, in seconds: larger than the gap between a cycle's two halves, and smaller than the cycle minus that gap. The timestamps are the writers' clocks, so the two topics are expected to come from one host (or hosts whose clocks agree well within the window).

    - name: visionpilot
      kind: steer_accel
      steering_topic: /vehicle/steering_cmd
      acceleration_topic: /vehicle/throttle_cmd
      pair_window_s: 0.03   # optional; null (the default) measures it

A trajectory's points are timed by header.stamp + time_from_start; one whose time_from_start does not increase (many planners leave it zero) is timed from its speeds instead.

docs.title: Arbitration
docs.text:
Every tick, of the sources whose last command arrived at most stale_s ago, the one with the highest priority drives; between equal priorities, the most recent command. Once every source is stale, on_stale decides: hold keeps applying the last command (what a relay node does when its upstream stops), brake brakes to a stop. Before any command has arrived, the ego is held on its brakes.

A command that is not all finite (a NaN or an infinity in a steering angle, a speed, an acceleration, a jerk, or a trajectory's poses, speeds or accelerations) is refused, with a warning: the active source's last good command of that kind drives on, and with none, the ego is held on its brakes.

ros2:
  domain_id: 0
  on_stale: hold
  sources:
    - name: planner
      kind: trajectory
      topic: /planning/scenario_planning/trajectory
      priority: 0
      stale_s: 0.3
  control: {}     # trajectory-follower gains, as driver.control

docs.title: The Open AD Kit safety-island demo
docs.text:
ros2=visionpilot_safety_island is the bench side of the Open AD Kit CES 2027 demo (openadkit#157): VisionPilot steers and accelerates, and a fresh command from the safety island (the CR52, restamped onto domain 1) overrides it.

uv run scenario ros2=visionpilot_safety_island
Source Kind Topics Priority visionpilot steer_accel /vehicle/steering_cmd, /vehicle/throttle_cmd 0 safety_island control /control/trajectory_follower/control_cmd 10

It selects ego.entity: ros2 on VisionPilot's vehicle (a Lincoln MKZ), DDS domain 1, and server.max_tick_rate_hz: 20.

docs.title: From Python
docs.text:
from autoware_carla_scenario.entity.ros2_entity import Ros2EgoEntity
from autoware_carla_scenario.ros2 import CommandSourceConfig, Ros2EgoConfig

scenario.ego_entity = Ros2EgoEntity(
    Ros2EgoConfig(
        domain_id=1,
        sources=(
            CommandSourceConfig(name="planner", kind="trajectory",
                                topic="/planning/scenario_planning/trajectory"),
        ),
    )
)

To test without DDS, pass transport=FakeRos2Transport(config) and queue commands with its deliver().

docs.title: How it speaks ROS 2
docs.text: A node on rmw_cyclonedds_cpp publishes a message as a DDS sample of a type named <package>::msg::dds_::<Message>_ on the topic rt/<name>. autoware_carla_scenario.ros2.messages declares the same structs, field for field from the .msg definitions, so the samples are wire compatible with no ROS 2 type support installed. They are written in XCDR1, the representation rmw_cyclonedds_cpp writes.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Only rmw_cyclonedds_cpp has been tried. Other RMWs speak the same RTPS, but matching them is not tested.
  • The ego's role name is Ego, where VisionPilot subscribes its camera under /carla/hero/...; whether CARLA's own ROS 2 topics follow the role name has not been checked against a server yet. A camera in cameras is published under the topic it names, whatever the role name.
  • A camera in cameras publishes no sensor_msgs/CameraInfo.
  • Commands are read in the local frame frame_id names; nothing transforms a plan published in another frame (a Lanelet2 map, say).
  • control and steer_accel hand the acceleration to CARLA's Ackermann controller as given, as VisionPilot's relay does; the controller's own settings (AckermannControllerSettings) are CARLA's defaults.

docs.title: Scenario Editor
docs.text:
The Scenario Editor is a web UI for authoring scenarios declaratively and exporting them as self-contained wheelhouses. It runs as its own application:

uv run scenario-editor          # http://localhost:9100
uv run scenario-editor --help   # its options (Configuration below)

It is deliberately separate from the Scenario Result Viewer (uv run viewer). Neither mounts the other, and running one does not start the other; integrating the two is a later phase.

docs.title: What it edits
docs.text:
The editor never edits Python. Its canonical representation is the Scenario IR -- a ScenarioDocument stored as YAML -- which the framework compiles into the existing runtime primitives:

ScenarioDocument -> ScenarioCompiler -> BaseAction / BaseCondition -> BaseScenario

There is no editor-only runtime. Every action a document names is built by autoware_carla_scenario.actions, every condition by autoware_carla_scenario.conditions, and every spawn constraint is evaluated by the same sweeper.constraints engine a --multirun sweep uses.

docs.title: Which map: the Map library
docs.text:
A scenario's map is named by a source URI pointing at a git repository, and the editor fetches and caches it. Map library in the header browses a repository -- HuggingFace, GitHub, your own -- and lists every map in it; the Scenario inspector shows, per scenario, whether the map is downloaded and whether its revision is pinned.

See HD Maps from a Git Repository. Two things are worth knowing here: a map Autoware's own setup already downloaded is used as it sits, and OpenDRIVE is not needed to author a scenario -- lanelets are.

docs.title: Where it happens: the places panel
docs.text:
One map carries every lanelet the scenario names -- each entity's spawn, the ego's goal, and the lanelet every condition watches. The canvas says what happens and in what order; it has no way to say where, and until this panel existed the answer was a scatter of ids across lane heads and condition cards that only meant something with the map open in another window.

It sits at the top of the right-hand rail, over the inspector:

+------------------------------------------+---------------------------+
| Arrangement (the timeline, full width)    | Places      < 1/133 >     |
| ACTOR | Init | 1  | 2  | 3  | 4  | 5      |   (o) NPC1 spawn BOUND    |
| Ego   |      | [] |    |    |    |        |   (o) Ego goal            |
| NPC1  |      | [] | [] |    |    |        |   (o) Ego spawn           |
| Env   |      |    | [] |    |    |        | [Ego spawn][Ego goal][..] |
| PASS  | ...                               +---------------------------+
| FAIL  | ...                               | Inspector                 |
+------------------------------------------+---------------------------+

Three things had to be true at once -- the map, the timeline and the inspector all on screen without scrolling -- and this is the arrangement that gets there without taking width from the thing that needs it. The timeline's axis is width: a card further right is later in the story, so narrowing it costs steps you can see. The map is roughly square and the inspector is a column, so both fit the rail; and "where" then sits directly over "what", which is what makes clicking a place and reading its object one movement of the eye.

The whole editor is one CSS grid (.ed-stage) for that reason. #editor-body stays the single htmx swap target and simply does not draw a box -- display: contents lifts the timeline and the inspector into that grid -- so the map can sit beside either of them while every edit still re-renders one element. Moving the panel is a change to one block of editor.css, not to a template.

Which glyph a place gets is the field's own declaration, not a guess from whatever holds it: FieldSpec.place is spawn, goal or watched, so the Set Goal action's lanelet draws as a destination exactly as the ego's own goal does. A primitive that registers a new lanelet field is drawn without the map learning anything about it.

Each place is a pin in its actor's track colour -- the same hue that actor's lane head and every condition naming it already wear -- with a glyph for what the place is: a target for a spawn, a flag for a goal, an eye for a lanelet something watches. The viewer has one highlight channel, so the outline says "this scenario touches here" and the pins say which of them is which.

Under the map the same places are chips, in document order. Clicking one opens the object that named it in the inspector and points the map at it; clicking a place on the map does the same, because the overview draws places the document already names and the only thing a click there can mean is "show me what named this". Nothing is edited here -- a lanelet is still set where it is written, in the picker its own field opens.

A label reads away from its dot, except on the right half of the map, where it reads back towards the middle: that edge is also where the viewer keeps its own zoom buttons, and a label running under them is a label nobody can read.

docs.title: An abstract scenario draws one bound pattern
docs.text:
A scenario whose lanelet is a constraint search does not name a place: it names a set, and the sweeper runs it once per member. Outlining all 133 matches draws the search, and none of those 133 runs looks like that picture. So one match is bound -- through the same swept_slot the exported config sweeps and the same constraint engine the sweep evaluates -- and the panel says which of how many is on screen. The arrows step through the runs a --multirun sweep would perform, one concrete scenario at a time.

Everything else keeps the id stored beside it, because that is exactly what a run that does not sweep uses: the sweeper enumerates a single target key, so at most one lanelet in a document is ever bound.

Binding means parsing the map on the server, which is measured in seconds, so it is a button (Bind a pattern) rather than something every page load pays for. Once the map is cached every later render binds without being asked, including the panel's own refresh after an edit.

docs.title: Where a pin goes
docs.text:
The labels are the server's -- rendered with the panel, beside the list that repeats them -- and only the coordinates are the viewer's. editor.js asks it through its public API: focusOn(id) centres the view on a primitive, so focusing one and reading getView() back reports that lanelet's centre in the map's own coordinates, and the view is then put back where it was. The alternative was projecting the .osm a second time in JavaScript, which is a second answer to "where is this" that can disagree with the drawing it is laid over. Each lanelet is measured once and kept on the frame, which is the frame reuseMap() parks across a re-render, so an edit re-places the pins without asking the map anything.

The panel frames itself on the places rather than on the whole city when the map loads, and a pan or zoom after that is the person's: a re-render carries it across, exactly as the picker's does. Tilted into the viewer's 3D view the pins hide themselves, because getView() then reports drawing coordinates and a point on a hill and the ground behind it are drawn in the same place.

This is a second parse of the same .osm while a picker is open, which is the cost the inspector's own map was removed to avoid. It is a different drawing rather than the same one twice: the picker answers "which lanelet is this field", and the overview answers "where is this scenario" -- a question nothing else on the page answers at all.

docs.title: The canvas
docs.text:
The main view is a swimlane DAG drawn as a DAW arrangement: one track per actor, with the horizontal axis reading as scenario progression, not time. Under the actors sits the Environment track, for actions no vehicle performs.

STEP >      | 1          | 2                 | 3
------------+------------+-------------------+------------------
Ego         | Drive      |                   |
------------+------------+-------------------+------------------
NPC1        | Follow     |                   | # Lane Change Left
            |            |                   |         ^
            |            |                   |   +-----+-----+
            |            |                   |   |    ALL    |
            |            |                   |  NPC1->Ego  NPC1->Ego
            |            |                   |  Distance   TTC
            |            |                   |  < 20 m     < 4 s
------------+------------+-------------------+------------------
Environment |            | Set Traffic Signal|
------------+------------+-------------------+------------------
PASS        | NPC1 enters the ego lane
FAIL        | Collision  | Timeout 30 s

docs.title: Which track an action belongs to
docs.text:
The action type decides, never the author. ActionSpec.scope is either actor or environment, and an environment action -- setting traffic lights, for instance -- is drawn in the Environment track whatever its actor field says. Nothing reads that field when such an action is built, so honouring it put the card in some vehicle's lane and claimed a relationship the run does not have. The editor no longer offers the field for one, refuses it on the way in, and drops a stale value on the next save; each track's + action menu offers only the actions that belong in it.

The Environment track is drawn even when it is empty, because it is where you go to add the first one. An action that merely has no actor yet is drawn there too: it is invalid, and a card nothing draws cannot be corrected.

The sequencer furniture is what makes the direction readable: track headers down the left, a numbered ruler across the top, a bar line before every slot and every other slot shaded. The ruler counts steps and not seconds, which is the whole reason it is a step ruler -- see the first rule below.

docs.title: What a step is
docs.text:
Nothing in Python has a "step". The runtime arms every action from the first tick and ticks them all every frame:

for action in scenario._pre_tick_actions:
    action.tick(world, elapsed)

An action fires when its own trigger says so, not when its column comes up, and an action with no trigger gets AlwaysTrueCondition -- so it fires on tick 1 however far right it is drawn. column_hint is read by nothing outside this editor: compiler.py, declarative.py and the exporters contain no reference to ui at all.

So a step is not a point in time. It is a set of actions nothing orders, and the canvas draws it that way:

  • Several actions can share one step, stacked in the same column. That is the honest picture of two actions that are both armed and neither waiting on the other -- spreading them across two columns would draw a sequence the runtime does not have.
  • An action may not share a step with anything its trigger waits on. Within a step nothing is ordered, so a dependency has to be visibly earlier. Adding an action_state trigger pushes the dependent right on the spot, moving a dependency right carries its dependents with it, and a move that would break the rule is repaired rather than refused -- the card lands as close to where it was aimed as its dependencies allow. validator.py reports a hand-edited ui block that says otherwise.

That makes the step axis mean exactly one thing: left of is "already finished, and something here is waiting on it". It still says nothing about how much earlier.

A step number means the same column on every lane, so there is no leading column an actor track has and the Environment or verdict lanes do not. A spawn is not a step -- it is the state a track starts in -- so it is stated in the lane head rather than given a slot on the ruler.

An action with no trigger fires on the first tick, wherever it is drawn. BaseAction defaults to AlwaysTrueCondition, so a card in step 5 with an empty trigger runs immediately and its position is simply wrong about it. The canvas writes "fires immediately" under the card, and the validator warns -- never errors, because a position is presentation.

Three rules make it readable:

  • The distance between cards means nothing. Column position is ui.column_hint, which is presentation only and never reaches the runtime. A clip in step 3 may only start after one in step 2 if something says so; how much later is not on screen because the document does not know.
  • There is no separate event lane. A condition is a trigger, drawn under the action it fires and joined to it by a solid line, so cause and effect are next to each other instead of being correlated across the screen. A Set Goal card can also hold conditions on its waypoints -- waypoint conditions, edited in its inspector with the same condition controls.
  • Two cards may not steer one entity at once. A card that commands an entity's speed, steering or lights takes that control domain while it runs, and a second card firing on the same domain ends the run in error. Tick Override a running action in the second card's inspector to have it stop the first instead (the canvas marks it overrides; overrides: true in the document). Cards that command no entity do not offer it.
  • A card fires once unless told otherwise. Untick Fire only once to have it fire again each time its trigger holds (once: false in the document). Cards whose action cannot fire again (Stalled Object, Construction Zone, Urban Construction Zone, Adversarial Traffic (NADE)) do not offer it, and the validator refuses once: false on them.
  • One actor reacting to another is a reference, not a coincidence. "Swerve once NPC1 has cut in" is a Lane Change clip on the ego track whose trigger is an Action state condition naming NPC1's cut-in and the state completeState. That reference lives in the document (params: {action: a_..., state: completeState}), so it is a fact the scenario contains rather than something the canvas infers.

The canvas draws that reference as a dashed line in the causing actor's track colour, running from the action to the condition waiting on it. The cut-in example reads as one chain across two tracks:

NPC1   ... [Cut in] ......
                     :         <- dashed: Cut in -> the condition waiting on it
Ego    ..............:...  [Evade right]
                          ^ Cut in · NPC1 | Action | completeState
                            solid: fires this action

Both line types are named in the legend above the canvas, because a dash pattern is not self-explanatory. Crucially the dashed line is drawn only from data-caused-by, the document's own reference -- never from where two cards happen to sit. Moving a clip can therefore neither invent a causal link nor erase one, and a condition that names no action (a distance check, say) is never drawn as caused by anything.

docs.title: Action states
docs.text:
The states are ASAM OpenSCENARIO 1.2's StoryboardElementState, applied to a single action:

State Meaning standbyState Instantiated, waiting for its start trigger startTransition The trigger fired and execute() ran -- held for one tick runningState The work is under way endTransition The completion criteria were met -- held for one tick completeState Finished (a repeating action returns to standbyState)

completeState is the one that makes "after the cut-in" verifiable. A forced lane change stays in runningState until the vehicle has actually settled onto the next lane -- a different lane id, within LANE_CHANGE_CENTER_TOLERANCE_M of its centre and LANE_CHANGE_HEADING_TOLERANCE_DEG of its heading. A lane id change alone is not enough: a car whose centre has just crossed the boundary is still diagonal, and a reaction triggered on that would fire mid-manoeuvre.

There is deliberately no failure state and no action-level timeout, because OpenSCENARIO has neither. A manoeuvre that never happens stays in runningState forever, so completeState cannot be reached by a lane change that did not occur; ending such a run is the scenario timeout's job, which is already a FAIL condition. The two transition states are each held for exactly one tick, so a condition watching startTransition sees it.

Which is also why a card can be moved into an empty step rather than only swapped with its neighbour: a reaction has to be placeable to the right of the cause on another track, and its own track is usually empty in between.

Every condition reads as subject -> target | metric | rule value, e.g. NPC1 -> Ego | Distance | < 20 m or Ego -> Lanelet 183 | Position | inside.

A target that is not an actor is named for the coordinate system it is in. This framework speaks both Lanelet2 and OpenDRIVE and their ids are written the same way, so Ego -> 183 would say nothing about which 183 is meant.

docs.title: Position: pick a frame, not a mixture
docs.text:
There are two position conditions, one per coordinate system, because the two need different fields:

Address Reads as Position (Lanelet2) a lanelet NPC1 -> Lanelet 183 \| Position \| inside Position (OpenDRIVE) a road, optionally a lane NPC1 -> Road 80 \| Position \| lane 2 \| inside

Either can be narrowed to a stretch of that lane with s from / s to and t from / t to. The runtime has always accepted these comparisons; the editor used to discard them. They are the abstract way to say "in the last 20 m before the junction": unlike an absolute region, s and t are measured along and across the lane, so the condition keeps its meaning wherever a constraint sweep puts the entity.

A lanelet already names one lane, so the Lanelet2 condition resolves it to an OpenDRIVE road and lane and there is nothing further to pin. An OpenDRIVE road does not: a road carries several lanes, so road and lane together are what address a place uniquely, and a road left without a lane says so on the card (any lane) rather than looking like a precise address.

docs.title: Lanelet2 ids are picked, never typed
docs.text:
Every field naming a Lanelet2 lanelet is edited only on the map. The number beside it is a readout, not an input: nobody knows lanelet ids by heart, so typing one is guesswork the map answers exactly, and making the map the single editor leaves one path a value can arrive by instead of two to keep in step. Edit opens the viewer over the whole window -- the inspector column is 384px wide, and a city map that size cannot be picked from -- and clicking a lanelet fills the field and closes it. This comes from the field's declared kind (lanelet), so any field naming a lanelet gets the picker without touching a template.

There is no "type it instead" fallback for a viewer that will not load, for the same reason the SVG map fallback was removed: the page fetches htmx from a CDN too, so an editor that cannot reach the network has no working controls at all.

Three fields still take typed ids, each because their value is not only a lanelet id, and a test in test_authoring_registry.py fails if a new one appears without being listed there with its reason:

Field Why it is not picked equals.value (spawn constraint) any matches every lanelet -- a sentinel the sweeper parses, not an id in_set.values (spawn constraint) accepts ${map.no_3d_model_lanelet_ids}, a reference resolved at sweep time traffic_signal regulatory element ids the viewer's regulatory layer reports the id of the linestring that draws a sign, not of the regulatory element -- a picker there would save a confidently wrong number

Two implementation notes, both of which cost an afternoon to find:

  • The picker is moved to <body> before it is shown. The inspector sits inside a position: sticky wrapper, and sticky creates a stacking context whatever its own z-index is -- so a z-index left in place ranks only against its siblings, and the canvas lanes (z-index: 2) paint straight over a modal asking for 80.
  • A set of lanelets works the same way, toggling on each click, and saves when the picker is closed -- sending the form on every toggle would re-render the inspector and tear the map down mid-selection.
  • Which viewer layers a click may land on is part of the field's declaration (FieldSpec.picks). The layers overlap: a click on a road usually lands on the direction arrow, and a hair to the side lands on a bound, which reports the id of a linestring, not of either lanelet it separates. Only the layers whose id is the lanelet's own are accepted.
  • /static is served with Cache-Control: no-cache. StaticFiles sends an ETag but no Cache-Control, which lets a browser invent a freshness lifetime and keep running an old editor.js without asking -- an editor visibly missing a feature the server is already serving. The ETag still makes the check a 304.

They are separate conditions rather than one with a coordinate-system switch because offering a lanelet and a lane on the same condition is what let the two contradict each other: on the nishishinjuku map lanelets 183 and 184 are lanes 2 and 1 of road 80, so pinning lanelet 183 and lane 1 asked for a place that does not exist. Compose them with ALL, ANY, NOT, Sticky and Persistent, which map onto AndCondition, OrCondition, NotCondition, StickyCondition and PersistentCondition.

docs.title: Fixed or searched: every lanelet, one question
docs.text:
Edit on any lanelet field opens the map, and the panel beside it asks the same thing wherever you opened it from — Fixed or Constraint search:

Where a lanelet is named Slot Hydra key a sweep writes An entity's spawn ego.spawn, npc1.spawn ego.spawn_lanelet_id, scenario.spawn_overrides.npc1.lanelet_id The ego's goal ego.goal ego.goal_lanelet_id A lanelet parameter of an action or a condition <node id>.<field> scenario.param_overrides.<node id>.<field>

A constraint is a statement about the map, so it is written with the map it searches in view, and the matches are outlined on that same map as they are counted. That is why the choice is in the picker and not in the 384px inspector column, which only states which mode is in force and offers Edit.

A set of lanelets — stop_lanelets, the map's exclusion list — is picked by hand and gets no such panel: a search names one lanelet per run, because that is what the sweeper enumerates, so offering the choice there would promise that a search fills the whole set.

Fixed pins the lanelet the field shows. For a spawn that is a lanelet and an offset:

Field Value Where Lanelet ID 183 the picker, by clicking the map Offset 12.5 m the picker, under the same heading

Constraint search hands the choice to the existing lanelet-constraint sweeper. The tree is edited in the picker, each node with its own parameters — the inspector column is behind the map while it is open — with the match count beside it outlining what it found on that same map, and is serialised straight into sweep.constraints under whichever key addresses the slot:

sweep:
  constraints:
    ego.spawn_lanelet_id:
      - type: and
        constraints:
          - type: has_adjacent
            value: left
          - type: lanelet_length
            rule: greater_than_or_equal
            value: 10.0
          - type: not
            constraint: {type: is_junction}
          - type: not
            constraint:
              type: in_set
              values: ${map.no_3d_model_lanelet_ids}

The id the field shows stays in the document under a search: it is the default a run that does not sweep falls back to, and the value the exported config declares so that Hydra's struct mode accepts the override at all.

One search per run. The sweeper enumerates a single target key, so a document may search for one lanelet; a second search is a validation warning rather than an error — the scenario still runs, with everything else pinned to its default — and names which slot is being driven.

Preview matches evaluates that tree against the real Lanelet2 map and reports, for example, 133 matched of 979 lanelets. It is counted when the picker is opened, not on every render: each lanelet field on the inspector has a picker in the page at once, and counting means parsing a city. Loading a map is opt-in and cached; if the map files are missing the count is unavailable but the constraint editor keeps working.

docs.title: The map
docs.text:
The drawing comes from simple_lanelet2's wasm map viewer — the same project that provides the lanelet2 Python API this framework runs on. The editor serves the scenario's .osm at /draft/<id>/map.osm, the viewer parses and renders it in the browser, and the editor drives it through two calls: setHighlight() with the matched IDs, and a select listener that turns clicking a lanelet into setting whichever lanelet field the picker was opened from.

Constraint evaluation stays on the server, in the framework's own sweeper — the viewer only draws. That split is deliberate: a second constraint engine in JavaScript could disagree with the sweep the scenario will actually run.

The module is loaded from the project's GitHub Pages build, because the wasm is built rather than committed. Point SCENARIO_EDITOR_MAP_VIEWER at the output of simple_lanelet2's tools/build_web.sh to serve it yourself. When it cannot be fetched the panel says so; the match count and the matched-ID list come from the server and are unaffected.

docs.title: The map is parsed once
docs.text:
htmx replaces the whole inspector on every edit, so the server sends a brand-new, empty map frame each time. Mounting that frame refetched the .osm and parsed it again in wasm — one fetch per edit, for a map that had not changed.

The frame that already holds the parsed scene carries a data-viewer-key, and reuseMap() in editor.js swaps it back in over the fresh one, copying across only what actually differs: which lanelets are outlined. The whole frame moves rather than the canvas inside it — the viewer keeps a reference to the element it was constructed with and observes it for resizes, so lifting the canvas out would leave it measuring a node that is no longer on the page. Panning and zooming survive an edit as a consequence, which re-mounting had been silently throwing away.

That is what makes the picker editable. An edit in its side panel — the fixed or searched choice, the constraints, a spawn's offset along the lanelet — posts like every other control and swaps the whole editor body, which builds a fresh copy of the modal while the open one hangs off <body>. The fresh copy is swapped in behind the person using it, and the key carries the parsed map across, pan and zoom included.

It is the only renderer. A server-rendered SVG used to sit behind it as an offline fallback, but the page loads htmx from a CDN and every control here is an hx- attribute, so an editor that cannot reach the network does not work at all — the fallback bought no offline capability while costing a second drawing of the same map on screen at once.

The viewer has a single highlight channel — one outline colour, no second class — so what is outlined follows the mode: a constraint search outlines its matches, a pinned lanelet outlines itself. The caption under the map names which of the two it is, rather than showing colour swatches the viewer does not use.

docs.title: Derived offsets
docs.text:
The longitudinal offset can be Fixed or Derived from the map. A derived offset is a sweep.bindings entry -- currently StopLineOffsetBinding:

Field Value Position on matched lanelet Derived Derived from Before stop line Distance 15 m 
sweep:
  bindings:
    ego.spawn_s:
      type: stop_line_offset
      offset: 15.0

The sweeper enumerates a single target key per run, so one entity's spawn can be searched per scenario; the editor warns when a document asks for more.

The ego reaches the runner through the framework's own ego.spawn_lanelet_id / ego.spawn_s keys, with its lateral offset and heading as ego.spawn_t / ego.spawn_heading. Other entities get a declared scenario.spawn_overrides.<entity> sub-tree so they are addressable by exactly the same plain key=value overrides.

docs.title: A logical scenario: the route search
docs.text: A document may describe the ego's drive as a pattern of road instead of lanelets -- a logical scenario. The scenario inspector's Route search section lists the pattern one segment per line ("lane 30-60 m, opposite lane: yes", "junction, turn left, traffic light: yes") with where the ego spawns and is sent, and edits it as the YAML the document stores (an empty box removes it; a malformed one is refused with the reason). A Follow Trajectory card's Path then offers Along the scenario's route, whose Route vertices are edited as text, one kind key=value ... per line, and the Route progress condition is offered for triggers, assertions and waypoint conditions. A Spawn card brings a hidden entity in (or, with no actor, adds a prop by name); trigger its Set Goal card on the Spawn card's action state.

docs.title: Ego: who drives, and where to
docs.text:
The ego's inspector opens with Driven by — the stack that drives it, exported as ego.entity:

Driven by ego.entity Goal TrafficManager (CARLA autopilot) autopilot optional — it reads none Autoware autoware required — it plans its route to the goal and will not move without one

(The framework's third value, carla_driver, needs a driver config group the editor does not author; a run can still select it from the command line.)

The Goal section sits beside the spawn, because the two are the ends of the same thing: where the run starts, and where the ego is meant to get to. A goal is picked from the map like a spawn is, and may be searched for like one — the sweep then writes ego.goal_lanelet_id. An Autoware ego without one is a validation error; an ego the TrafficManager drives may be given none — a cut-in or a red-light run is about what happens on the way — and Clear goal puts it back to that.

A goal is not a card. A card happens during a run, and a goal is what the ego needs before one can start: Autoware localizes at the spawn, plans a route to the goal, and only then engages. The framework asks the same of a hand-written scenario — BaseScenario.require_goal(), asked by register_route_to_goal and by ScenarioRunner once setup() returns — so the editor stores the goal on the ego and exports it as the framework's own keys:

ego:
  spawn_lanelet_id: 183
  spawn_s: 0.0
  spawn_t: 0.0
  spawn_heading: 0.0
  entity: autoware
  goal_lanelet_id: 265
  goal_s: 12.5

The goal keys are written only when a goal is set, leaving the ego group's own null in place otherwise.

The Set Goal card still exists, for changing a destination mid-run or for a vehicle that is not the ego. One owned by the ego and left in the initialization phase is warned about: the ego's own goal is already delivered there, so the card would send a second destination in the same phase. Only a vehicle that plans its own route reads a goal at all, so a goal stored on any other entity is a validation error rather than something quietly dropped at export.

The Set Goal card is also how any road user moves through waypoints (written out, each with a time or a waypoint condition) and Driven by says who moves it: its own driver, a controller, or a replay (Routes, Trajectories and Recorded-Scene Replay). The Despawn card (despawn, a vehicle or a pedestrian, never the ego) takes a road user out of the world when its trigger holds -- typically an Action state condition on its own Set Goal card reaching Complete, so it leaves where its route ends instead of driving on wherever its traffic takes it.

docs.title: Metadata-driven GUI
docs.text:
Actions, conditions, constraints and bindings keep growing, so the templates render metadata, never a type switch. Adding a primitive is a Python-side change in autoware_carla_scenario.authoring.registry:

register_action_spec(
    ActionSpec(
        type_id="lane_change",
        title="Lane Change",
        category="Vehicle / Motion",
        builder="build_lane_change_action",
        visual_kind="instant",
        fields=(FieldSpec("direction", "Direction", "select", "left", _DIRECTIONS),),
    )
)

plus a matching factory in authoring.builders that returns the framework's own class. The inspector, the canvas, validation and the compiler all pick it up with no template edit. test_authoring_registry.py fails if a spec names a builder that does not exist, or a visual that names a field the primitive lacks.

docs.title: A list of records
docs.text:
A field of kind record_list holds an ordered list of records, each a mapping of its own item_fields -- for a list whose order means something and whose entries repeat, such as NADE's adversities, where the first to fire wins:

FieldSpec(
    name="adversities",
    label="Adversities",
    kind="record_list",
    default=(),
    item_fields=(
        FieldSpec("kind", "Kind", "select", "brake_check", _KINDS),
        FieldSpec("probability", "Probability", "number", 0.01),
    ),
)
  • Inspector: one block of controls per record, with buttons to add one and to remove or move each.
  • The buttons are submits of the inspector's own form.
  • The form posts each record's fields as <field>.<i>.<sub>, the row count as <field>.__rows, and the button pressed as <field>.__op.
  • Validation and compiling: each record is validated and coerced by its fields, as a node's params are.
  • required means at least one record.
  • An unset list is an empty one.
  • Entity references inside a record are resolved as top-level ones are.
  • Generated builder: it builds one item per record. The item class comes from the constructor's annotation (list[AdversitySpec]), and each item field feeds the item constructor's keyword of the same name, enums lifted.
  • Restrictions: a record holds no lanelet field, whose map lives outside the form, and no record list.
  • Overrides: a run overrides one record's field with scenario.param_overrides.<node id>.<field>.<index>.<sub>=<value>.

docs.title: The map path is a document field
docs.text:
/draft/<id>/map.osm serves the file the document names, and that name is typed by whoever is using the editor -- which may bind 0.0.0.0 (--host). Handed straight to a FileResponse it was an arbitrary local file read for anyone who could reach the port. A path is accepted only when it resolves inside SCENARIO_EDITOR_MAP_ROOTS (the working directory unless set) and names a .osm, so what the route can serve is bounded by where the editor was started rather than by what the process can read.

That is a bound, not authentication: the editor still has none, so it belongs on a network you trust.

docs.title: Save Draft vs Export Wheelhouse
docs.text:
Save Draft writes the working document to scenario_drafts/<id>.yaml.

Export Wheelhouse produces a .zip the browser downloads, holding every wheel the scenario needs:

cut_in-wheelhouse.zip
`-- cut_in_scenario_wheelhouse/
    |-- cut_in_scenario-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl     # the scenario itself
    |-- autoware_carla_scenario-*.whl              # the framework, at the pinned commit
    |-- typesafe_carla-*.whl                       # the CARLA client, CPython package prebuilt
    |-- typesafe_carla_toolchain-*.whl             # the Codon compiler it pins
    |-- ... every transitive dependency, ~94 wheels
    |-- requirements.txt                           # the whole set, pinned
    `-- README.md                                  # how to install it

Install it with pip and nothing else -- no uv, no git, no network, no resolution:

unzip cut_in-wheelhouse.zip
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install --no-index --find-links cut_in_scenario_wheelhouse cut-in-scenario
.venv/bin/scenario scenario=cut_in map=nishishinjuku

The CARLA client is typesafe_carla, and the typesafe-carla wheel in the wheelhouse is the released one from PyPI, which carries its CPython package (typesafe_carla.carla) prebuilt -- one build for every Python 3.10+. So pip is the whole installation, here as everywhere: nothing is compiled on the target, and an offline vehicle needs neither cc nor a build step. Only if that prebuilt package does not match the installation -- a typesafe-carla-toolchain other than the one the wheel was built with, say -- does the first import typesafe_carla.carla, the first scenario run, build it with the Codon compiler from the toolchain wheel (15 to 30 minutes, about 14 GB of RAM, cc, but no network) into ~/.cache/typesafe_carla/pycarla (TYPESAFE_CARLA_PYCARLA_DIR moves it); typesafe-codon pycarla does that ahead of time, and reports that there is nothing to build when the prebuilt package applies.

That is the point of the format. Where scenarios run is often a venv built from python3-venv and python3-pip -- the two things rosdep can resolve -- with neither uv nor, on a vehicle, a network route. A uv project needs all three; a wheelhouse needs none.

The scenario's document and Hydra config travel inside its wheel, so an installed scenario is self-contained: there is no directory that has to be kept beside it.

docs.title: What the wheelhouse is built from
docs.text:
The exporter still generates the uv project it always did -- pyproject.toml with the framework pinned to an exact commit, uv.lock, the document, the Hydra config, the package's own tests -- and still runs uv sync --locked and those tests against it. That project is now a build input: the wheels are resolved from its lockfile and the project itself does not leave the server.

The CARLA client needs no special handling: typesafe-carla is a plain dependency of the framework, published on PyPI, so the package requests no extra, vendors no wheel, and the lock resolves the client like any other dependency.

There is no destination field. The editor is routinely used from another machine on the LAN, where a path typed into it would name a directory on the host running the server -- not one the person exporting can reach. Everything is built in a temporary directory, the wheelhouse is zipped, and the build tree is removed, so the only thing that outlives the request is the archive, and re-exporting never has to overwrite a half-written one.

The response is still the report -- warnings, the tool log, whether the package's own tests passed -- with the download link in it. Making the response the file itself would throw away the very things an export is checked for.

docs.title: One platform, every supported interpreter
docs.text:
A wheelhouse is resolved for a platform: the wheels are the ones the exporting machine selected, so installing them on a different platform fails on the first wheel with no matching tag -- export from a matching machine instead.

The interpreter is not that kind of constraint. Resolution is done once per interpreter the package supports, all into the same directory. Which interpreters those are is the CI-tested range -- 3.10 through 3.14 -- narrowed to what the package's requires-python admits; the package inherits the framework's, so normally all five. The pure-Python wheels are shared between the passes and the compiled ones sit side by side with their own tag, so pip installs whichever matches. That is what lets one export serve ROS 2 Humble, whose Python is 3.10, and Jazzy, whose Python is 3.12: the alternative is a python3.12 that Ubuntu 22.04 does not package at all.

It is large -- the CARLA client and its Codon toolchain, OpenCV and the lanelet2 bindings, the compiled ones once per interpreter. That is the cost of not needing a network at install time, and of not needing to know which Python the target runs before exporting.

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text:
What Pinned by autoware-carla-scenario exact version, or an exact commit SHA typesafe-carla the framework's own requirement (>=0.3.0,<0.4), locked in uv.lock like everything else Python .python-version, exact patch version uv [tool.uv] required-version, when uv's version could be read Everything else uv.lock, and then the wheels built from it

A branch is never emitted -- main, master and HEAD all move, so a package pinned to one stops being the package that was tested as soon as somebody pushes. When no immutable pin can be determined the export fails rather than guessing. A local-path dependency is only produced by an explicit development export, which says so in its README and manifest.

Set SCENARIO_EXPORT_FRAMEWORK_VERSION to pin a published release instead of the current checkout's commit.

docs.title: Export is atomic
docs.text:
The exporter builds into a temporary directory and runs uv lock, then uv sync --locked, then the generated package's own tests, then the wheelhouse. If locking, verification or the wheelhouse fails, nothing is written -- a package whose dependencies never resolved, or that no environment can install, is not a successful export.

The manifest records only values that were actually observed:

format_version: 3
scenario: {id: cut_in, title: Cut in, document_version: 1, package: cut-in-scenario}
runtime: {python: 3.12.10, uv: 0.12.0, requires_python: '>=3.10,<3.15'}
wheelhouse:
  directory: cut_in_scenario_wheelhouse
  install: pip install --no-index --find-links cut_in_scenario_wheelhouse cut-in-scenario
  wheels: 104
  python: ['3.10', '3.11', '3.12', '3.13', '3.14']
autoware_carla_scenario:
  source: git
  repository: https://github.com/hakuturu583/autoware_carla_scenario
  commit: 0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567
  subdirectory: autoware_carla_scenario
files:
  document: src/cut_in_scenario/document.yaml
  hydra_config: src/cut_in_scenario/conf/scenario/cut_in.yaml
notes: []

Anything that could not be determined is null with a note, never a plausible guess.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Option Variable Default Meaning --drafts SCENARIO_EDITOR_DRAFTS ./scenario_drafts Where drafts are stored --export-dir SCENARIO_EDITOR_EXPORT_DIR ./scenario_packages Where an export's wheelhouse .zip is staged, in a directory per draft, until the browser fetches it — SCENARIO_EDITOR_MAP_ROOTS the working directory Directories a Lanelet2 map may be read from, :-separated --host SCENARIO_EDITOR_HOST 127.0.0.1 Bind address --port SCENARIO_EDITOR_PORT 9100 Bind port (the result viewer uses 9000) — SCENARIO_EDITOR_MAP_VIEWER GitHub Pages build URL of simple_lanelet2's viewer.js

An option defaults to its variable, so a flag on the command line wins over the environment (uv run scenario-editor --host 0.0.0.0 --port 9200). An unknown option is an error (exit 2) and serves nothing.

The editor listens on this machine only by default

The editor has no authentication, so it binds 127.0.0.1 unless told otherwise. It used to bind 0.0.0.0, every interface; to serve other machines as before, pass --host 0.0.0.0 (or set SCENARIO_EDITOR_HOST=0.0.0.0) on a network you trust. The editor prints a warning when it listens on anything but a loopback address.

docs.title: Running an authored scenario
docs.text:
An exported scenario plugs in through the same entry point any scenario package uses (see Architecture) -- installed from its wheelhouse, the scenario command is on the venv's PATH:

.venv/bin/scenario scenario=cut_in map=nishishinjuku

# Sweep every lanelet the spawn constraints match:
.venv/bin/scenario --multirun scenario=cut_in map=nishishinjuku \
    hydra/sweeper=lanelet_constraint

The CARLA client needs no separate install: typesafe-carla is a dependency of the framework, so it is in the lock and in the wheelhouse alongside everything else, with its CPython package prebuilt, so nothing has to be compiled on the machine that runs the scenario (see Save Draft vs Export Wheelhouse).

docs.title: Offline
docs.text:
Only two things in the editor come from the network, and neither is load-bearing for editing:

htmx every interaction; the editor needs it simple_lanelet2's map viewer the map drawing only — the panel says so when it cannot be fetched

The stylesheet is served by the app itself rather than by a CDN, so a blocked egress rule cannot take the layout with it.

docs.title: Running a Batch on SLURM
docs.text:
A batch (scenario 'scenario=<glob>', and with --multirun every case of each scenario's sweep) runs its cases one after another, in one process, on one CARLA. On a machine or cluster with SLURM, the same batch can run its cases as the tasks of a SLURM array job instead, several at once, each on a CARLA of its own:

uv run scenario --multirun 'scenario=cut_in/*' +sweep.odd_sample.count=24 \
  launcher=slurm launcher.array_parallelism=2 launcher.gres=shard:1 launcher.mem=12G

It is off unless a run selects it. The launcher config group is not part of the default config: a run that does not name it composes the same config as before, and the batch runs here, exactly as it always has. launcher=local says the same explicitly.

The batch writes what a local batch writes, where a local batch writes it (outputs/<date>/<time>/), under the same names: every case's {Scenario}_result.json, {Scenario}.trajectory.jsonl, coverage, ODD archive, environment and CARLA recording, and batch_results.json with the summary table at the end. A case's outputs do not depend on which task ran it or when.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
On the machine you run scenario on (a SLURM submit host):

  1. The batch is expanded, labelled, built and statically checked exactly as a local batch is: the ODD sampling, the case labels, the static check (once a config shape), the map fetched. A config error is refused here, before anything is submitted.
  2. A manifest is written into the batch's output directory (slurm/manifest.json): every case's scenario and overrides, its resolved config, and the file stem it is to be named by.
  3. sbatch --array=0-(N-1)%K submits the cases, launcher.cases_per_task to a task, at most launcher.array_parallelism tasks at once.
  4. By default scenario follows the array (squeue, and the outcome each task records) until it ends, then prints the summary and writes batch_results.json, as a local batch does, and exits 0 when every case passed. Ctrl-C cancels the batch's jobs, waits (up to 60 s) for their tasks to leave the queue, and collects. With --no-wait (launcher.wait=false) it submits and exits, and a small job that runs once the array has ended (--dependency=afterany) collects the batch; should that job not be submitted, scenario says so, with the array's job id, and exits non-zero (scenario-slurm wait collects the batch instead).

Each task, on its node:

  1. takes a slot of ports no other task on the node holds and nothing listens on (Ports);
  2. composes each of its cases' configs from the manifest's scenario and overrides, and refuses to run one that no longer resolves to the config it was submitted with (a job that does not run in the submitting environment);
  3. builds them (not checked again: the submitting process did), starts a CARLA on its ports and runs its cases one after another through the same queue a local batch uses, writing their files into the batch's directory under the names a local batch gives them;
  4. records each case's outcome as soon as it has run (slurm/results/<case>.json), and its own progress in slurm/tasks/<submission>-<task>.json (host, ports, state, peak resident memory); with rerun.enabled=true it also converts each case's trajectory log into its Rerun recording ({stem}.rrd) and records whether that failed, so collect reports the recordings as a local batch does (Seeing a run). The submitting process only checks that the rerun extra is installed; the nodes need it too;
  5. stops its CARLA however it ends: at the end, on scancel, on the signal SLURM sends launcher.signal_grace_seconds before launcher.time runs out, and -- through the job script -- when the worker itself was killed, even by the SIGKILL that ends a scancel after SLURM's KillWait (CARLA runs in a session of its own, which that signal misses): a small watchdog process of its own, started once the slot is taken, stops CARLA when the worker ends without having done so, and keeps the slot locked until then.

docs.title: Following, collecting, resubmitting
docs.text:
scenario-slurm takes the batch's output directory:

scenario-slurm status   outputs/2026-10-18/12-00-00   # cases, jobs, tasks
scenario-slurm wait     outputs/2026-10-18/12-00-00   # follow, then collect
scenario-slurm collect  outputs/2026-10-18/12-00-00   # summary, batch_results.json
scenario-slurm resubmit outputs/2026-10-18/12-00-00   # the cases with no result
scenario-slurm cancel   outputs/2026-10-18/12-00-00   # scancel the batch's jobs

A case that has no outcome -- its task was cancelled, ran out of time, was killed for memory, or its node failed -- is reported as ERROR with a message saying so, and collect lists them. resubmit submits again the cases with no outcome and those that raised on every attempt (ERROR); --failed adds the ones that ran and failed, --cases a,b names them (labels or indices; a case named twice runs once), and --array-parallelism/--cases-per-task change how they are spread. A case run again replaces its earlier files: before it runs, the task removes every output of its stem (run_outputs), its T4 dataset directory ({stem}.t4) included, so none of the last attempt's is left beside the new result. So resubmit refuses while a job of the batch is queued or running, or while squeue cannot tell whether one is (--force submits all the same). collect can be run any number of times.

sacct is not needed: the batch is followed through squeue and the files the tasks write.

The result viewer does the same from its pages: its run panel submits a batch with launcher=slurm, and a SLURM batch's page shows its cases, jobs and tasks as they run and resubmits, collects or cancels it (Running through SLURM).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
launcher=slurm selects conf/launcher/slurm.yaml; every key can be set on the command line (launcher.mem=12G), or in a config.

Key Default partition, account, qos null sbatch --partition/--account/--qos time null sbatch --time; the task is sent SIGTERM signal_grace_seconds before it runs out mem, cpus_per_task, gres null sbatch --mem/--cpus-per-task/--gres (gpu:1, or shard:1 to share a GPU) array_parallelism null at most this many tasks at once (--array=...%K); null: no cap cases_per_task null cases a task runs on its CARLA; null: the cases spread evenly over array_parallelism tasks (one case a task without a cap) job_name null acs-<date>-<time> of the output directory extra_sbatch_args [] further sbatch arguments export null sbatch --export; null: ALL, or NONE with remote_cwd env_passthrough null variables recorded at submission and set again in the job; null: see below, or none with remote_cwd setup [] shell lines the job runs before the worker (module load, source .venv/bin/activate) env {} variables set in the job, last python null the interpreter the jobs run (the tasks and the collect job): an absolute path, a path relative to the job's working directory (.venv/bin/python), ~/... (the home on the node), or a command on the node's PATH (python3); null: the submitting one remote_cwd null where the jobs work on the nodes, for a submit host that sees their file system at another path (A submit host with other paths); null: the directory scenario runs in headless true unset DISPLAY in the job, so CARLA renders off-screen start_stagger_seconds 0 no task of the batch starts sooner than this after another did: the first wave, the tasks started as slots free up, a resubmit's (Shared state) wait true follow and collect; false (or --no-wait): submit and exit poll_seconds 15 how often wait asks squeue cancel_on_interrupt true Ctrl-C while waiting cancels the batch's jobs collect_job true with wait: false, a job that collects once the array ends collect_mem 2G its --mem signal_grace_seconds 120 --signal=B:TERM@N port_base, port_slots 20000, 1000 where the tasks' port slots are (Ports); port_slots at least 1 port_lock_dir null where the slots' locks are; null: /dev/shm/acs-slurm-ports-<uid>, else /tmp (Ports)

cases_per_task trades a task's start -- CARLA takes about 50 s to start, and a driver policy about as long to load -- against how evenly the cases spread and how many a lost task takes with it.

docs.title: The job's environment
docs.text:
A task runs with the Python the batch was submitted from (sys.executable, or launcher.python) and its environment:

  1. sbatch --export=ALL (launcher.export) hands the job the environment of the shell sbatch runs from;
  2. the job script then sets again, as they were when the batch was submitted, the variables launcher.env_passthrough matches: PATH, LD_LIBRARY_PATH, PYTHONPATH, PYTHONHOME, VIRTUAL_ENV, CONDA_PREFIX, CARLA_* (CARLA_EXECUTABLE), AUTOWARE_*, ONEPLANNER_*, TYPESAFE_CARLA_*, GLIBC_TUNABLES, MALLOC_*, CUDA_HOME, CUDA_PATH, CUDAToolkit_ROOT -- so scenario-slurm resubmit from another shell runs the cases as they were submitted;
  3. launcher.setup runs;
  4. launcher.env is set.

A driver policy's variables belong on env_passthrough (a pattern: launcher.env_passthrough=[...] replaces the list) or in launcher.env. No token or credential is on the default list, and a name with TOKEN, SECRET, KEY, PASSWORD or CREDENTIAL in it (in any case) is not recorded through a pattern (AUTOWARE_*) either -- only when env_passthrough names it exactly, or launcher.env sets it: the manifest and the job scripts holding the values are files in the batch's output directory (both the user's alone, mode 0600 and 0700). With export: NONE, the job has only what steps 2 to 4 give it.

With launcher.remote_cwd set, none of this comes from the submit host: the job has the environment SLURM gives it on the node (export: NONE), the variables env_passthrough names only when it is given, then setup and env (A submit host with other paths).

A config that reads the environment (${oc.env:ONEPLANNER_MAP_DIR}) is resolved in the task too; a case whose config resolves differently there than where it was submitted is refused, naming the keys that differ.

docs.title: A submit host with other paths
docs.text:
By default the jobs run where scenario was run: the directory it ran in, the interpreter it ran with and the batch's output directory are recorded by their absolute paths, which the nodes must see as the submit host does. A submit host that sees the nodes' file system somewhere else -- a workstation that mounts a node's ~/workspace/OnePlanner with sshfs or NFS at ~/mnt/node/OnePlanner, under another user's home -- names the nodes' paths instead, none of them absolute:

# On the submit host, in its mount of the node's ~/workspace/OnePlanner:
cd ~/mnt/node/OnePlanner
uv run scenario --multirun 'scenario=cut_in/*' +sweep.odd_sample.count=24 \
  launcher=slurm launcher.partition=main launcher.gres=shard:1 \
  launcher.remote_cwd=workspace/OnePlanner \
  launcher.python=.venv/bin/python \
  "launcher.setup=['source ~/workspace/opt/env.sh']"
  • launcher.remote_cwd is where every job -- each task and the collect job -- works on the node. A relative path is relative to the job user's home on the node, ~/... is that home too, and an absolute path is used as it is. It is expanded by the job script on the node, never here: the home is the one the node's passwd database gives the job's user (whatever $HOME the job was handed), so the user name and home may differ from the submit host's.
  • launcher.python is then required: the submit host's interpreter is not the node's. A relative path (.venv/bin/python) is relative to remote_cwd, a bare name (python3) is looked up on the node's PATH as setup leaves it.
  • The batch's output directory must lie under the directory scenario runs in (outputs/<date>/<time>/ does), which is what the node sees at remote_cwd; scenario refuses a batch elsewhere. The manifest records it relative to that directory (batch_dir_relative, a version 2 manifest), and the jobs find it under their own working directory. On the submit host, scenario-slurm takes the batch's directory as this host sees it (scenario-slurm wait ~/mnt/node/OnePlanner/outputs/<date>/<time>), and resubmit submits with the settings the batch was submitted with.
  • Nothing of the submit host's environment reaches the job: export is NONE (the job starts with the environment SLURM gives it on the node, which on most clusters is the user's login environment) and env_passthrough is empty, unless either is set. Set the node's environment with setup, which runs in remote_cwd and may read unset variables (source ~/workspace/opt/env.sh, module load cuda, source .venv/bin/activate), and env.
  • SLURM writes a job's output before the job knows where the batch is: each job starts in /tmp with its output there (/tmp/acs-slurm-<user>-<job>_<task>.out on the node) and sends it on to the batch's slurm/logs/ once it is in remote_cwd. The file in /tmp keeps what came before (a remote_cwd the node does not have) and what SLURM itself writes (a time limit, a cancel).
  • A case's config that resolves to absolute paths -- an ODD file in a scenario package, a map -- resolves to the node's paths there; see below for when that is still the same config.

Without remote_cwd the batch is submitted and run exactly as before (a version 1 manifest).

A value that is a path may differ and still be the same config. That is the case when it is the submitting directory's path seen from the job's working directory (<cwd>/x there, <remote_cwd>/x here), or when it names a file with the content it had where the batch was submitted: scenario records the SHA-256 of every file an absolute path in a case's config names (the manifest's files), and the task compares the file its own config names. A file missing on the node, or with other content, is refused, naming the key and both paths. This holds with or without remote_cwd: a package installed in another environment names its files at other paths too.

docs.title: Ports
docs.text:
Each task's CARLA needs ports no other CARLA on the node uses, and a user may run one on the defaults (2000, TrafficManager 8100). A task takes a slot of 10 ports from port_base:

Port base+0 CARLA RPC (server.port) base+1 CARLA streaming (-carla-streaming-port) base+2 CARLA secondary (-carla-secondary-port) base+3 TrafficManager (traffic_manager.port) base+4 the Autoware bridge the run hosts (autoware.address) base+5 the driver bridge the run hosts (driver.bridge.address)

The slot a task tries first is its array job id plus its task id, so the tasks of an array start on different slots. It takes one only when no other task holds it (an exclusive lock, <lock dir>/autoware_carla_scenario-port-<base>.lock, which goes when the task's process does) and none of its ports is bound; else the next. The lock directory must be one every job on the node sees, which /tmp is not where SLURM gives each job a private one (job_container/tmpfs): it is /dev/shm/acs-slurm-ports-<uid> (or /tmp where that cannot be made), or launcher.port_lock_dir. The default range, 20000-29999, is below Linux's ephemeral ports.

driver.address is not changed: a policy the run serves itself (driver.policy) listens on a port the OS picks, and one it does not is a server someone else runs, which every task dials. driver.transport is not changed either: with direct a task calls the policy it serves without a socket, and with unix it serves it on a socket in a directory of its own (under $TMPDIR, which SLURM does not set by default, so usually /tmp), so neither needs a port of the slot and tasks sharing a node never meet; a unix: driver.address someone else serves is dialled by every task, as a TCP one is.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Memory. A task runs a CARLA (about 6 GB resident) and a scenario process (about 6 GB with a TensorRT driver policy loaded). Without cgroups, SLURM uses --mem only to schedule, so set it, and array_parallelism, to what the node has.
  • Shared state. The tasks share the map caches (~/autoware_data/maps), the map files a driver policy reads (driver.map_dir) and the batch's output directory, so these must be on a file system every node sees.
