Option Default micro_radius_m 200 a mesoscopic vehicle this close to a focus point comes back meso_radius_m 1.25 × micro_radius_m a microscopic one further than this from all of them leaves update_interval_s 1.0 simulated seconds between two decisions; the queue model steps every tick scenario_vehicles false let the scenario's vehicles SUMO drives (scenario_vehicles=sumo) leave CARLA too headway_s, jam_spacing_m 1.5, 7.5 the queue model's capacity per lane, and the road a queued vehicle takes up junction_control true hold a mesoscopic vehicle at a red SUMO signal

A vehicle leaves only from a normal edge, never from inside a junction, and comes back with its route, its type, length, width and top speed, and a speed it was told to keep. A scenario's vehicle that is mesoscopic takes set_desired_speed and turn_at_junction in the queue model; it cannot change lanes there, and says so. scenario_vehicles is off by default because such a vehicle has no actor while it is far: a scenario that reads it -- a condition on its speed -- should check entity.simulation_fidelity, or call entity.require_microscopic(world) first. SUMO's FCD output records the microscopic vehicles only.

Manoeuvres of SUMO-driven vehicles become TraCI calls: change_lane → changeLane (SUMO obeys a solid line, and says so), set_desired_speed → setSpeed, turn_at_junction → a route onto the junction's outgoing edge in that direction. With the default, they go to the TrafficManager. follow_route goes to the TrafficManager only: a vehicle SUMO drives keeps its route, since the route's lanelets are not mapped to SUMO edges.

The coupling follows TeraSim's CARLA co-simulation; its adversarial behaviour generation is left to scenarios.

docs.title: Routes, Trajectories and Recorded-Scene Replay
docs.text:
RoutingAction sends a vehicle or a pedestrian through waypoints to a goal. Each waypoint may carry when: an arrival time or a departure condition. Who moves the entity is its mode:

mode Who drives Between waypoints Timing RoutingMode.DRIVER (default) The entity's own driver: the TrafficManager or SUMO for a vehicle, the pedestrian route walker, Autoware for an Autoware ego Lanelet2 routes (walkable lanelets for a pedestrian) Met by speed commands to the driver (below); an Autoware ego takes the route only RoutingMode.FOLLOW The action's own controller (OpenSCENARIO's trajectory following, FOLLOW) Straight legs Kept by the controller on the trajectory's clock RoutingMode.POSITION Nobody: the entity is placed every tick (POSITION) Straight legs Exact (a kinematic replay)

It is what lets a recorded drive be written down as a scenario: a recording is transcribed into one trajectory per road user, and each one is replayed around the ego (follow or position), or handed to the road user's own driver to keep its timing (driver).

Breaking change (19.0.0): FollowTrajectoryAction is gone

FollowTrajectoryAction and the editor's Follow Trajectory card (follow_trajectory) were removed; RoutingAction and the Set Goal card (routing) do everything they did. In Python write RoutingAction(entity, trajectory=..., time_reference=..., mode=RoutingMode.FOLLOW) (or POSITION) for FollowTrajectoryAction(entity, trajectory, time_reference, TrajectoryFollowingMode.FOLLOW). In a document change type: follow_trajectory to type: routing and following_mode to mode (follow / position as before, or driver), and state time_domain (the card's default is now none). A document that still has a follow_trajectory card is refused with a message saying so; there is no automatic conversion.

Reading a dataset is left to tools outside the framework (see Replaying a recorded scene), so the framework carries no dataset format.

docs.title: The action
docs.text:
A goal and Lanelet2 waypoints are what an ego is given (RoutingAction("ego", Lanelet2Pose(42, 10.0), waypoints=[Lanelet2Pose(17, 0.0)])); a trajectory writes the waypoints out, the last one the goal:

from autoware_carla_scenario import (
    Lanelet2Pose,
    MapPose,
    ReferenceContext,
    RoutingAction,
    RoutingMode,
    Trajectory,
    TrajectoryTimeCondition as At,
    TrajectoryTiming,
    TrajectoryVertex,
)

path = Trajectory(
    "npc1_path",
    [
        TrajectoryVertex(Lanelet2Pose(lanelet_id=120, s=0.0), At(0.0)),
        TrajectoryVertex(Lanelet2Pose(lanelet_id=120, s=30.0), At(4.0)),
        TrajectoryVertex(MapPose(x=81234.5, y=50123.0), At(7.0)),
    ],
)
self.register_pre_tick(
    RoutingAction(
        "npc1",
        trajectory=path,
        time_reference=TrajectoryTiming(ReferenceContext.RELATIVE),
        mode=RoutingMode.POSITION,
        label="npc1_follows_path",
    )
)

A trajectory has the same four parts as OpenSCENARIO's trajectory following:

OpenSCENARIO Here Notes Trajectory (name, closed, shape) Trajectory(name, vertices, closed=False) Only the Polyline shape. A recording is a sequence of samples; a clothoid or NURBS fitted to one would add an approximation between the data and the vehicle. Vertex (time, Position) TrajectoryVertex(position, advance=None) A vertex's time is its departure condition, advance=TrajectoryTimeCondition(t) (read back as vertex.time); any other condition can take its place -- see Waypoint conditions. Either every vertex has a time or none has, a vertex with another condition counting as having one. TimeReference time_reference=None or TrajectoryTiming(domain, scale, offset) None is <None/>: the vertex times are ignored and the entity keeps the speed it had when the action started. With a timing, a vertex at time τ is reached at τ * scale + offset seconds after the scenario (ABSOLUTE) or the action (RELATIVE) started. TrajectoryFollowingMode mode=RoutingMode.POSITION or FOLLOW (or DRIVER) See below. initialDistanceOffset initial_distance_offset Start that many metres along. With a timing, the clock starts at the time the trajectory reaches that point.

A vertex's position may be written in any frame the framework addresses:

  • Lanelet2Pose, OpenDrivePose and CarlaWorldPose -- as everywhere else;
  • MapPose(x, y, yaw=None, z=None) -- an absolute pose in Autoware's map frame (the Lanelet2 file's projected frame), which is the frame a recording states its poses in. A missing yaw is taken from the direction of the path; a missing z puts the entity on the road surface under it;
  • RelativeLanePose(ds=0.0, offset=0.0, d_lane=0, yaw=None, entity_ref=None) -- a pose relative to an entity, in lane coordinates (OpenSCENARIO's RelativeLanePosition); see below.

Positions are converted to CARLA world coordinates when the action first runs, through the loaded map. Vertices of different kinds may be mixed in one trajectory.

docs.title: Lane-relative vertices
docs.text:
A RelativeLanePose writes the shape of a manoeuvre -- pull out, overtake, cut in ahead of the ego -- once, to be played from wherever it begins:

from autoware_carla_scenario import EGO_ROLE_NAME, RelativeLanePose

overtake = Trajectory(
    "overtake",
    [
        TrajectoryVertex(RelativeLanePose(), At(0.0)),  # where npc1 is
        TrajectoryVertex(RelativeLanePose(ds=20.0, d_lane=1), At(2.0)),
        TrajectoryVertex(RelativeLanePose(ds=60.0, d_lane=1), At(5.0)),
        # 10 m ahead of the ego, in its lane: a cut-in.
        TrajectoryVertex(RelativeLanePose(ds=10.0, entity_ref=EGO_ROLE_NAME), At(7.0)),
    ],
)
self.register_pre_tick(
    RoutingAction(
        "npc1",
        trajectory=overtake,
        time_reference=TrajectoryTiming(),
        mode=RoutingMode.FOLLOW,
        label="npc1_overtakes",
    )
)
Field OpenSCENARIO Meaning entity_ref entityRef role_name of the reference entity, a str or an EntityRole (stored as its string). None (default) is the entity the action moves. ds ds Metres along the reference entity's lane, from where it is; negative goes back. d_lane dLane Lanes across: +1 one lane to the left, -1 one to the right, 0 the reference's own lane. offset offset Metres from the target lane's centreline, positive to the left -- the sign of Lanelet2Pose.t. The reference entity's own lateral position does not carry over. yaw Orientation (relative) Radians from the target lane's direction, positive to the left (anticlockwise) -- the sense of Lanelet2Pose.heading. None faces along the path, as for MapPose.

How a vertex is placed, on the Lanelet2 map and its routing graph:

  1. The reference's lane. The lanelet the reference entity is on, and the exact distance along its centreline. Where lanelets overlap (a junction) or meet (a seam), the one whose direction is nearest the entity's heading wins, then the one nearest its elevation, then the lowest id.
  2. ds along the lane. Past a lanelet's end the distance carries on into the lanelet that follows it in the routing graph; a negative ds past its start into the one before it. Where several follow (a fork) or precede (a merge), the one that turns least is taken, then the lowest id -- the "straight on" a route most often takes, and deterministic. A ds that runs off a lanelet nothing follows is an error naming that lanelet.
  3. d_lane across. At the point ds reached, one step per lane through the routing graph's left or right neighbour -- lane-changeable or not (a solid line still has a lane beyond it), but only lanes of the same direction of travel. The point keeps abreast: its distance along the neighbour is where the point projects onto it, so the outside of a bend is not shortchanged. A missing neighbour is an error naming the lanelet and the side. Lanelet2 only knows a neighbour that shares the lanelet's whole side, so where the two lanes are split into lanelets at different points (one 20 m lanelet beside two 10 m ones) there is no neighbour to step to, and the vertex raises the same error.
  4. offset and yaw are applied on that lanelet, which gives a Lanelet2Pose, converted to CARLA coordinates like any other.

When. A trajectory with relative vertices is placed when the action starts -- the first tick of a run, against where each reference entity is at that tick -- and is then fixed: the vertices do not move with the reference entity afterwards, so the rest of the action (timing, both modes, hiding) works on it exactly as on absolute vertices. A repeating action (once=False) places it again at the start of every run. A reference entity that is not in the world yet puts the start off until it is -- for as long as it takes: the action neither ends nor fails meanwhile, and warns once per run; a lane the map does not have raises a ValueError naming the trajectory and the vertex. These lane checks can only be made then: they depend on where the reference entity is.

docs.title: Modes
docs.text:
• DRIVER hands the route to the entity's own driver -- see Driver mode and timing.
  • POSITION places the entity on the trajectory every tick, with the velocity the trajectory implies (so speed conditions and the recorder see the recorded speed). It is a kinematic replay: it reproduces a recording exactly, whatever the vehicle could actually do.
  • FOLLOW drives the vehicle there with the pure-pursuit and speed controller of the external driver interface (TrajectoryFollower, on the vehicle's own powertrain model), by default with its time_indexed longitudinal controller, which keeps the vehicle where the trajectory's clock has it. The motion is the vehicle's own, so it can lag or cut a corner. A pedestrian is walked towards the path.

docs.title: Driver mode and timing
docs.text:
In driver mode the route starts where the entity is -- the nearest point of its path within 6 m, a hidden one having been brought in by a SpawnAction -- and passes every waypoint after it, each placed on the lanelet under it (a walkable one for a pedestrian). A vehicle the traffic backend drives is handed it as a path (BackendDriven.route_to), a pedestrian walks it (PedestrianEntity.route_to), an Autoware ego is given it as a mission.

Timing. When waypoints carry times (with a time reference) or departure conditions, the action keeps running until the entity reaches the goal and, every tick, sets the driver's speed to meet them (TrafficManager set_desired_speed, SUMO setSpeed, the walker's step speed):

  • the next waypoint with a time: the distance left to it along the planned path over the time left, clamped to [0, limit] (the lane's speed limit, 2 m/s for a walker) and smoothed. A late entity goes at the limit to catch up. The driver still stops for lights and yields; the speed is a target;
  • the next waypoint with a departure condition: a rising route_progress condition (what a logical scenario times its road users by) is predicted -- its entity's progress rate says when it will hold -- and the entity is paced to arrive then. Any other condition, or a measured entity that is not moving forward, is approached at cruise speed (speed, else the limit) braking to stop 2 m short of the waypoint, where it holds until the condition does;
  • with nothing due ahead: speed if given, else the limit.

A hold can deadlock

An NPC holding before a waypoint until the ego has progressed, while it stands in the ego's way, waits for ever: the ego cannot pass it. Prediction slows the NPC down long before it would hold, so a route_progress condition on a moving ego seldom holds it; a condition that cannot be predicted does. Place waypoints that wait for the ego out of its path.

An Autoware ego takes no speed: it is given the route only, and the action warns once that its waypoints' times and conditions cannot be met.

Arrivals. In every mode, each waypoint with a time or a condition is logged when reached -- when it was due (its time; the moment its condition first held) against when the entity arrived -- as a waypoint_arrival record of the trajectory log, so a run can be scored on its timing.

Keeping to the recorded lanes. A vehicle's written-out waypoints are not routed one by one onto the nearest lane: the whole track between them is sampled every 2 m and matched to the lanes it runs along -- road lanelets within 4 m running within 60 degrees of its heading, joined on the routing graph by following on, a lane change or a short path, the closest sequence chosen (traffic.route_match) -- and the route goes through where it leaves each one. A track that cannot be matched falls back to its waypoints one by one, leaving out those no lane route reaches, with a warning. The TrafficManager is given the route with its own lane changes off, and a route ending in a junction is carried on along the lane after it until it is clear of the junction, so it is never handed an empty path.

When it ends. A route given as a goal (and Lanelet2 waypoints) with nothing to time ends as soon as the vehicle has it (as an ego's initial goal always has); a route written out as waypoints, timed or not, runs until the vehicle is within 1 m of its end along the planned path (a timed one then sets its driver's speed back to the cruise speed); a pedestrian's ends when it arrives.

docs.title: Who drives in follow and position modes, and when it ends
docs.text:
For the length of the run the action is the entity's only driver. A vehicle is taken back from the traffic backend first (TrafficBackend.release); an ego driven by an external stack (Autoware, a driver policy) is refused, because two authorities on one vehicle is not a scenario anyone wrote.

The action stays runningState until the entity reaches the end of the trajectory: the last vertex's time with a timing, the end of the path without one (never, for a closed trajectory), within ARRIVAL_TOLERANCE_M (1 m) of it in FOLLOW mode. A timed path that ends at rest -- a brake check's, 2 s of braking that stops a few metres on -- lasts its time in FOLLOW mode too: a vehicle that reaches its end early stands there on the brake until the last vertex's time. Then a vehicle is braked to a stop and a walker stood still where the trajectory ended. Pass until= to end it on a condition of your own. stop_at_end=False (an extension) leaves a vehicle moving as it arrived instead -- in POSITION mode with the last segment's velocity -- for an action that hands it straight back to traffic, as the adversarial actions do (resume_traffic).

RoutingAction routes an entity that is in the scene; it does not bring one in or take it out (appear_on_start and hidden_outside_trajectory are gone from it as of 1.0). A road user that enters a recording late is spawned hidden and brought in by a SpawnAction (the spawn card): put on its place, physics on, facing its heading, moving at speed; its routing card is triggered on the spawn card completing and starts where it stands. Triggered by a RouteProgressCondition it enters when the ego has come as far as it had when the road user was first seen; a PlaceClearCondition on the same place in its trigger waits for the place to be clear, and shift_max lets it take the nearest clear place further on along its lane once the trigger gives up waiting. The run writes a spawn record to the trajectory log on the tick it is brought in (a prop the action adds has none). One that leaves early is removed by a DespawnAction.

Vertices may also be placed against a logical scenario's route (RouteLanePose, RouteOppositePose, RouteCrossingPose, RouteCrosswalkPose, RouteRoadsidePose; path_source: route in a document) -- see Logical Scenarios from Routes.

docs.title: When a road user leaves: DespawnAction
docs.text:
A route's end is where the road user's recording ends, but its driver does not know that: a vehicle the TrafficManager drives carries on wherever its traffic takes it. DespawnAction(entity, condition) (card Despawn, despawn) takes a vehicle or a pedestrian -- never the ego -- out of the world when its condition holds: the traffic backend lets go of it (and stops protecting it), the collision log stops listening to it, its actor is destroyed and the entity is unregistered. An action still naming it afterwards logs that once and does nothing (a routing run on it ends); a condition reads it as absent. The run writes a despawn record to the trajectory log.

- id: npc1_leaves
  type: despawn
  actor: npc1
  trigger:
    type: action_state
    params: {action: npc1_drive, state: completeState}

A driver route written out as waypoints runs until the entity reaches its last one, timed or not, so its completion is the moment it arrives.

A road user the ego has left behind for good can leave too: one standing at least 30 m behind the ego along the road reads, in a trigger,

type: any
children:
- {type: action_state, params: {action: npc1_drive, state: completeState}}
- type: all
  children:
  - {type: action_state, params: {action: npc1_drive, state: runningState}}
  - {type: standstill, params: {entity: npc1, duration: 5.0}}
  - type: entity_distance
    params: {source: ego, target: npc1, measure: lane, signed: true,
             rule: less_than_or_equal, distance: -30.0}

signed (lane frame only) measures how far the target is ahead of the subject along the road, the way the subject faces, negative behind it (coordinate.lane_distance.lane_offset), so it reads the same whether the ego is moving or stopped.

A pedestrian routed in driver mode is walked by CARLA's own walker controller (controller.ai.walker) where the map has a pedestrian navigation mesh: it keeps to the pavements, crosses at crossings (waiting at the kerb, as CARLA's walkers do), and walks round what stands in its way. It is sent along its route a target every 10 m (reached 2 m short of it along the walk, or 2 m from it), its top speed the walk's pace; a walker held by its route's timing is taken off the controller while it stands (CARLA sends a walker standing 4 s somewhere random) and its target is sent again every 2 s. Whether it may cross a road away from a crossing is its own: the RoutingAction's cross_factor (the card's Crosses away from crossings), the probability its route may use the road anywhere -- 1 for a recorded walk that crossed there, 0 keeps it to crossings, empty is CARLA's default (0). CARLA keeps one such factor for the world and reads it only as a walker's controller starts (Navigation::AddWalker), so it is set to the walker's own just then and put back straight after. A map without a navigation mesh is said once, and its walkers are stepped along their routes as before. The navigation mesh comes with the map's import (roadgen's <Name>Package.py builds it with CARLA's RecastBuilder). A vehicle driven by the framework's own controller (follow mode, a final approach), which the TrafficManager does not drive, brakes for a walker in its way within its stopping distance (utils.clearance). A walker that falls over all the same is taken out of the world once it has lain there 5 s (npc_collisions.FALLEN_DESPAWN_S, the monitor's despawn_fallen_after_s; never the ego), with a despawn record of reason fallen.

A pedestrian's written-out waypoints a few metres apart (no more than 10 m from one to the next: a recorded walk) are walked as written, from where it starts; farther apart they are routed between on the walkable lanelets.

docs.title: Waypoint conditions
docs.text:
Each vertex is departed on one condition, its advance: when it holds, the entity leaves the vertex for the next one. A vertex with none is passed through on arrival.

  • Time is one kind of condition. TrajectoryTimeCondition(t) departs the vertex when the trajectory's clock reaches t -- the scenario clock mapped through the action's TrajectoryTiming (domain, scale, offset) and its initial_distance_offset. That is what a vertex time has always meant, and vertex.time reads it back. Without a time reference times are ignored, as OpenSCENARIO's <None/> says, and such a vertex is passed through.
  • Any other condition -- one the framework has now, one it gains later, or your own: an elapsed time, the distance to another entity, a speed, a traffic signal, an ActionStateCondition on another action, and AndCondition / OrCondition / StickyCondition / PersistentCondition compositions of them. The action asks it only what every condition answers, check(world, elapsed), and as for a trigger anything but None counts as satisfied. elapsed is the scenario's elapsed time, so ElapsedTimeCondition(30.0, label=...) reads "not before the scenario is 30 s old". (A TrajectoryTimeCondition inside a composition has no trajectory clock to read and compares the scenario's elapsed time; the editor refuses it there.)

A vertex cannot carry two: a time and another condition are combined, if that is what is meant, by giving the vertex an AndCondition of an ElapsedTimeCondition and the other.

Between two vertices. After vertex i is departed at scenario time T:

  • if vertex i + 1 has a time whose scenario time is not before T, the entity arrives there exactly then, moving linearly in between. When i was departed on its own time this is exactly the timed interpolation a recording is replayed with (a zero-duration segment is a jump), so a trajectory of times alone moves as it always did;
  • otherwise -- no time on i + 1, or one already past because the entity waited -- it goes at the action's speed: speed= (m/s) when given, else the speed the entity had when the run started. At (near) zero that segment is never finished, and the action warns when the run starts.

So after a late departure, a next vertex whose time is at or just after the departure is reached at once -- a jump in POSITION; in FOLLOW the vehicle cannot keep up and drives as fast as its controller lets it. That is the rule "arrive at its time if that is not before the departure" doing what it says.

Waiting. In POSITION mode a condition is checked from the tick the entity reaches its vertex -- not before -- then on every tick while it waits there, standing still with zero velocity. Once it holds the vertex is departed for the rest of that run; it is not asked again. If it already holds on arrival the entity does not stop. A condition that never holds keeps the entity there until until= ends the run. On the last vertex of an open path a condition means "end the run when it holds" (a time: when the clock reaches it, as ever); arriving at a last vertex with none ends the run. On the first vertex it is the departure from the start (a time: wait at the start until then). Vertices before the point a run starts from (initial_distance_offset) are not checked. A repeating action (once=False) re-arms every condition at the start of each run, and a closed path -- which cannot carry times -- checks its conditions again on every lap in POSITION mode. Whatever state a condition object keeps is its own: a latched StickyCondition stays latched.

from autoware_carla_scenario import (
    EGO_ROLE_NAME,
    ComparisonRule,
    ElapsedTimeCondition,
    EntityDistanceCondition,
    MapPose,
    RoutingAction,
    RoutingMode,
    Trajectory,
    TrajectoryTimeCondition as At,
    TrajectoryTiming,
    TrajectoryVertex,
)

crossing = Trajectory(
    "walker_crossing",
    [
        TrajectoryVertex(MapPose(81200.0, 50100.0), At(0.0)),
        # At the kerb: wait until the ego is within 25 m, then step out.
        TrajectoryVertex(
            MapPose(81205.0, 50100.0),
            EntityDistanceCondition(
                "walker1", EGO_ROLE_NAME, 25.0, ComparisonRule.LESS_THAN,
                label="ego_close",
            ),
        ),
        # Across by 11 s -- or, if the ego came late, at 1.4 m/s.
        TrajectoryVertex(MapPose(81205.0, 50110.0), At(11.0)),
    ],
)
self.register_pre_tick(
    RoutingAction(
        "walker1",
        trajectory=crossing,
        time_reference=TrajectoryTiming(),
        mode=RoutingMode.FOLLOW,
        speed=1.4,
        label="cross",
    )
)

# A trajectory built elsewhere (a recording, a lanelet route): `gated` replaces
# what the vertices named depart on, a time included.
held = recorded.gated({12: ElapsedTimeCondition(20.0, label="not_before_20s")})

By mode.

  • DRIVER: see Driver mode and timing -- the entity is paced to arrive when the condition holds, or held 2 m short of the waypoint until it does.

  • POSITION places the entity where that timeline has it every tick; waiting, it stands on the vertex itself.

  • FOLLOW (vehicle): a vertex whose condition has not held yet is a stop line -- the controller's plan ends on it, slowed to come to rest there at 2 m/s². A car cannot stop within a tick, so here the condition is checked before arrival, from as far off as stopping there takes (braking distance, a second's travel and the arrival band); one that holds then is passed, letting the vehicle through at speed and costing the schedule nothing -- even if it would no longer hold by the time the vehicle gets there, and a PersistentCondition starts counting from that distance. The last vertex of an open path is the exception: it is checked only on arrival, since departing it ends the run. Otherwise it is looked at every tick; within ARRIVAL_TOLERANCE_M (1 m) along the path the vehicle has reached the vertex and waits on the brake. The plan after it is stamped from the timeline above.
  • FOLLOW (walker): looked at early in the same way, walked onto the vertex, slowing as it gets close; within 0.3 m it has reached it and stands.
  • On a closed path FOLLOW finds where the entity is by projecting it near where it was, and that projection does not wrap from the end of the path to its start -- so in FOLLOW mode a closed path's conditions are reliable on the first lap only. POSITION has no such limit.

RoutingAction.held_vertex names the vertex (0-based) the entity waits at for a condition other than a time, or None.

Breaking change

TrajectoryVertex no longer takes time= (or a time as its second argument), and the editor's vertex rows no longer have a time column: write TrajectoryVertex(position, TrajectoryTimeCondition(t)), and in a document a trajectory_time waypoint condition on the vertex. The old forms raise an error that says so.

docs.title: In the Scenario Editor
docs.text:
Set Goal (category Vehicle / Motion) is a card like any other, for the ego, a vehicle or a pedestrian. Driven by is its mode (Driver, Follow, Position). Its route comes from one of five sources:

  • Goal lanelet, via lanelets (the default) -- a goal lanelet and s along it, and the lanelets to pass on the way: what an ego is sent to. It takes no waypoint conditions and no time reference.
  • Vertices (map frame) -- written in the card, one vertex per line: x, y[, yaw] (metres, radians; 81234.5, 50123.0 leaves the yaw to the path). The line above the text says how many vertices and how long. Their times are waypoint conditions (below). This is what a recording transcribes to, so a replayed road user's card can be edited like any other.
  • Along lanelets -- the lanelets picked on the map, followed along their centrelines at a lateral offset and timed at a constant speed.
  • Along the scenario's route -- route vertices, see Logical Scenarios from Routes.
  • Relative to an entity's lane -- lane-relative vertices, one per line: ds[, offset][, d_lane][, yaw] (metres, metres, lanes, radians; only ds is required, d_lane is a whole number), measured from the entity chosen in Relative to -- or, left empty, from the card's own actor. The document stores them as rows [ds, offset, d_lane, yaw] and the reference as an entity id, which the compiler turns into that entity's role name. Deleting the reference entity clears the field, so the card is then measured from its own actor.

Waypoint conditions -- what each vertex departs on, its time included -- are under the card's fields in the inspector: + waypoint condition takes a vertex number -- counted from 1: the Nth vertex of the list (map-frame or relative), blank and comment lines not counted -- and a condition type, and adds an ordinary condition tree there, drawn and edited exactly as a trigger is (click it for its fields, add children to an All / Any). A vertex's time is the type Trajectory time (trajectory_time, one field: time on the trajectory's clock), read "depart vertex N at". A second condition added to the same vertex is combined with the first in an All (a Trajectory time cannot be combined: it is only ever a vertex's whole condition). The vertex number of each can be changed in place, and the bin removes it; a recording's long list of times folds away. The card on the canvas says how many it has, and Speed where no time paces sets the action's speed. In the document they are a list on the action, each a vertex and a condition node:

actions:
- id: a_walker
  type: routing
  actor: walker1
  params:
    path_source: vertices
    mode: follow
    vertices: [[81200.0, 50100.0, null], [81205.0, 50100.0, null],
               [81205.0, 50110.0, null]]
    time_domain: relative
    speed_ms: 1.4
  advance_conditions:
  - vertex: 1
    condition: {type: trajectory_time, params: {time: 0.0}}
  - vertex: 2          # the second vertex
    condition:
      type: entity_distance
      params: {source: walker1, target: ego, rule: less_than, distance: 25.0}
  - vertex: 3
    condition: {type: trajectory_time, params: {time: 11.0}}

The compiler builds each condition with the same builders as a trigger, and the validator checks them as it checks a trigger, plus where they sit and the timing rules: a vertex the card has, one condition per vertex, every vertex departing on something once any has a time, times that do not decrease, a time reference only with times, a Trajectory time only as a vertex's whole condition, no condition waiting for its own action to leave the running state (the action runs for as long as the entity waits), and only for vertices written in the card -- a lanelet path's vertices are generated every 2 m, nothing anyone could count, so it takes none (its speed times it). A condition that names an entity or action you delete goes with it, as a trigger does. The own-action rule is deliberately conservative: any reference to the card's own action but "is running" is refused, even under a Not where it could not deadlock. A row with a time cell, as documents had before, is refused with a message that gives the trajectory_time condition to write instead.

The other fields are the action's: the time reference (from the action start, from the scenario start, or none -- the default), its scale and offset, the mode, how far along to start, and whether the entity is out of the world outside the trajectory's time. The validator checks what the fields only mean together: a time reference needs vertex times (or a speed, for lanelets), and keeping the entity out of the world needs the Position mode and a time reference. For relative vertices it checks the numbers, the timing and that the reference entity exists; whether the lanes they name exist is only known when the action starts.

An entity's Spawn out of the world option (non-ego entities) spawns it under the map with its physics off, for a card that brings it in at its first vertex: a road user a recording picks up late, placed where it first appears, could otherwise collide at spawn with whatever stood there when the run began.

docs.title: Replaying a recorded scene
docs.text:
A transcribed recording becomes an ordinary scenario document -- the one the editor edits and the declarative runtime runs -- with nothing beyond the parts above:

  • the ego spawns where the recording's ego started and is sent where it went;
  • every road user is an entity spawned on the lanelet it was first seen on, with one Set Goal card: map-frame vertices, each departed at its recorded time (a trajectory_time waypoint condition) on the scenario clock (time_domain: absolute, time_offset moving the recording's first frame to t = 0), in Position mode and hidden outside its trajectory;
  • a road user first seen after the start spawns out of the world (spawn.hidden) and appears at its first vertex.

Open it in the editor to add the conditions the test is about -- a road user can wait for the ego by replacing one of its vertex times with another waypoint condition.

Note

Transcribers written for the earlier format (a time column in the vertex rows) have to write trajectory_time waypoint conditions instead; a document with a time column is refused with a message saying so.

T4 scenes are transcribed this way by scenario-import-t4 of the separate scene_to_scenario_transpiler package, which depends on the framework, never the other way round.

Warning

Map-frame vertices are Autoware's map frame, so a document replaying a recording has to run on the map the scene was recorded on, loaded with the same projector.

docs.title: Trajectory Log
docs.text:
Every run writes {stem}.trajectory.jsonl next to its _result.json: the vehicles, pedestrians and traffic lights of the world, once per world.tick(), and what the run made of them -- the map it ran on, the ego's plan, its conditions tick by tick and its verdict -- one JSON object per line. TrajectoryRecorder (autoware_carla_scenario/trajectory_recorder.py) writes it, and the carla-hub run report replays it. The file holds everything needed to show the run again without CARLA, the ego's plan and the path it drove included: the autoware_carla_scenario_rerun package (the rerun extra; rerun.enabled=true runs it on each log as its run ends) makes a Rerun recording of it, which is how a run is seen (Seeing a run). scenario-t4scene writes it as a T4Scene, the scene exchange format of tier4/e2e-devkit (T4 Scene).

Its format is published as a JSON Schema of one line, the contract for readers in any language: schemas/trajectory.schema.json in the package and in the wheel (JSON Schema 2020-12, tuples as prefixItems). From Python, find it with importlib.resources.files("autoware_carla_scenario") / "schemas" / "trajectory.schema.json", which needs no CARLA client. Code that already imports the recorder can use trajectory_recorder.SCHEMA_PATH. trajectory_recorder.schema.json, next to the recorder, is the same schema in draft-07 (trajectory_recorder.DRAFT7_SCHEMA_PATH), for the generators that cannot read 2020-12 tuples.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text: The format has a version, schema_version in the world line: 2. Version 2 added the records map, warmup, actor_gone, markers, condition, action and result, and schema_version itself; a file of version 1 has no schema_version and none of those records, and still follows the schema. The records marked (2) in the table below that are not in that list (rear_axle, turn_indicators, plan, adversity, waypoint_arrival, collision, walker_fallen, spawn, despawn) came later within version 2: a reader of version 2 that does not know one skips it. So did the tick's optional angular_velocity field: a file written before it has none. Every change keeps the records there are: a new version adds records (and optional fields), so a reader that skips the types and ignores the fields it does not know reads any later file.

docs.title: Records
docs.text:
Each line is one of twenty records, told apart by type. A file starts with one world line and one map line, then one traffic_light line per light and one warmup line. After that come the ticks: each tick line is preceded by an actor line for every vehicle or walker appearing in it for the first time (an ego's followed by a rear_axle line) and an actor_gone line for every one that has gone since the last, and followed by a turn_indicators line when a vehicle's turn indicators changed on it, a markers line when the ego's plan changed on it (and a plan line after it, the plan timed), a condition line for each condition that changed and an action line for each action that moved on. A run that reached a verdict ends with result.

not for a prop) frame, t, label (the action's), entity (role), id (its actor's, or null) despawn (2) on the tick a DespawnAction removed an entity, or the run a walker that lay fallen 5 s frame, t, label (the action's), entity (role), id (its actor's, or null), reason (action/fallen) result (2) last, when the run reached a verdict passed, message, elapsed_seconds, conditions [{label, role, condition_type, satisfied, message}] (_result.json's, without the details)

Fixed-length arrays are tuples: the schema gives each position its meaning, and generated types keep them as tuples where the target language has them.

docs.title: Frames, units and time
docs.text:
• Positions and rotations are in CARLA's left-handed world frame (x east, y south, z up; see Coordinate frames). Positions are in metres, angles in degrees, and velocities are world-frame m/s (an angular velocity, world-frame deg/s, a pseudovector: into a right-handed frame its x and z flip, not its y). Every float is rounded to 3 decimals.
  • A walker's velocity is measured from where it stood the tick before: one walking on CARLA's walker controller reports 0. Every other actor's is the one CARLA reports.
  • t is simulated time since the scenario clock started, the time pass/fail conditions see. It is not wall time. Warm-up ticks are not recorded: the warmup line says how many there were, so a frame of the CARLA recording, which starts with them, is frame - warmup.start_frame.
  • Ticks are 20 Hz (FIXED_DELTA_SECONDS).
  • A plan line has two clocks: t, the tick it is written on, and planned_at_us, the driver's own (a policy's from its session's start, an Autoware ego's command stamps), which its points' dt count from. A plan is written on the tick it is made on, except one made before the first recorded tick (while the run waits for the ego to be ready), written on that tick: compare plans by planned_at_us, not by t.

To move a pose into the Lanelet2 / Autoware map frame from Python, build a CarlaWorldPose and call coordinate.transform.to_map_frame (see Coordinate transforms). In other languages, apply the same conversion with the map's MGRS offset (ox, oy) and elevation offset z_offset (MapManager.mgrs_offset and MapManager.z_offset):

x_map   =  x + ox
y_map   = -y + oy
z_map   =  z + z_offset
yaw_map = -radians(yaw)      (pitch negated likewise; roll unchanged)
vy_map  = -vy

A file of version 2 carries these offsets in its map line (mgrs_offset, z_offset), with the Lanelet2 and OpenDRIVE files the run read and their SHA-256, so a reader can load the very map the run was on.

docs.title: What a reader has to handle
docs.text:
• Light states are deltas. lights holds only the lights that changed since the last written tick (all of them in the first tick), and is absent when none changed. Carry each light's state forward. A turn_indicators line is a delta the same way, per vehicle.
  • Ticks can be missing. A tick without any vehicle or walker is not written, so frame and t can skip.
  • Entities brought in late are marked. An entity spawned hidden is in actors from the start, parked out of sight under the map; a spawn line says when a SpawnAction put it on its place, as a despawn line says when one was taken out.
  • Actors that go are marked. A vehicle or walker that is destroyed or despawned stops appearing in actors, and from version 2 an actor_gone line says so before the first tick it is missing from.
  • Markers, conditions and actions are deltas too. A markers line holds until the next one, and a plan line until the next plan line (markers that carry no plan clear the drawing, not the plan); a condition line until the next of the same role and index; an action line until the next of the same phase and index (startTransition and endTransition hold for one tick). The run stops checking conditions at the first that decides it, so the last tick may have no line for the ones after it.
  • Episode ids are 64-bit. episode is a random uint64, so it is often past 2^53: read it as an unsigned 64-bit integer (it only tells episodes apart).
  • Map keys are strings. control and lights are keyed by actor id as a decimal string ("1"), a JSON object key.
  • Integers are plain JSON numbers. Nothing is quoted: unlike the protobuf JSON mapping, which writes 64-bit integers as strings, the file and its schema keep them numbers. The schema caps frame (uint64 in LibCarla) at 2^53 - 1 and actor ids (uint32) at 2^32 - 1; episode, a random uint64, is capped at 2^64 - 1 (see above). Any reader, including JavaScript's double-only JSON.parse, holds them exactly; a value past the cap fails validation rather than silently losing precision.
  • Only egos have controls. control carries actors whose role is ego or hero (any case). steer is normalised to [-1, 1]; it is not a wheel angle.

docs.title: Reading it from another language
docs.text:
Generate types from the schema with the generator for your language:

Language Generator Notes TypeScript json-schema-to-typescript A discriminated union on type, with tuple types Python datamodel-code-generator Pydantic models; tuples become length-checked lists Rust typify Reads 2020-12; an enum on type (the schema's discriminator), tuples as tuples C++, Go, Rust, C#, ... quicktype Reads the draft-07 copy; merges the records into one type with optional fields; tuples become arrays 
npx json-schema-to-typescript -i schemas/trajectory.schema.json -o trajectory.d.ts
uvx --from datamodel-code-generator datamodel-codegen \
  --input schemas/trajectory.schema.json --input-file-type jsonschema \
  --output-model-type pydantic_v2.BaseModel --output trajectory_log.py

Any JSON Schema 2020-12 validator checks a file line by line, for example jsonschema in Python:

import json
import jsonschema
from importlib.resources import files

schema = files("autoware_carla_scenario") / "schemas" / "trajectory.schema.json"
validator = jsonschema.Draft202012Validator(json.loads(schema.read_text()))
with open("CutInScenario.trajectory.jsonl") as f:
    for line in f:
        validator.validate(json.loads(line))

The top level is a oneOf of the records, each fixing type with a const, and names the field in an OpenAPI-style discriminator (propertyName: type, with the mapping from each type to its record), which validators ignore and generators that know it use for a tagged union. x-schema-version is the format version the schema describes. The draft-07 copy says the same with definitions and items arrays.

docs.title: Changing the format
docs.text:
A change to a record in trajectory_recorder.py needs the same change in schemas/trajectory.schema.json, and the draft-07 copy written again from it:

uv run python autoware_carla_scenario/scripts/trajectory_schema_draft7.py

The recorder's tests check every line they record against both schemas, which forbid fields they do not list (additionalProperties: false), and that the copy is the one the script writes, so they fail until both have the change. A change that a reader of the last version could not skip over is a new schema_version (SCHEMA_VERSION, and x-schema-version in the schema).

docs.title: Tutorial: Writing Your First Scenario
docs.text:
This tutorial shows two paths to creating a scenario:

  1. Quick Start (recommended) — Use the bundled Claude Code plugin. Describe what you want in plain text and let Claude generate all files.
  2. Manual walkthrough — Understand every file by building one yourself.

docs.title: Quick Start with Claude Code Plugin
docs.text: This repository ships a write-scenario plugin inside .claude/local-marketplace/. It is pre-enabled in .claude/settings.json — no extra setup is needed. Just open Claude Code in the repository root and the plugin is ready to use.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Type /write-scenario followed by a natural-language description of the test you want. Claude walks you through a 7-stage workflow automatically:

Stage What Claude does 1. Understand Parses your description, asks clarifying questions 2. Discover Scans the codebase for available Conditions, Actions, Constraints, and Bindings 3. Write Generates all four files: Python class, config dataclass, YAML, and run.py registration 4. Debug Runs the scenario in CARLA, reads logs, fixes failures iteratively 5. Review Analyzes parameter orthogonality and sweeper compatibility 6. Sweep Adds sweep.constraints / bindings to the YAML for parametric testing 7. Multirun Provides the exact command to execute the logical scenario across the map

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
> /write-scenario I want to test that the ego stops at a stop sign,
  waits 3 seconds, then proceeds through the intersection.

Claude will:

  1. Identify StandstillCondition and TimeoutCondition from the codebase
  2. Generate my_scenario.py, update configs.py, create YAML, register in run.py
  3. Run the scenario, analyze the result, and iterate until it passes
  4. Propose sweep constraints so the test generalizes to every stop sign on the map

You do not need to memorize the framework API — the plugin discovers everything dynamically.

docs.title: Other Plugin Commands
docs.text:
Command When to use /write-scenario Create a new scenario from scratch /debug-concrete-scenario An existing scenario fails — analyze logs and fix /review-scenario Before adding sweep — check parameter design

The rest of this page explains the manual process. Read on if you want to understand what the plugin generates under the hood.

docs.title: Key Concepts
docs.text:
Term What it is File type Abstract scenario Reusable Python class that defines what to test (conditions, actions, entities). *.py Config dataclass Typed parameters the scenario accepts (timeout, speed, lanelet IDs, ...). *.py Concrete scenario YAML file that binds an abstract scenario to specific parameter values. *.yaml

One abstract scenario can have many concrete variants (straight, left turn, right turn, etc.).

docs.title: Step 1 — Create the Config Dataclass
docs.text:
Add your config to src/autoware_carla_scenario/examples/configs.py:

@dataclass
class MyScenarioConfig:
    """Parameters for my custom scenario."""

    name: str = "my_scenario"

    #: Lanelet IDs the ego should visit.
    expected_lanelet_ids: list[int] = field(default_factory=lambda: [460])

    #: Fail-safe timeout in seconds.
    timeout_seconds: float = 10.0

Every field becomes overridable from the YAML side via Hydra.

docs.title: Step 2 — Create the Abstract Scenario
docs.text:
Create src/autoware_carla_scenario/examples/my_scenario.py:

from __future__ import annotations

from autoware_carla_scenario import (
    EGO_ROLE_NAME,
    AndCondition,
    BaseScenario,
    EgoConfig,
    EntityLanePositionCondition,
    GroundProjectionConfig,
    Lanelet2Pose,
    StickyCondition,
    TimeoutCondition,
)

from .configs import MyScenarioConfig


class MyScenario(BaseScenario):
    """Verify the ego visits every expected road."""

    def __init__(
        self,
        ego_config: EgoConfig,
        spawn_pose: Lanelet2Pose,
        config: MyScenarioConfig | None = None,
        ground_projection: GroundProjectionConfig | None = None,
    ) -> None:
        super().__init__(
            ego_config, spawn_pose=spawn_pose,
            ground_projection=ground_projection,
        )
        self._config = config or MyScenarioConfig()

    def setup(self) -> None:
        # 1. Snap ego spawn to CARLA road surface
        self._setup_ego_spawn()

        cfg = self._config

        # 2. Build pass condition — "ego visited all expected roads"
        stickies = []
        for ll_id in cfg.expected_lanelet_ids:
            stickies.append(
                StickyCondition(
                    EntityLanePositionCondition(
                        EGO_ROLE_NAME,
                        Lanelet2Pose(lanelet_id=ll_id, s=0.0),
                        label=f"ego_on_lanelet_{ll_id}",
                    )
                )
            )
        self.register_pass_condition(AndCondition(stickies))

        # 3. Fail-safe timeout
        self.register_fail_condition(
            TimeoutCondition(cfg.timeout_seconds, label="timeout")
        )

    def is_done(self) -> bool:
        return False

docs.title: Anatomy of setup()
docs.text:
Every scenario follows the same structure:

  1. Spawn — call self._setup_ego_spawn() (snaps the Lanelet2 pose to the CARLA road surface).
  2. Pass conditions — register one or more conditions via self.register_pass_condition(). The scenario passes as soon as any pass condition fires (returns a result), not when all of them have. To require several things, combine them in one AndCondition, wrapping each state that only has to be visited once in a StickyCondition, as the example above does.
  3. Fail conditions — register via self.register_fail_condition(). If any fail condition fires, the scenario fails. On each tick the pass conditions are checked before the fail conditions, so a pass and a fail on the same tick ends the run as a pass.
  4. Actions (optional) — e.g. TurnAction, TrafficSignalAction.

Discovering available Conditions and Actions

Run grep -r "class.*Condition" src/autoware_carla_scenario/conditions/ and grep -r "class.*Action" src/autoware_carla_scenario/actions/ to see everything the framework provides.

docs.title: Step 3 — Register the Scenario
docs.text:
In src/autoware_carla_scenario/examples/run.py, add the import and registration:

from .my_scenario import MyScenario
from .configs import MyScenarioConfig

register_scenario("my_scenario", MyScenario, MyScenarioConfig)

The first argument ("my_scenario") is the name referenced in YAML's scenario.name field.

Prefer a separate package for reusable scenarios

register_scenario (and register_conf_dir) are part of the public API: from autoware_carla_scenario import register_scenario. If your scenario is not meant to ship inside the framework, put it in its own package instead of editing run.py — see Packaging Scenarios in a Separate Package.

docs.title: Step 4 — Write a Concrete Scenario (YAML)
docs.text:
Create src/autoware_carla_scenario/examples/conf/scenario/my_scenario/default.yaml:

# @package _global_
scenario:
  name: my_scenario
  expected_lanelet_ids: [460, 265]
  timeout_seconds: 8.0

ego:
  initial_speed_kmh: 5.0
  spawn_lanelet_id: 242
  spawn_s: 25.0

# @package _global_

This Hydra directive is required on the first line. It tells Hydra to merge the file into the root config, not into a nested key.

docs.title: Minimal checklist
docs.text:
• [x] scenario.name matches the registered name ("my_scenario")
  • [x] ego.spawn_lanelet_id is a valid lanelet ID in the target map
  • [x] ego.spawn_s is within the lanelet length

docs.title: Step 5 — Run It
docs.text:
# Single run
uv run scenario scenario=my_scenario/default

# Batch — run all variants under my_scenario/
uv run scenario scenario='my_scenario/*'

# Override a parameter on the fly
uv run scenario scenario=my_scenario/default scenario.timeout_seconds=20.0

docs.title: Step 6 — Check Results in the Viewer
docs.text:
# Start the viewer (defaults to port 9000)
uv run viewer

# Or scan another project: the directory containing outputs/ and multirun/
uv run viewer --base-path /path/to/project

Open http://localhost:9000 in your browser. The viewer has three levels of navigation:

docs.title: 1. Session list
docs.text:
The top page lists every test session with its timestamp, run type (multirun / single), scenario name, and overall result.

Each row is color-coded: green for all-passed, red if any scenario failed. Click a session to drill down.

docs.title: 2. Session detail
docs.text:
Inside a session you see every concrete scenario that was executed. For multirun (sweep) sessions, this can be hundreds of rows — each with its parameter overrides, individual PASS/FAIL badge, and execution time.

The progress bar and counter at the top (e.g. 127/127 All passed) give an at-a-glance summary. Use the PASS / FAIL / N/A filter buttons to narrow the list.

docs.title: 3. Concrete scenario detail
docs.text:
Click any row to open the detail view for a single concrete scenario. Here you can see:

  • Pass/Fail status and elapsed time
  • Condition tree — the evaluated condition expression showing exactly which sub-conditions were met
  • Trajectory log — the path of the run's trajectory.jsonl, which the autoware_carla_scenario_rerun package (convert) turns into a Rerun recording to watch the run in the Rerun viewer (Seeing a run); the screenshot below predates 15.0.0, when this was a video

The Re-run button in the top-right corner lets you re-execute the same scenario directly from the viewer.

docs.title: 4. Running scenarios from the viewer
docs.text:
You can also launch scenario runs directly from the browser without using the CLI. Click the Run Scenarios dropdown in the top-right corner to open the run form.

The form lets you configure:

  • Scenario — a glob pattern to select which scenarios to run (e.g. */* for all scenarios)
  • Extra Overrides — Hydra overrides applied to every scenario in the run (one key=value per line, e.g. server.host=192.168.1.100)
  • Sweeper — select lanelet_constraint to run a multirun sweep across matching lanelets

Click Start to begin execution. The generated command is shown at the bottom of the form for reference. Results appear in the session list below once the run completes — click Update to refresh.

docs.title: Additional notes
docs.text: • The viewer scans outputs/ (single/batch runs) and multirun/ (sweep runs) for *_result.json files. Click Update if you ran a scenario while the viewer was open.

docs.title: Adding Sweep (Parametric Testing)
docs.text:
To test the same scenario across many lanelets automatically, add a sweep section to the YAML:

# @package _global_
scenario:
  name: my_scenario
  expected_lanelet_ids: [460, 265]
  timeout_seconds: 8.0

ego:
  initial_speed_kmh: 5.0
  spawn_lanelet_id: 242
  spawn_s: 25.0

sweep:
  constraints:
    ego.spawn_lanelet_id:
      - type: and
        constraints:
          - type: lanelet_length
            rule: greater_than_or_equal
            value: 10.0
          - type: not
            constraint:
              type: is_junction

Run as a multirun:

uv run scenario --multirun scenario=my_scenario/default \
  hydra/sweeper=lanelet_constraint

The sweeper evaluates constraints against the Lanelet2 map and generates one job per matching lanelet. Results appear under multirun/ in the viewer.

docs.title: Packaging Scenarios in a Separate Package
docs.text:
The manual walkthrough above adds scenarios inside autoware_carla_scenario (examples/configs.py, examples/my_scenario.py, examples/run.py, conf/scenario/...). That is fine for scenarios shipped with the framework, but for your own scenarios it is often better to keep them — and their config dataclasses — in a separate, installable package that depends on the framework. This keeps your scenarios reusable and versioned independently, with no fork of autoware_carla_scenario.

A ready-to-copy template lives at examples/scenario_package_template/.

docs.title: Quickest path — generate one with scenario-new
docs.text:
Instead of copying the template by hand, generate a fresh package (the files below are rendered from Jinja2 templates):

# scenario-new <package-name> [--scenario NAME] [--output-dir DIR]
scenario-new reach_goal_pkg --scenario reach_goal

This writes a ready-to-install package:

reach_goal_pkg/
├── pyproject.toml                     # name + entry point filled in
└── src/reach_goal_pkg/
    ├── __init__.py                    # register() wired up
    ├── reach_goal.py                  # ReachGoalScenario
    ├── configs.py                     # ReachGoalConfig
    └── conf/scenario/reach_goal/default.yaml

The scenario module sits beside __init__.py, configs.py and conf/, and importing it binds its name in __init__.py, so configs, conf and the names __init__.py defines (register, register_scenario, register_conf_dir) cannot be scenario names; scenario-new refuses them (including when they come from the package name, as in configs_package).

uv pip install -e reach_goal_pkg
uv run scenario scenario=reach_goal/default map=nishishinjuku

# Static check, before CARLA starts: only this package's scenarios.
uv run scenario-check scenario='reach_goal/*'

scenario-check compiles the scenario with Codon and reports a type error, a misspelled config key or a bad value at its line; see Static check. The generated package has a tests/test_typecheck.py that runs it under pytest.

The same generator is available programmatically:

from autoware_carla_scenario.scaffold import create_scenario_package

create_scenario_package("reach_goal_pkg", scenario_name="reach_goal",
                        output_dir="~/pkgs")

The rest of this section explains what the generated files contain.

docs.title: What a scenario package needs
docs.text: Piece Where API used Scenario class your package *.py subclass BaseScenario Config dataclass your package configs.py plain @dataclass Concrete YAML your package conf/scenario/<name>/*.yaml Hydra Registration your package __init__.py register_scenario, register_conf_dir Discovery your pyproject.toml autoware_carla_scenario.scenarios entry point

docs.title: Register at import time
docs.text:
Everything you need is part of the framework's public API — import it from the top-level package, not from examples:

# my_scenario_package/__init__.py
from pathlib import Path

from autoware_carla_scenario import register_conf_dir, register_scenario

from .configs import MyScenarioConfig
from .my_scenario import MyScenario


def register() -> None:
    register_scenario("my_scenario", MyScenario, MyScenarioConfig)
    register_conf_dir(Path(__file__).parent / "conf")

Shared parameters (ego, map, server, entity, ...) are also public, so your config module reuses them instead of redefining them:

from autoware_carla_scenario import EgoVehicleConfig, MapConfig, ServerConfig

docs.title: Advertise the entry point
docs.text:
In your package's pyproject.toml, declare the entry point so the scenario CLI discovers your register() automatically when the package is installed:

[project.entry-points."autoware_carla_scenario.scenarios"]
my_scenario_package = "my_scenario_package:register"

docs.title: Run it — no framework edits required
docs.text:
uv pip install -e path/to/my_scenario_package

# Your scenario is discoverable by name, exactly like a built-in:
uv run scenario scenario=my_scenario/default map=nishishinjuku
uv run scenario scenario='my_scenario/*' map=nishishinjuku

At start-up the runner calls load_scenario_plugins(), which loads every installed autoware_carla_scenario.scenarios entry point (registering your scenarios and conf/ directory). A bundled Hydra SearchPathPlugin then adds every registered conf/ directory to Hydra's search path. The map, ego, server, and entity config groups still come from the framework's built-in conf/, so your package only ships the scenario/ group it actually owns. The result viewer (uv run viewer) loads the packages the same way: its Run panel lists your scenarios, matches them in globs such as my_scenario/*, and expands their sweeps.

No entry point? Register explicitly.

If you prefer not to rely on entry-point discovery (e.g. from a custom runner script), just call your register() — or register_scenario / register_conf_dir directly — before invoking the runner. The entry point is only what lets the stock scenario CLI find you automatically.

docs.title: Static Check (Codon)
docs.text:
Before a scenario runs, the runner compiles it with Codon, a statically typed compiler for Python syntax, and refuses it when it does not compile. A misspelled method, a str where a float belongs, a condition missing its label, a turn direction passed where a lane-change direction is expected, or a YAML value of the wrong type is reported with the file and line it is on, before CARLA is started:

$ uv run scenario scenario=intersection_passing/straight scenario.timeout_seconds=fast
autoware_carla_scenario.examples.intersection_passing.IntersectionPassingScenario: static check failed:
  scenario.timeout_seconds: error: 'str' does not match expected type 'float'

The scenario still runs as Python, exactly as before: the check compiles the same source, never runs what it compiled, and changes nothing at run time. The CARLA API a scenario calls is typesafe_carla, the statically typed CARLA client this framework runs on. A scenario imports it as import typesafe_carla.carla as carla: at run time that is typesafe_carla's CPython package, and for the check it is typesafe_carla's Codon library, so the same names are checked that run.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
The runner checks every scenario registered with register_scenario() when it builds it, so a run, a batch (scenario='lane_change/*') and every job of a sweep are checked before anything starts. To check without running anything:

uv run scenario-check                                   # every scenario config
uv run scenario-check scenario=intersection_passing/straight
uv run scenario-check scenario='lane_change/*' scenario.timeout_seconds=20

scenario-check composes each config exactly as the runner does, so the same overrides apply. scenario='*' is every config, like no scenario=; a package author checks only theirs (scenario='my_package/*', about 15 s per config), as every built-in config takes minutes. It exits with 0 when every scenario passed, 1 when one failed, and 2 when it could not run: there is no Codon compiler, no config matches scenario= (the message lists the configs), or an override names a key the config does not have (scenario.timout_seconds=3 is reported with the closest key, scenario.timeout_seconds; +key=value adds a new one; HYDRA_FULL_ERROR=1 shows the traceback). A scenario package can make the same check in its own tests, with no simulator (the template and scenario-new packages have one in tests/test_typecheck.py):

from autoware_carla_scenario.typecheck import typecheck_scenario

def test_my_scenario_compiles() -> None:
    result = typecheck_scenario(MyScenario, MyScenarioConfig, {"timeout_seconds": 10.0})
    assert result.ok, result.format()

docs.title: When it runs: the typecheck key
docs.text:
Value Effect auto (default) Check when a Codon compiler is installed; warn and run unchecked when none is. required Refuse to run without a Codon compiler. off Do not check.

Set it like any other key (uv run scenario ... typecheck=required) or with AUTOWARE_CARLA_SCENARIO_TYPECHECK, which takes precedence. A scenario registered with register_scenario_builder() (a custom builder, such as the packages the Scenario Editor exports) is not checked: only its builder knows how it is constructed.

docs.title: Keeping verdicts between runs
docs.text:
A process compiles a program once and keeps the verdict for as long as it runs. The program is keyed by its shape: the driver with each config value replaced by its type (a bool, a float, an int, a string, an enum's class), since Codon types it statically and reads no value at compile time. The cases of a sweep that differ only in their values are therefore one program, compiled for the first case and reused, verdict and diagnostics, for the others (logged as "reusing the static check made for the config with the same types"); a failure refuses each of them. scenario-check checks configs side by side, and one whose program is being compiled when it starts waits for that compile rather than starting its own. What changes the shape compiles again: another key or order of keys, a value of another type (an int where the first case had a float in a field not typed float, None where it had a value), another length of a list, a mapping the config converts in one case and not in another. A value whose literal Codon could refuse on its own (an int beyond 64 bits, a string with an escape) is kept as it is.

Verdicts are kept beyond the process, one file per program, in $XDG_CACHE_HOME/autoware_carla_scenario/typecheck (~/.cache/... without an absolute XDG_CACHE_HOME): a later process with the same inputs reads the verdict instead of compiling. Set AUTOWARE_CARLA_SCENARIO_TYPECHECK_CACHE to use another directory, or to an empty string to keep each verdict for its process only (as happens anyway without a home directory, or with one that cannot be written). A verdict read back is the program's, and is reported for the check that read it (#652): a scenario check's line names that scenario, and a library check's names the modules this run was given and says cached, with the time this run took rather than the compile's. A Codon crash is kept for its process only. A compile that timed out, or a Codon killed with SIGKILL (the out-of-memory killer), is no verdict and is kept nowhere: the next check of the same program, such as the next case of a sweep, compiles it again (#694). Nothing prunes the directory; delete it, or its files not accessed for a while, to reclaim the space. The key covers everything the verdict depends on. For the compile, that is the scenario's (or the framework's) modules, the generated driver's shape, the model, typesafe_carla's Codon library, and the compiler's version and standard library. For the None check, which the scenario, ODD and library checks all run, it is every Python source and stub of the framework, the checker included (mypy reads them for the types of what a scenario calls, and the CARLA stubs are written by its carla_stubs.py from typesafe_carla's Codon library, already in the key), the name and version of every other installed distribution (mypy follows a scenario's imports into numpy, lanelet2 or typesafe_carla), the mypy version, and the Python version. Where a version says nothing of what mypy reads, the files are in it by path, size and modification time: the .py, .pyi and py.typed files of each distribution installed editable and of each directory on MYPYPATH and PYTHONPATH, which mypy searches (a relative entry is taken from the directory the check runs in; symlinked directories are followed). Of the packages being checked, whose modules the key has by their text already, only their stubs count there, so an edit to one scenario of an editable or PYTHONPATH package does not stale the verdicts on the others. And it includes what the checks made in Python found before the compile: an import the framework's Python lacks, or an abstract class that is built. These digests are taken once a process (about 100 ms, more with a large PYTHONPATH such as a ROS workspace's). mypy runs with --config-file= and in an empty directory of its own, so neither a configuration file nor a module of the directory the check runs from reaches the verdict. A scenario package is therefore found as an installed or editable distribution, or through MYPYPATH: give a namespace package (one without __init__.py) an __init__.py, as the scaffolded packages have. What the key still leaves out: a distribution installed in development mode without PEP 610's direct_url.json (an old setup.py develop, a .pth file written by hand); clear the directory after editing one. A crash is never kept, and an entry that cannot be read counts as a miss. A verdict read from the directory has its file's times touched, so the directory can be pruned by access time.

The test suite shares such a directory between its xdist workers. CI keeps one from run to run, so a run compiles only the programs whose inputs changed.

docs.title: Builds wait for their memory
docs.text:
Codon's peak memory grows with what it compiles: about 1.9 GB for a scenario or a module of the framework, about 9.3 GB for the whole library check (2.8 million characters of source). Builds started side by side -- the xdist workers of the test suite, the checker's own pool of four -- would otherwise together outgrow a 16 GB machine, and the out-of-memory killer would take a build (a SIGKILL, above) or, on a CI runner, the runner itself ("The runner has received a shutdown signal").

So each build first waits for its share (typecheck/memory_gate.py). The builds of a machine record what they hold in one directory ($TMPDIR/acs-codon-gate-<uid>), and one is started when what the running builds hold plus its own estimate fits the machine's memory (or its cgroup's limit) less 1.5 GB, or when none is running: a build too large for the machine still runs, alone. The holds of a process that died are forgotten. Set AUTOWARE_CARLA_SCENARIO_CODON_GATE to another directory to share it differently, or to 0 to start every build at once.

docs.title: Installing Codon and typesafe_carla
docs.text:
The check needs typesafe_carla (the typesafe-carla package, from PyPI) and the Codon compiler it pins (typesafe-carla-toolchain, 0.19, which typesafe-carla depends on). Both ship for Linux x86_64 and aarch64, and both are run-time dependencies of the framework anyway: typesafe_carla is its CARLA client (see installation).

The checker finds Codon the way typesafe_carla's typesafe-codon launcher does (it calls typesafe_carla's own lookup), so one setup serves both: $TYPESAFE_CODON (a codon executable), the typesafe-carla-toolchain package, $CODON_DIR/bin/codon, ~/.codon/bin/codon, then codon on PATH. It runs it with the launcher's environment (CODON_DIR, and LD_LIBRARY_PATH for the bundled runtime). The check is written for Codon 0.19: a Codon of another release series counts as no Codon at all, so auto warns and required refuses. So does a missing typesafe-carla.

docs.title: What is checked
docs.text:
The checker copies the scenario's own modules (the module defining the scenario class, its config class, and every module of the same package they import) into a scratch directory, next to a typed model of the framework, and compiles a small program that does what the runner does:

config = MyScenarioConfig()          # then one line per YAML value:
config.timeout_seconds = 10.0        #   scenario.timeout_seconds
scenario = MyScenario(ego, config=config, spawn_pose=..., ground_projection=...)
scenario.setup()
scenario.is_done()

A value for a bool, int, float or str field, at the top level as in a nested dataclass, is first passed to a function that takes that type only, on a line of its own (#598): Codon converts any value with __bool__ that is assigned to a bool field, so scenario.enabled=no (which Hydra, like a quoted "false" in YAML, reads as the str "no") would otherwise pass, and the feature would be on. It is refused at scenario.enabled, whether the field has a default or not. An int for a float field still passes.

Codon checks a function only when something calls it. The program checks everything setup() and is_done() reach: the calls into the framework, the scenario's own helpers, and, through register_pass_condition() and the other register_* methods, the check() of a custom condition and the execute() of a custom action.

Then it compiles the rest of the scenario's own modules too (#192). Each module the checker copies gets the library check's function appended (What is compiled), and the program calls it after the lines above:

def _acs_library_check():                      # appended to my_scenario.py
    MyScenario(_acs_value(EgoConfig), _acs_value(Lanelet2Pose), ...)
    _acs_value(MyScenario)._goal_ids(_acs_value(int))    # a helper setup() never calls
    _acs_value(MyScenario).initial_speeds_mps(_acs_value(Optional[carla.Actor]))
    unused_probe(_acs_value(carla.World))                # a module-level function
    _acs_cls_default_9: int = "three"                    # MyScenario.RETRIES: int = "three"

So an error is reported wherever it is in those modules, not only on the path setup() takes: in a private helper or a public method nothing calls yet, in a hook override the runner calls later (initial_speeds_mps()), in a module-level function, in a class-level default, or in the config class's methods. Each call passes a value of each parameter's annotated type, and a defaulted parameter's default is compiled by one more call that leaves it out.

The result of a hook override is checked against the framework's type (#238). Codon compiles an override against its own annotation only, and the framework code that calls it is a stub of the model, so check() -> bool, initial_speeds_mps() -> list[float] or is_done() -> str compiled, and failed or misbehaved when the scenario ran. So each appended call of a method passes its result to the model, which checks it strictly against the return type of the method it overrides, when the class derives from BaseScenario, BaseCondition, BaseAction or EgoVehicle (directly, or through a built-in condition or another class of the scenario's modules):

    _acs_hook_return(MyScenario, "is_done", _acs_value(MyScenario).is_done())
    _acs_hook_return(GapCondition, "check",
                     _acs_value(GapCondition).check(_acs_value(carla.World), _acs_value(float)))

Every method and property each of the four classes declares is such a hook, with the return type the model declares for it (test_typecheck_model.py keeps the two in step): setup() returns None, is_done() a bool, initial_speeds_mps() a Dict[int, float], check() an Optional[ScenarioResult], execute() None, debug_markers() a DebugMarkers, and so on. The check is strict where an annotated assignment is not (Codon 0.19 converts any value with __bool__ in done: bool = x): an override must return the type itself or what Python's typing takes for it -- a subclass of a class, an int for a float, a bool for an int, and, for an Optional[X], an X, an Optional of one, or only None (a condition that never decides). A str, an int or an Optional[bool] for a bool is refused, at the override's def line:

scenario.py:62: error: BaseScenario.is_done() returns bool, and this override returns another type
    reached by <scenario check: MyScenario.is_done()>
    during the realization of _acs_expect_return(r: str, T: bool, ...) [scenario_base.codon:230]

A method of a class deriving from none of them, or one its base does not declare (a helper of the scenario), is not checked this way, and neither is an abstract one (@abstractmethod) or one that only raises (raise NotImplementedError()): it returns no value, which Codon types None whatever its annotation says. The program also checks what the scenario's own setup() and is_done() return, after the module checks, for one the appended calls leave out.

A wrong call or return is reported in the author's terms (#527, #528,

docs.title: 529, #530). Codon says `no function 'SetSpeedAction.init' with arguments
docs.text:
(SetSpeedAction, EntityRole, str, str)for a call it cannot match, and'float' does not match expected type 'str'(the two types swapped) for areturnof the wrong type. The check reads the call or thereturn` in your file, binds it to the real Python signature of the class, method or function, and says what is wrong, at the argument:

scenario.py:28:62: error: SetSpeedAction(): target_speed_kmh: expected float, got str
scenario.py:28:60: error: TimeoutCondition(): 'lable' is an invalid keyword argument (did you mean 'label'?); TimeoutCondition takes (timeout_seconds: float = 60.0, *, label: str)
scenario.py:36:9: error: val() returns str, but the function is declared -> float

A message that cannot be tied to a parameter is X() takes (...); got (EntityRole, str, label=str), with self dropped and a keyword argument marked. A static string type prints as 'str' (not ''3''), the frames of the model's own helpers (_keyword_only, _required_str, actions.codon) are left out of the trace, and a literal None given where a type is expected is told that the parameter does not take None rather than to test the value.

Some common slips get a hint after Codon's message (#599), each only where both the message and your source at the line say it is that slip:

You write Codon says The hint range(len(ids) / 2) range() cannot be called with (float) range() takes ints, and / always gives a float: divide with //, or convert with int() ids[len(ids) / 2] __getitem__() cannot be called with (float) an index must be an int: divide with // ",".join(ids) of a list[int] 'Generator[int]' does not match expected type 'Generator[str]' ",".join(map(str, ids)) or ",".join(str(v) for v in ids) self.register_pre_tick(lambda: None) (also register_post_tick, register_init, a register_measure read function, a register_cover expression, or a def of no parameter) a lambda() takes 0 arguments (1 given) the callback is called with the world: lambda world: ... self.register_measure("flag", lambda w: True) expected a float (or an int) names the measure and what its read function returns (a bool is no number to a measure: 1.0 if ... else 0.0, or a cover)

A range() or index of a float without a / written there, and a join of something that is not a call of join at that column, get none.

Two declared return types Codon does not enforce are refused from the syntax, before Codon runs (#529): a return of a literal, an f-string or a display in a function declared -> bool (Codon converts it to a bool; Python returns the str), and a function declared to return a type other than None, Optional[...], Any or NoReturn whose body can run off its end. The flow analysis follows if, while, for, try, with and match; a while True without a break, a raise, assert False, sys.exit() and a call of a function declared NoReturn end a path, and a body that is only ..., pass or a docstring (an abstract method, an overload) is not checked. A returned expression whose type is not obvious from its syntax (return some_str) is not judged.

Then mypy checks that an Optional is tested for None before it is used (#239). Codon unwraps an Optional[T] implicitly wherever a T is needed, so cfg.min_speed_kmh / 3.6 of a float | None field compiled, and raised TypeError in Python when the field was None.
