Codon 0.19 has no ascii() ("name 'ascii' is not defined"); repr gives the same str type, and only the checked copy changes, so the escaping of non-ASCII characters is unchanged at run time zip(a, b, strict=True) zip(a, b): the check types the loop, it does not run it s.startswith((a, b)), s.endswith((a, b), start) with the tuple written in the call (#439) (s.startswith(a) or s.startswith(b)); a receiver or item that is not a name, attribute or constant is bound once by a lambda the tuple is held in a name (s.startswith(PREFIXES)), is empty, or the call has *args / keywords; each item is still checked as a str format(x, spec), format(x) (#439) x.__format__(spec), str(x) format is bound where the call is: by the module (an assignment, import, def or class at module level) or by an enclosing function or lambda (a parameter or local); a method named format or a class attribute binds nothing there, so it does not disable the rewrite (#471) ascii(x) (#439) repr(x): the same str type; the check does not run it, so the escaping of non-ASCII characters is unchanged at run time ascii is bound where the call is, as for format (#471) getattr(x, "name", default) with a literal name, x a name or an attribute chain, the default on one line (#590) ((default), x.name if hasattr(x, "name") else (default))[1]: Codon's getattr takes no default, and Codon decides hasattr when it compiles, so only the branch x's type takes is compiled, typed as that branch (the attribute's type where the class declares it, the default's where it does not). The first item keeps the default compiled either way, as Python evaluates it either way (getattr(x, "name", x.typo) is refused). hasattr on an Optional is decided on the Optional (see "Making a module compile"), so the default's branch is the one compiled there. Inside an f-string field the name is quoted with the quote the f-string does not use (f'{getattr(o, "a", 1)}' gives hasattr(o, "a")), as is every string a rewrite writes into a field (#609): Codon's parser ends the f-string at its own quote a name built at run time, another receiver (a call, a subscript), a default over several lines or hasattr bound where the call is: refused with getattr() takes 2 arguments (3 given) and a hint to write the hasattr test t.count(x), t.index(x[, start[, stop]]) with t a name or an attribute chain (#601) (t.count(x) if hasattr(t, "count") else _acs_count(t, x)): Codon's tuple has no count / index and cannot be extended, and only Codon knows t's type, so a list, a str or a class of yours keeps its own call, compiled as written, and only a tuple goes to the helper (an item of another type than x never equals it). A tuple display, (1, 2).index(2), goes to the helper directly. A tuple narrowed from an Optional (t.count(1) if t is not None else 0) is still Optional to Codon: the helper unwraps it (#609). Where Codon crashes with no diagnostic in a module that has these rewrites (an earlier error left the helper a wrong type, as lst = [None, a] then lst.index(a)), the module is compiled once more without them, and that compile's error is reported; a rerun that passes, crashes too or refuses a tuple's count / index (the crash had another cause) leaves the crash reported the receiver is a module (itertools.count), a builtin type (str.index(s, "a")), a call or a subscript (f().count(x), rows[0].index(x): bind it to a name), or the call spans lines; then a tuple's is refused ('Tuple[int,int]' object has no attribute 'count') d.keys() & e.keys(), \|, -, ^; d.items() <= e.items(), <, >, >=, ==, != (#601) set(d.keys()) & set(e.keys()), the other operand of &, \|, -, ^ a set too (a view takes any iterable there, and gives a set); a comparison makes a set of each view and leaves the other side as it is (a view orders only against a set) the view is held in a name (k = d.keys(), then k & e): write set(d) & set(e) super(Derived, self).__init__(k) in a method of Derived whose first parameter is self (#601) super().__init__(k): Codon's super takes no arguments another class (super(Base, self), which skips Derived's bases up to Base), a @classmethod / @staticmethod, the class or self rebound in the method, or the call inside a nested function, lambda or comprehension: Codon's super() takes 0 arguments (2 given) round(x), round(x, None), round(number=x, ndigits=None) (#585) int(round(x)): Codon's round(x, n=0) always returns a float, Python's an int when ndigits is left out or None, so xs[round(x)], n: int = round(x) and range(round(x)) check. round(x, ndigits=2) is round(x, 2) (Codon's has no Python keywords). round(x, 2) stays a float, also for an int x (Python returns an int there). Being an int, round(x) is refused inside a list[float] or dict[str, float] display ([round(x), 1.5]), as any int is: write float(round(x)) there round is bound where the call is, as for format (#471); an ndigits that is a variable is passed as it is: an int \| None one is read as a float, one bound to None only fails in Codon's round (__pow__() cannot be called with (None)) sorted(xs), xs.sort(), min / max of a class that defines __lt__ only the class gets __gt__ (other < self) and __ge__ (not self < other), which Codon's sort calls the class defines no ordering (use @dataclass(order=True) or key=) a if x else None, a if x is not None else None, None if x is None else a (also not x), where a reads the narrowed x: m.group(1) if m else None, npc.speed if npc is not None else None (#597, #621) _acs_some_if(lambda: a, x) if not isinstance(x, Optional[NoneType]) else None. Codon cannot unify the type of a with the None ('Optional[str]' does not match expected type 'str'), and where that type is known only later (an attribute or a method of an Optional) it left the expression an unresolved Optional[T], so a later str(), round() or format spec of it was refused or crashed Codon. Codon decides the isinstance test from the type, so it compiles only the branch it picks (the None where x is always None, as Python never evaluates a there) and unifies nothing; _acs_some_if returns a as an Optional (one that already is one is kept), the type Python gives the expression. In a class body, or where a cannot be in a lambda (a walrus, yield, await, super() or super(Cls, self)), the branch is _acs_some(a) a.__eq__(b), a.__ne__(b) (#596) (a == (b)), (a != (b)): Codon cannot call by name an __eq__ that overrides an inherited one (the identity __eq__ the check gives a plain class, or the model's BaseCondition), as a __ne__ written return not self.__eq__(other) does; == is how Python calls it, too super().__eq__(b), A.__eq__(a, b) and a parenthesized receiver are left alone a class that defines __eq__ but not __ne__ (a value object in a set or as a dict key) the class gets __ne__ (not (self == other)): Python derives it, Codon does not and its hash table calls it (a @dataclass already has one) namedtuple("P", "x y") / "x, y" the string becomes the list ["x", "y"] (Codon crashes on a string) field names that are not a literal (a variable, .split()), and rename= / defaults= / field_names= / module= as keywords, and field names Python rejects (a duplicate, a keyword, a leading underscore); a namedtuple the module defines or imports from elsewhere is left alone; use a list written in the call or a typing.NamedTuple class @functools.total_ordering the decorator and its import are dropped, and the class gets the comparisons it would add from its __lt__, __le__, __gt__ or __ge__ (and ==, or identity without __eq__) the class is not at module level, or defines none of the four lambda x, k=k: x + k (a default that is not a literal) (lambda k: lambda x: x + k)(k): the default is bound by a call, once, as in Python a def in a function whose parameter default is a local of an enclosing function (#612): for name in names: def log_it(world, n: str = name), scale = 2; def f(k: int = scale) (name,)[0]: Codon refuses the bare name ("name 'name' cannot be captured") but evaluates any other expression once, when the def runs, as Python does. The tuple holds the same value and type, and the parameter can still be passed a default that is no bare name is left as written (Codon takes it); a method of a class defined in a function is not rewritten. Another cannot be captured is hinted: bind the value with functools.partial(f, n=value), or read the local in the body an f-string in a decorator (#616): @tag(f"lane-{N}"), @tag(f"plain") str() parts joined by +, as in a lambda above: @tag(("lane-" + str(N))). Codon reads an f-string there as an attribute of the string ("'str' object has no attribute 'prefix_f'"), with or without fields. An f-string in a default, an argument or a body is no decorator and is left as written a brace or a nested f-string inside an expression (as above) def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb) (annotated type[BaseException] \| None, BaseException \| None, object, ... or not) each parameter without a default gets =None: Codon calls __exit__() with no arguments, even when the block raised (#435). An annotation of BaseException or Exception (alone or \| None, Optional[...]) is kept as X \| None; any other annotation is dropped fs: list[Callable[[int], int]] = [inc, lambda x: x * 2], table: dict[str, Callable[[int], int]] = {"a": inc, "b": dbl}, or a return of such a display from a function annotated so (a dispatch table) each function, module function (mod.f) or lambda element is wrapped in Codon's Callable[Tuple[int], int](...), so they share one type (#436) the element is a bound method, a lambda using a local variable of its function, or a call (not wrapped, then Codon's own refusal and a hint); the table is a set, an attribute of a class, is unannotated, or is built another way than a display (a comprehension) a class constant read in its own class body (#433): DOUBLE = LIMIT * 2, x: int = SIZE (a dataclass default), def f(self, n=LIMIT), @register(LIMIT) Class.LIMIT (Outer.Inner.LIMIT in a nested class) the constant is annotated and not a single-line literal (LIMIT: int = 2 * 3), it is assigned again later in the body, the class is defined in a function, the read is a NamedTuple field default, or it is an Enum member with a non-literal value a comprehension or generator in a class body (#469): SQ = [i * i for i in range(3)], field(default_factory=lambda: [d.name for d in Mode]), lambda: tuple(gen), lambda: list(Mode) a module-level function above the class (def _acs_hoist_Q_2(): return (...)) that the attribute or field default calls, on the same lines (Codon does not bind a comprehension's variable in a class body, and crashes on an Enum iterated there) the expression reads its own class, or an enclosing one (range(LIMIT) with LIMIT a constant of the class): build it in a module-level function. A class nested in a class is hoisted too (#482, _acs_hoist_Outer_Inner_5, above the outermost class); one inside a function is not a lambda assigned in a class body (#482): f = lambda self, v: v * 2, key = lambda v: str(v) + "!" def f(self, v): return (v * 2) on the same line, as Python makes it a method. A lambda whose first parameter is not self / cls is a @staticmethod (a decorator line is added, mapped to the lambda's line): it is called as C.key(3), and Codon would otherwise bind v to the instance (Codon cannot call a method through the class with an explicit instance for this, T.f(3) is refused for a plain def). Python binds the instance to v on T().f(3) and raises a TypeError, which the check accepts: write self when the lambda is meant as a method. In a nested class too a lambda on the line of its class (class C: f = lambda: 1) or a multi-target assignment is left as written staticmethod(lambda a, b=2: a + b), classmethod(lambda cls: ...) in a class body (#482) an @staticmethod / @classmethod def of the same name a lambda default of a method (#482): def sort(self, xs: list[int], key=lambda v: -v) a module-level function above the outermost class (def _acs_lambda_P_3_27(v): return (-v)) that the default names; Python evaluates a default once and the lambda reads only globals, so it is the same value the class is inside a function or a block, or the lambda has defaults that are not literals: write a module-level def and name it as the default dict(a=1) {"a": 1} (Codon's dict takes no keywords). In an f-string field, f"{dict(a=1)}", the f-string becomes a + of its parts first (str({"a": 1})): a brace ends the field for Codon's parser (#609) dict(base, a=1) (#613) (dict(base) \| {"a": 1}): the same dict, the keywords winning (in an f-string field, the f-string is lowered first, as for dict(a=1)) dict(base, **more), or a dict the module binds itself filter(None, xs) (#613) (_acs_v for _acs_v in xs if _acs_v): the truthy items, as Python's filter yields them (Codon's takes a function) a filter the module binds itself; the items still need a truth value (an enum member has none, see Iterating an enum) items: list[int] = [], tags: dict[str, int] = {}, seen: set[str] = set() (annotated, in a class body, a function or the module, #611) an empty one of the annotated type, List[int](): Codon types a display from its elements, and an empty one is a container of None (a class with no __init__ of its own was refused at its constructor call) an annotation Codon cannot name there (Any, a TypeVar, a class defined further down outside a function) pairs: list[tuple[int, ...]] = [] (a local of a function, #625), then tuple displays of more than one length appended or inserted in that function: pairs.append((1, 2)), pairs.insert(0, (3,)) pairs = List[List[int]](), pairs.append(List[int]([1, 2])): the tuple[X, ...] inside is the List[X] a class-level one is checked as (Codon's tuples have a fixed length), so tuples of different lengths go in, and the elements are still checked. Dropped, the annotation left Codon to type the list from its first append. Given tuples of one length only, the annotation is dropped as before (the list of fixed-length tuples Codon types then takes a tuple held in a name, extend, in with a tuple display), and so is a tuple[X, ...] in a dict, a set, a nested list or an Optional a list given tuples of more than one length that is also given a tuple from a name (pairs.append(t)), or another way (+=, extend), or tested with (1, 2) in pairs: refused with a hint to build it with tuple([...]); a module-level one, or one a nested function appends to, is typed from its first append as before lst: list[Npc \| None] = [None, a], d: dict[str, Npc \| None] = {"x": None, "y": a} (a display whose first element or value is None, #611) the elements put into a list (dict) of the annotated type, each None the Optional's (_acs_list_into(List[Optional[Npc]](), Optional[Npc](), a)): Codon types a display by its first element as above Plan(lanes=(1, 2, 1)), replace(Plan(), lanes=(1, 2)), replace(self, lanes=()), for a dataclass field lanes: tuple[int, ...] (or Sequence[int]) of the module (#614) List[int]([1, 2, 1]) / List[int](), the list the field is checked as, as for its default a tuple held in a name, a positional argument of a dataclass with a base, ClassVar or init=False field, or replace() of an object whose class is not told by a constructor call or self: refused with 'Tuple[int,int,int]' does not match expected type 'List[int]' and a hint to write tuple([1, 2, 1])

Notes:

  • Codon calls __exit__() with no arguments, so a parameter is None in the check. A branch on a parameter annotated type[...], object or TracebackType (if exc_type is not None:, if tb is not None:) is therefore dead code to Codon, not compiled and not type-checked: Python runs it as written. Annotate the exception parameter exc: BaseException | None (or Exception | None) and test that one (if exc is not None:): its annotation is kept, so the branch is compiled and checked (str(exc)). from types import TracebackType is refused (types has no model): annotate tb as object. __enter__ returning self (-> "Ctx", or no annotation) compiles as it is, and so does -> bool (suppression). __exit__(self, *args: object) needs no rewrite. The canonical signature __exit__(self, exc_type: type[BaseException] | None, exc: BaseException | None, tb: object) -> bool raises no "Codon cannot express" warning: the dropped parameters are the ones the check leaves to their None default (#482).
  • Codon gives every function and lambda a type of its own, so a list or dict of different ones does not compile without the annotation, even if you annotate nothing else. Annotate where the table is assigned or returned; an element of another signature than the annotation is refused, a set of functions is refused whatever the annotation (Codon cannot hash a function), as is a dict keyed by functions (a dict with functions as values is fine): the error carries a hint to use a list or a dict keyed by name. An unannotated fs = [inc, dbl] or a class attribute is refused with a hint: write an if/elif chain or a match on the key instead (if key == "a": return inc(x)). A bound method (self.run) or a lambda using a local variable cannot be converted: use a module-level function that takes the object, or the chain.
  • __ge__ of a class that defines __lt__ only is more than Python gives it (a >= b is a TypeError there): the check accepts it because Codon's sort needs it. It does not change what runs.
  • A rewritten lambda no longer takes the captured parameter: fs[0](1, 5), which passes k, is refused (with a hint naming this). A default after a non-literal one is bound the same way, so positional calls keep their meaning. Use functools.partial where you pass the captured value.
  • Codon's f-strings have no {{ / }}: an f-string with a literal brace becomes a + of its parts, the brace a string of its own (f"{name} {{x}}" is (f"{name} " + "{" + "x" + "}")), whether or not another of its fields is rewritten (#696).
  • Codon has no ascii(), so the !a conversion of a field is checked as !r (#701): the type is the same str; only the checked copy changes.
  • An f-string that is rewritten (a literal brace, a spec Codon does not parse, !a) is written back as double-quoted strings, so a field whose expression holds a double quote or a backslash (d["it's"], d['a\\b']) cannot stay a field. It becomes a call instead, whatever its conversion (#704): str(e) with no conversion or !s, repr(e) with !r or !a, and with a spec that call's __format__, or (e).__format__(spec) with no conversion: f"{x:+d} {d['a\\b']!r:>9} {{" is ((x).__format__("+d") + " " + repr(d['a\\b']).__format__(">9") + " " + "{"). The value and its str type are the same as Python's.
  • F-string format specs (#434). Codon's parser takes a fill and align, #, 0, a width, , / _, a precision and a type (f"{x:>8.3f}", f"{n:#010x}", f"{n:,}", f"{x!r:^10}", f"{x=:.2f}") as they are. It has no sign (+, space, -), no field inside the spec ({x:>{w}}), and it refuses a spec it does not know ({x:q}). Those fields are rewritten as above; the other fields of the same f-string stay f-string fields. The rewrite calls __format__ on int, float, str and a class that defines it: a bool or a class without __format__ has none in Codon (the error is hinted: int(flag)). The spec is read at run time, so a spec Python rejects ({x:q} on a float, a sign on a str) compiles in the check, which does not run; Python raises its ValueError when the scenario runs. Only the checked copy changes.
  • A brace or a nested f-string inside an f-string expression is refused, at the line of the f-string: a dict or set display or comprehension (f"{len({1, 2})}"), a string holding { or } (f"{'{}'.format(x)}") and an f-string inside an f-string. Codon's parser ends the field there and reports a position that is no line of your file. Bind the value to a local first (label = "{:>3}".format(x), then f"{label}"). A syntax error Codon still reports inside an f-string field is shown at the line of the f-string that has it (the first f-string with a format spec, else with a literal brace, else the file's only f-string line), with no column, and never at a line before the file: with no one f-string to blame, it is shown with no line rather than at a guessed one.
  • A type error inside an f-string field is shown at the f-string's line, with no column (#610). Codon reports it on the line after the line the f-string starts on, at the faulting expression's column plus the length of the field's text: a column past the end of that line, or no line of the file when the f-string is on its last line. The check moves such an error back when nothing on the reported line starts at the reported column, of any width (Codon locates an error on that line itself there; its width of a call on several lines counts the characters across the line breaks, that of a with or for statement is one more than Python's), and an f-string that starts on the line before has a field holding an expression of that width that ends at or before the column (and, on a one-line f-string, no further from it than the f-string's end). The line shown is the expression's own (a field on a later line of a triple-quoted f-string is shown on its line). An error of the line itself always has such an expression (a comprehension's for c in n clause, which Codon locates from its for, is matched by where it ends), so it stays where it is, column and all. An implicitly concatenated f-string ("a" f"b{n + 'x'}", also on several lines, #616) is reported on the line after its first literal's line too, at a column the bound above does not hold for: the first literal's 0-based column, plus the offset of the field's { in its own literal, plus the field's length, plus the expression's offset from the {. The check computes that column for each field of an f-string that starts on the line before (a triple-quoted literal, a field on several lines and a line that is not ASCII excepted) and moves an error that matches it, column and width, to the field's line, with the same guard (anything that starts on the reported line at that column keeps it).
  • A class constant read in the class body (#433): Python resolves the name in the class scope, Codon in the module's (name 'LIMIT' is not defined), so the check writes Class.LIMIT. It rewrites exactly what Python resolves there: a name an earlier assignment of the same body bound, read by another statement of the body, a dataclass field default, a method's parameter default or a decorator. A method body, a lambda body and a comprehension (but for its first iterable) do not see the class scope, so a bare LIMIT there is the module's and stays; a nested class sees only its own body; a parameter or comprehension variable named LIMIT shadows nothing at the default, which is read in the class scope. In an Enum a member read by a later statement is its value in Python (B = A makes an alias), so the check writes the literal; any other name of the body is qualified as above.
  • The constant has to be a class attribute in Codon. A name annotated at class level (LIMIT: int = 5, Final[int], ClassVar[int]) is a typed field of the instance, not an attribute of the class, so a read of it cannot be qualified: when its value is a single-line literal the check writes that literal where the name is (n: int = 5; Python reads the same value), and otherwise the read is refused with a hint: write LIMIT: Final = 5 (a bare Final is dropped, leaving a class attribute) or no annotation, or use a module-level constant. A NamedTuple field default cannot read its own class constant either (x: int = LIM is "no module named"): its other statements and methods can.

docs.title: The names of typing a scenario may import
docs.text:
Codon has no typing module of its own beyond a few names, so the check brings a shim (typecheck/codon/typing.codon). A scenario may import these names from typing (#364); test_typing_names keeps this list and the shim in step:

TYPE_CHECKING, Sequence, MutableSequence, Iterable, Collection, Mapping, MutableMapping, AbstractSet, FrozenSet, Any, TypeVar, Protocol, runtime_checkable, Literal, IO, Iterator, Deque, DefaultDict, Counter, Final, Annotated, NoReturn, Type, Sized, Hashable, cast, Optional, List, Dict, Set, Tuple, Callable, Union, ClassVar, Generator, overload, Self, override, TypeAlias, NewType, Never, assert_never, TypeGuard, TypeIs, Container

  • from collections.abc import Sequence, Callable (what ruff's UP035 suggests) is read as from typing import Sequence, Callable (#586), on the same lines. The names of collections.abc the check has are Callable, Collection, Container, Generator, Hashable, Iterable, Iterator, Mapping, MutableMapping, MutableSequence, Sequence, Sized and Set (typing's AbstractSet); any other (KeysView, MutableSet, Awaitable) is refused at its import line with that list. import collections.abc and from collections import abc (annotations spelled collections.abc.Sequence, abc.Sequence) are refused too, with the hint to import the names.
  • typing_extensions has the same names as far as typing has them, so a scenario for Python 3.10 imports Self, override, Never, assert_never and TypeIs (which typing gained later) from there; any other name of it (deprecated, ReadOnly) is refused with a hint to this list.
  • The type-only names are rewritten before Codon reads the code (#514), and none of them is checked: @override is dropped (not that the method overrides one); X: TypeAlias = T is X = T; Self in an annotation of a class is the class (-> Self is -> Counter, so a subclass's method is checked as returning its base, and a call of Twice(1).inc().twice_only() is refused although Python accepts it); NewType("LaneId", int) is LaneId = int and LaneId(v) is (v), so the new type is checked as its base (a LaneId is any int, as Python runs it); assert_never(x), as a statement or a return, is raise AssertionError(...), and anywhere else (a ternary, a lambda body, an argument) it is refused, since Codon types the call as None; Never and Container annotations are dropped, like NoReturn and Sized; TypeGuard[X] and TypeIs[X] are bool, which they are at run time.

  • A TypeVar with a bound= or constraints (TypeVar("B", bound=Base), TypeVar("N", int, float)) is rewritten to TypeVar("B") (#513): Codon's takes a name only, and makes a function generic over its unannotated parameters anyway, so the bound or the constraints are not checked.

  • Final and Annotated are read as what they wrap (Final[int] and Annotated[int, "m"] are int; a bare Final is dropped). NoReturn, Type, Sized, Hashable, Any and Callable annotations are dropped, so they are not checked. The exception is a Callable[[A], R] parameter whose function body stores it (self._cb = fn, self._cbs[key] = fn, self._cbs.append(fn), or hands it to a method of the same class that stores it, self._add(fn)), with argument and result types Codon can express: it is kept, written as Codon's Callable[Tuple[A], R], so a callback registry (a class-level _cbs: list[Callable[[int], int]] that register() appends to) has the same type on both sides. A generic parameter put in a typed Callable container made Codon abort with std::bad_alloc and no location (#488). A named function or a lambda passed to it converts, and one of the wrong signature is refused at the call. Two limits, both Codon's: a closure reading a local variable of its function cannot be converted (Codon's own refusal, with the dispatch-table hint), and neither can a lambda that takes no arguments (lambda: None; it is refused at its line after the crash, with the hint to pass a named function). A parameter the body only calls, or passes on, stays dropped, so a closure still checks. An optional callback (Optional[Callable[[A], R]], Callable[[A], R] | None) is kept the same way when the body stores it, written as the plain Callable[Tuple[A], R] (Codon converts a function, a lambda and None to it, but a function or a lambda to an Optional of it not), the = None default staying. The class-level attribute is written Optional[Callable[...]] (the | between a Callable and None cannot be evaluated by Codon when it imports the class, #495), so if self.cb is not None: self.cb(v) checks. Codon accepts a call of it without that test; the check does not refuse it. A lambda's type, which Codon names %_lambda_N, shows in a message as "a lambda".

  • A Codon abort with std::bad_alloc names the Callable attributes of the checked modules at their lines; a function passed where a Callable of another signature is expected is named at the call that passes it (Codon 0.19 reports no type error for that, only a code generation failure).
  • cast(T, x) is x typed as T (as in Python, nothing checks that x is a T); when T cannot be named in Codon (a Callable, a class defined further down) it is x as it is.
  • A class-level Y: Final[int] = 4 stays a typed field, not a class attribute, as any annotated class-level name does; write Y: Final = 4 for a class attribute read as C.Y. A read from outside the class (Q.LIMIT with LIMIT: int = 5 or ClassVar[int]) gets Codon's 'Q' object has no attribute 'LIMIT' with a hint to write LIMIT: Final = 5 (#471); the check does not rewrite it, since in a @dataclass the annotated name is an instance field in Python too.
  • Iterator is Codon's generator type, and Deque, DefaultDict and Counter are collections.deque, defaultdict and Counter.
  • Any other name is refused at its import line. Generic and TypedDict cannot be modelled: leave the type parameters of a class or function unannotated (Codon makes it generic over them) instead of subclassing Generic, and write a @dataclass (or a Dict[str, X]) instead of a TypedDict.

docs.title: Python 3.12+ syntax (#624)
docs.text:
The package runs on Python 3.10 to 3.14. Codon 0.19 parses Python 3.11's syntax, so the check rewrites the newer syntax first, with every line and column kept:

Python 3.12+ What the check makes of it Refused (with a hint, at its line) A string in an f-string's field quoted with the f-string's own quote (PEP 701): f"{cfg.name.replace("_", "-")} {d["k"]}" the string quoted with the other quote, f"{cfg.name.replace('_', '-')} {d['k']}" (Codon's parser, as Python's before 3.12, ends the f-string at its own quote, and reported unexpected dedent a line later) a string that holds the other quote too (f"{d["it's"]}"), a string of either quote that holds the quote of a single-quoted f-string around it (f'{d["it's"]}', which Codon's parser ends at that quote too), and a backslash anywhere in a field (f"{"\n".join(names)}"), which Codon's parser refuses whatever the quotes: bind the value to a local first. In an f-string that is rewritten anyway (a literal brace, a spec Codon does not parse, !a), such a field becomes a call and is not refused (#704). A nested f-string is refused as before ("A brace or a nested f-string") type LaneIds = list[int] (PEP 695), at any level LaneIds = list[int], as X: TypeAlias = T is a generic alias, type Pair[T] = tuple[T, T]: Codon has no generic alias; write the type out, or make the alias concrete Type parameters of a function, a method or a class (PEP 695): def first[T](xs: list[T]) -> T, class Box[K, V]: kept: they are Codon's own generics syntax. A bound, constraints or a default ([B: Base], [N: (int, float)], [T = int]) are dropped, as a TypeVar's are, since Codon reads [T: int] as a static integer parameter *Ts and **P (PEP 646, PEP 612): Codon has no variadic generics

A generic function or class is compiled, and checked, where the scenario uses it (Box("a").get() + 1 is refused): like a function annotated with a module-level TypeVar, it is not called on its own, and a warning says so ("parameter xs is annotated with a TypeVar", "the class is generic"). On Python 3.10 and 3.11 this syntax does not parse, so a scenario using it needs Python 3.12 or later to run at all.

docs.title: Python constructs Codon refuses (#379)
docs.text:
Each of these is valid, mypy-clean Python that Codon 0.19 cannot compile and that the check cannot cheaply rewrite. The check refuses it at its line with a hint, and the working spelling is below. What runs is your code as written; only the check needs the other spelling.

You write Codon says Write instead case int(n):, case Pt(x=x, y=y):, case Pt(a, b): (a class pattern with arguments), or case Pt(): of a class of your own name 'n' is not defined, or it reads the pattern as a call of Pt (__init__() missing 1 required positional argument) if isinstance(v, Pt):, then read the attributes (v.x, v.y); case int():, case str(): and the other builtin types compile case {"k": v}:, case {"k": _}:, case {**rest}: (any name or _ inside the mapping) name 'v' is not defined if "k" in d: and read d["k"]; a mapping pattern whose values are literals, values or or-patterns (case {"k": 1 \| 2}:) compiles case [a, *rest]:, case [*_]: unexpected star expression a fixed length (case [a, b]:), or test len(xs) and slice case [a, b] as whole: unexpected indentation match without as and use the name the subject already has def show(h: HasArea) called with a class that has area() but does not derive from the Protocol HasArea 'Sq[float]' does not match expected type 'HasArea' (also List[Sq] against List[HasArea]) derive from it (class Sq(HasArea):), give the classes a common base class, or annotate Union[Sq, Circle]; Codon lists are invariant: annotate a list with the class it holds (list[Sq]) f(*xs) with a list, f(**d) with a dict argument after * must be a tuple, not 'List[int]' / argument after ** must be a named tuple, not 'Dict[str,int]' pass the elements (f(xs[0], xs[1]), f(a=d["a"], b=d["b"])), or make the parameter a list or dict; a tuple (f(*(1, 2))) is accepted try: ... except* ValueError as eg: (exception groups, #439) scenario.py:70:1: error: unexpected dedent, at the line after the handler except ValueError: (one handler per exception type); Codon has no syntax for except* s.startswith(PREFIXES) with a tuple held in a name (#439) 'Tuple[str,str]' does not match expected type 'str' any(s.startswith(p) for p in PREFIXES); a tuple written in the call is rewritten d.update(c=3) (#439) no function 'Dict.update' with arguments (Dict[str,int], int) d.update({"c": 3}) (the check cannot rewrite it: it does not know d is a dict, and obj.update(dt=1) of your own class is valid) int.from_bytes(b, "big"), n.to_bytes(2, "big") (#439) 'int' object has no attribute 'from_bytes' shifts and masks (n = (n << 8) \| byte); Codon's bytes is a str "{a}".format_map(d) (#439) '{a}' object has no attribute 'format_map' an f-string, or "{a}".format(a=d["a"]) b.decode(), b.hex() on a bytes value (#439) 'str' object has no attribute 'decode' Codon's bytes is a str: it is already text A class decorator other than those the check drops (@register, adding the class to a registry, #603) unsupported class decorator drop it, and choose the class with an if/elif chain (or a match) on the name: Codon cannot hold a class as a value. @dataclass, @enum.unique, @typing.runtime_checkable and @functools.total_ordering are handled by the check async def, await, async for, async with anywhere in a checked module, called or not (#603) async not yet supported a plain def: the runner calls the scenario synchronously; or move the coroutine to a module the scenario does not import if obj: (not obj, bool(obj)) on an object of a class with no __bool__: a plain object, or one with only __len__ (#603) 'Bag[List[int]]' object has no attribute '__bool__' say what is meant: obj is not None for a value that may be missing, len(obj) > 0 for a container, or define __bool__ on the class class Registry(dict[str, int]), class Bag(list), class Meters(int): a class deriving from a builtin type alone (dict, list, set, frozenset, tuple, int, float, str, bytes, or their typing names), #613 __init__() missing 1 required positional argument: '_n_buckets', at the call (Codon's builtins are its own classes); refused at the class line hold one as an attribute (items: dict[str, int]) and give the class the methods it needs; a class with another base besides (class Mode(str, Enum)) and exceptions are left alone x = a if c else 3 with branches of different types (#603) 'str' does not match expected type 'int', at the conditional expression one type for both branches (str(3), float(n)), or an if/else statement that uses each value in its own branch lambda a, *, k=1: a * k, a lambda with keyword-only parameters (#629) a syntax error (unexpected dedent); refused at its line before Codon runs a nested def f(a, *, k=1): return a * k, whose keyword-only parameters the check compiles (#622) A call of a method that a subclass of yours overrides, passing a keyword (b.m(1.0, s=3.0)), or leaving out a parameter with a default (b.m(1.0)), keyword-only parameters included (#629) 's' is an invalid keyword argument for class_thunk_dispatch(), or cannot typecheck 'b.m(1.0)', with a hint pass every argument by position: Codon calls an overridden method through a dispatch thunk, which takes no keyword and fills in no default. A keyword-only parameter cannot be passed by position, so in an overridden method make it a positional one with its default, in the base and in each override A function with keyword-only parameters in a table annotated Callable (fs: list[Callable[[int], int]] = [key_of, dbl] with def key_of(x, *, rev=False), #629) no function 'Callable.__new__' with arguments (key_of[int,T2,bool]), with a hint naming it a lambda that calls it, [lambda x: key_of(x), dbl]. An annotated variable (g: Callable[[int], int] = key_of) and a Callable parameter take it as it is A nonlocal variable that may be None used as its value, even narrowed (out = y + 1 if y is not None else None in the inner function, #629) unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'Capsule[Optional[int]]' and '1', with a hint copy it into an annotated local of the inner function (cur: int \| None = y), and test and use that; an unannotated copy is a Capsule too

Plain value, or-pattern, guard, sequence (without *) and enum-member (case Mode.A:) patterns compile, as does case int(): of a builtin type.

A Protocol is not structural in the check: Codon compares class names, so a class is a HasArea only if it lists HasArea among its bases. Python runs the same code either way, because a Protocol base is only a marker there.

docs.title: What Python raises for that Codon compiles (#602, #603)
docs.text:
Codon checks types, so a call it compiles may still raise in CPython. Three kinds are decided from the syntax and refused at the call, before Codon runs (typecheck/static_raises.py):

  • sum() with a str start (#625): sum(["a", "b"], ""), sum(parts, start="-"), a start that is an f-string or str(...), and likewise a bytes or bytearray one. CPython refuses it before it adds anything ("sum() can't sum strings [use ''.join(seq) instead]"); Codon concatenates. Use "".join(parts). A start held in a variable is left to the run.

  • isinstance / issubclass with a subscripted generic (#603): isinstance(v, list[int]), issubclass(C, dict[str, int]), isinstance(v, typing.List[int]), also inside a tuple of classes ((str, list[int])), a | union (int | list[int]) or a typing.Union / Optional. Python raises TypeError ("isinstance() argument 2 cannot be a parameterized generic"; for typing.List[int] and the other aliases of typing, "Subscripted generics cannot be used with class and instance checks"); in a tuple or a union, once the value is none of the classes before it (a | union on Python 3.10: at once). Test against the bare class (isinstance(v, list)) and check the elements separately; for a Literal[...], compare the value. isinstance(x, int | float), an unsubscripted typing.List, Optional[int] and an index into a tuple of classes (TYPES[0]) are left alone, and so is a name the module binds itself (a parameter called list).

  • A framework class built with literal arguments it refuses (#602): MetricCondition("no_such_metric", label="m"), ElapsedTimeCondition(1.0, label=""), RouteCrossingPose(approach="Left"), RouteRoadsidePose(side="kerb"). When every argument of a call is a literal (a constant, or a tuple, list, set or dict of them, by position or by keyword) and the callee is imported from the framework, the check builds the class with those literals and reports the ValueError it raises, in the framework's own words:
scenario.py:71:34: error: RouteCrossingPose(...) with these literal arguments raises ValueError when the scenario runs: RouteCrossingPose.approach must be one of ['left', 'right', 'opposite'], got 'Left'

The validation is the constructor's own, so the check refuses what the run would and nothing else. Only classes whose constructor just validates and stores its arguments (no CARLA, world or map) are built: AlwaysTrueCondition, ElapsedTimeCondition, MetricCondition, OffRoadFractionCondition, RouteProgressCondition, TimeoutCondition, RouteCrossingPose, RouteCrosswalkPose, RouteLanePose, RouteOppositePose and RouteRoadsidePose (LITERAL_CHECKED). A call with any argument that is not a literal (a config field, a constant's name such as OFFROAD, an enum member such as ComparisonRule.LESS_THAN, *args) is left to the run, as is a TypeError (Codon reports the type) and a literal of another type than its parameter declares (a str for a float, an int for a str: Codon reports the mismatch, though the constructor would raise ValueError for it; an int for a float fits). The check imports these classes only for a module that calls one of them by name. The conditions import typesafe_carla.carla: where its first import would build the CPython package (no prebuilt one applies, 15-50 min), the check does not build it, and leaves the conditions to the run.

docs.title: Standard library names Codon lacks
docs.text:
Codon ships its own functools (only partial), itertools, collections, math, random and statistics, and a name it lacks fails with a bare "cannot import name". The check supplies these (#378, #515, #516); test_stdlib_names keeps this list, the check's additions and the tests in step:

functools.reduce, functools.lru_cache, functools.cache, functools.cached_property, itertools.pairwise, collections.OrderedDict, collections.deque, math.dist, math.isqrt, math.comb, math.perm, math.cbrt, math.exp2, math.hypot, random.Random, random.choices, random.triangular, statistics.fmean, re.Match, re.Pattern

  • functools.reduce (with or without an initial value) is a function of the model, which the check puts in place of the name.
  • lru_cache (with or without arguments), cache and cached_property are decorators the check drops, as caching changes no type; cached_property becomes a property. Nothing is cached, so f.cache_clear() and f.cache_info() are refused, and so is assigning to a cached_property attribute (self.area = 3 is legal in Python, not on a property). A name the module binds again (a parameter reduce, a def cache) is left alone. The names are handled where the module imports them, not in a function.
  • A decorator the check drops (lru_cache, cache, @abstractmethod, @override) may sit under one it keeps (@property, @staticmethod, @classmethod), as in @property over @abstractmethod (#595). Codon's parser refuses a blank or comment-only line inside a decorator list, so the check removes the dropped decorators' lines, and any comment or blank line, between the first kept decorator and the def, and moves the kept decorators down to the def: the def and every line after it keep their line numbers, and an error on a kept decorator is reported at the line it was written on. A decorator is its whole logical line, from its @ to its end (@( / name / ) on three lines).
  • The initial value of reduce must have the type of the accumulator the function returns: reduce(add, [1.5, 2.5], 0) is refused (write 0.0).
  • itertools.pairwise is added to Codon's itertools, and collections.OrderedDict is a dict, which keeps its insertion order; move_to_end() and popitem(last=...) are not declared, and are refused when called.
  • collections.deque gets what Codon's lacks: deque(iterable, maxlen), extend, extendleft, rotate, count, index, insert, remove, reverse, item assignment and deletion and ==/!=, all as Python's (maxlen drops items from the other end, rotate(-n) turns left). Codon's own deque(maxlen=n) kept one item too many when n + 1 was a power of two; the check's is fixed. deque(iterable, maxlen=None) and reversed(d) are not declared, and d.maxlen is -1, not None, for a deque with no limit (Codon's).
  • math.dist, isqrt, comb and perm are Python's (the same ValueErrors); an int is 64 bits in Codon, so comb and perm overflow where Python's would not. math.cbrt and math.exp2 are Python 3.11 functions: the check accepts them on 3.10 too (run time is where 3.10 refuses them), so a scenario meant for 3.10 has to avoid them itself. nextafter and ulp are not declared. math.hypot takes any number of coordinates (Python 3.8's, #590), hypot(x, y, z) included; Codon's took exactly two, and a call with two keeps Codon's (and its float32 one).
  • statistics.fmean(data) is Python's mean of the values as floats (#590); Codon's own is commented out. fmean(data, weights) is the weighted mean of Python 3.11, accepted on 3.10 too, like math.cbrt. The rest of statistics is Codon's (mean, median, stdev, ...), which takes a list[float].
  • re.Match.group(n), group(a, b), m[n], groups() and groupdict() are str (#597), as typeshed declares them (str | Any), so m.group(1) if m else "" compiles; Codon's are Optional[str], and their Optional[str] and the "" did not unify. The caveat is typeshed's too: a group that did not take part in the match ((-x)?) is None in Python, which the check does not see: test an optional group with is not None before using it as a str (the check compiles the test), or read it through groups(default) / groupdict(default), which keep Codon's Optional[str]. re.Pattern.split keeps its Optional[str] items, a group that did not take part splitting off as None, as in Python. The rest of re is Codon's.
  • random.Random.choices (and random.choices) take weights of ints or floats, or cum_weights=, and k=, as Python's do, and triangular(low, high) (the method and the function) takes the midpoint as the mode. Codon's choices wanted int weights and all four arguments. cum_weights and k can be passed by position here, where Python makes them keyword-only.

These are refused at the import line, with a hint saying what to write instead:

dataclasses.asdict, dataclasses.InitVar, dataclasses.KW_ONLY, functools.wraps, math.ulp, contextlib.contextmanager, warnings, json.JSONEncoder, types, textwrap, traceback, io, csv, uuid

  • dataclasses.asdict returns a dict[str, Any]: build the dict from the fields you need. The dataclasses shim declares only dataclass, field and replace (a call is rewritten and checked per field, see "Your own dataclasses, enums and named tuples").
  • dataclasses.InitVar and KW_ONLY (#590): Codon's constructor of a dataclass takes every annotated field and does not call __post_init__, so an init-only value has nowhere to go and the KW_ONLY marker would be a field. Pass an InitVar's value to a @classmethod (or a function) that computes the fields and builds the instance, or keep it as an ordinary field; drop KW_ONLY and pass the fields by keyword (a field without a default then goes before the defaulted ones).
  • functools.wraps (and any other name of functools, itertools, collections, math or random not listed above, such as math.ulp) is not modelled.
  • contextlib declares suppress only: write a class with __enter__ and __exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb) for contextmanager (the check rewrites the signature, see "Python the check rewrites for Codon"). warnings: log with logger.warning. json declares dumps, dump, loads, load and JSONDecodeError only (see the shims below), not JSONEncoder or the rest. types: name the type itself. textwrap: build the string with str methods. traceback: log with logger.exception. io: use a str, or a pathlib.Path opened with open(). csv: read the file with Path.read_text().splitlines() and split(",") each line, and write one with ",".join(fields) and Path.write_text(). uuid: use a counter, or os.getpid() for an id that differs per process.
  • time.strftime() and datetime.strftime() are not modelled (Codon's datetime has neither, nor __format__): the error says so; format the fields instead, f"{now.year:04d}{now.month:02d}{now.day:02d}" for now = datetime.datetime.now().
  • A name of os, os.path, shutil or a member of pathlib.Path that the shims below do not declare is refused with Codon's cannot import name or 'Path' object has no attribute, to which the check adds that it is not modelled (the shim declares only the names listed below), so it does not read as invalid Python.

docs.title: Iterating an enum
docs.text:
For an Enum class, a scenario's own (any of Enum, IntEnum, StrEnum, Flag, IntFlag, (str, Enum)) or one of the framework's (TurnDirection, ComparisonRule, TickTiming, ...), the check rewrites, as Python reads it:

  • for m in Mode and a comprehension over Mode, and *Mode;
  • list(Mode), tuple, set, frozenset, sorted, len, reversed, enumerate, iter, min, max, zip, map and filter (with a function) of Mode;
  • x in Mode and x not in Mode;
  • Mode["A"], a member looked up by name.

Inside the enum's own methods the class has other spellings, and the check reads them as the class (#481). In a @classmethod, the first parameter (cls, or whatever it is called) is the class, so [g.name for g in cls], list(cls), len(cls), x in cls and cls["A"] work. In an instance method, type(self) and self.__class__ are the class too (for m in type(self)). These hold only in a method written directly in the class body: a @staticmethod, a function outside the class and a class that is no enum are left alone, and so is a parameter the method rebinds (an assignment, a loop or comprehension variable, an import, a nested def), a nested function or lambda that declares a parameter of the same name, and a type the module or function binds.

Iteration yields the members in definition order. A member whose value repeats an earlier one is an alias, and is skipped, as in Python. A Flag or IntFlag yields its single-bit members only, as Python 3.11 and later do: a composite (RW = R | W, BOTH = 3), a zero member and an alias are skipped, though Perm["RW"] finds them. Only the name of the class (and the spellings above) is rewritten, so a parameter or local called like the class is left alone, and the enum may be defined in another module of the package.

The framework's enums are @tuple classes in the model (typecheck/codon/). Each declares _acs_members() and _acs_by_name(), and the check takes the enums to rewrite from the model files, so a new model enum is iterable once it declares them. test_typecheck_model.py keeps both equal to the Python enum's members, in its order. A scenario class of the same name as a model enum that is no enum is left alone, and so is a module-level variable, function or non-framework import of that name (#471); a parameter or local of the name shadows it only inside its function.

What does not work:

  • the class under another name or as a value: k = cls and then for m in k, or f(cls), and cls.__members__. They stay as written (the first is refused with a hint to write the class's name: 'Mode' object has no attribute '__iter__');
  • the class passed as a value, f(Mode), or Mode.__members__: both stay as written, which Codon does not resolve (no function 'List.__init__' with arguments (List[T], type[Mode]) for list(e) in f, and 'Mode' object has no attribute '__members__');
  • sum, any and all of the class, and filter(None, Mode): Codon needs __bool__ or + on the member (sum(int(m) for m in Mode), any(m == x for m in Mode));
  • an enum with no member ('Empty' object has no attribute '_acs_members').

docs.title: Flag and IntFlag
docs.text:
A scenario's own Flag or IntFlag (also class M(int, Flag)) combines as in Python: A | B, &, ^, ~ and A in x (every bit of A is set in x) make a value of the same class, an IntFlag takes an int on either side too (P.R | 4, 4 | P.R), and bool(x) is false for no bit set. Two combinations of the same members are equal, hash alike and compare equal to the member that has their value (P.R | P.W == P.RW). A Flag does no other arithmetic, order or int(); an IntFlag compares, orders and converts as an IntEnum does, and P.R + P.W is refused (use .value). ~x flips the bits of the single-bit members for a Flag, and every bit up to the highest of any member for an IntFlag, as Python 3.11+ does. The operators are usable at module level and in a class body or default (RW = P.R | P.W).

A combination is no member: the check builds it from the combined int, so it has an empty name, and P.R | P.W is P.RW is not modelled (compare with ==). A value written as an expression of the class's own members, even a composite or an auto() one, is worked out when the check reads the class (RW = R | W, ALL = A | B | C, HIGH = 1 << 4, ALL = ~0); auto() is the power of two above the highest bit so far. Operators of two different flag classes, and of a framework enum such as TurnDirection.LEFT | TurnDirection.RIGHT (not a Flag, so Python refuses it too), are refused.

docs.title: What the check does not catch
docs.text:
The check compiles the scenario and never runs it, so it says nothing of what a value is at run time (a division by zero, a missing key, an actor that is not spawned yet), and it accepts some code that fails in Python. The known gaps:

  • An Optional unwrapped implicitly, where mypy cannot see it. Codon unwraps an Optional[T] wherever a T is needed (arithmetic, an attribute, an argument), and mypy's pass (#239, What is checked) catches what mypy can type, CARLA's results included (from stubs of typesafe_carla's Codon library, #267). It does not see a value mypy reads as Any: one from a package with no type information (an import it cannot follow, which it ignores, such as lanelet2), a CARLA result whose type the stubs leave Any (an enumeration, carla.command, a pointer, a method whose overloads return different types), or the result of a function with no return annotation. Neither does it check the arguments of a CARLA call: an Optional passed to one is Codon's to unwrap (world.get_actor(maybe_id) compiles).
  • A union of the scenario's own classes used as one of its members. The None check's pass refuses only a union made of the members of one of the framework's (#309, What is checked): a union of classes the scenario defines (a class-level tuple[A | B, ...], held as List[Union[A, B]]) is converted at run time as Codon converts any union, and an un-narrowed use of one member's attribute compiles.
  • An attribute set on some paths only. Codon zero-initialises every field, and the class rules (#587, #588) follow no paths: an __init__ that calls super().__init__(...) in one branch only, or an attribute assigned in a method that may run after its first read, compiles and can raise AttributeError in Python. A class that is not a module-level name (one defined in a function) is not given the rules at all.
  • A helper with **kwargs or *args that nothing calls and that reads **kwargs by key is not compiled, with a warning: the check has no keyword to call it with (#266). One the scenario calls that reads them is compiled only with the keywords and the number of values its callers pass, and, as a call is known by its name only, not at all when the only calls of its name are another's (d.update(...) for a helper update) or are in a function the check does not compile.
  • A value converted by an annotated assignment. Codon 0.19 converts any value with __bool__ in an annotated assignment: done: bool = "no" compiles, and is True. (A literal returned from a function declared -> bool is refused, #529.) The check binds hook results strictly (#238) and class-level bool defaults through _expect_bool (#190), but an annotated local of the scenario's own code is converted as written. A local x: bool = some_str is no bool in Python.
  • An int where a float is expected is accepted, in a call and a hook result alike, as Python's typing takes it; not inside a container ([1, 2] for a list[float] is refused).
  • A function the check cannot call (a parameter with no annotation, or one of Any, object, Callable[..., R] or a TypeVar, or a return annotation naming Any) is compiled only where setup() and is_done() reach it, with a warning (What is checked).
  • A hook a class takes from a mixin listed before its framework base (class Gap(CheckMixin, BaseCondition), with check() defined in CheckMixin) is compiled as the mixin's own method, not checked against the hook's return type: define the override in the class itself.
  • A None default is not checked against its annotation: speed: float = None is an Optional[float] to Codon (mypy, in the scenario package's own pre-commit, reports it; the None check reports only its uses).
  • What only a tuple does: a tuple[X, ...] is checked as a List[X], so its hash, its equality with another tuple and its immutability are not checked.
  • An int is 64 bits, and no value is computed (#613): Codon's int is a 64-bit integer, and the check compiles the code without running it, so an overflow (2**64, math.factorial(25)) and 2 ** -1 (a float in Python) assigned to an int are not caught.
  • bytes is read as str: path.read_bytes() + "text" compiles, and CPython refuses it.
  • A values= that only Codon iterates (register_cover(), OddAttribute, #279). Codon 0.19 cannot tell a class passed as an argument from one of its objects, so an enum member passes where an enum class is meant (values=TurnDirection.LEFT). A frozen dataclass of the framework (a @tuple, so iterable to Codon) passes too, and so does an element type expression never returns.
  • An enum member looked up by value (ActionState("completeState")) is typed, but not resolved to the member. Lookup by name and iteration work for a scenario's own enum, within the limits of Iterating an enum.
  • typesafe_carla's Python-API compatibility shortcuts (a Vehicle method called on a plain Actor) compile, as they do outside its strict mode.
  • A scenario registered with register_scenario_builder() is not checked at all: only its builder knows how it is built.
  • The None branch of a conditional expression chosen statically (#629). The check makes Codon decide a if x else None (and None if x else a) from x's type (#597): where x is always None to Codon, only the None branch is compiled. When the test does not narrow as Python does (None if x else x.a, which evaluates x.a exactly when x is None), the error in the other branch is not compiled. mypy's pass reports it where x is annotated (Item "None" of "Npc | None" has no attribute "a"); an unannotated parameter only ever given None passes.
  • A sum() whose str start is a variable (sum(parts, sep)), which CPython refuses: only a start written as a string, an f-string or str(...) is decided from the syntax (#625).
  • A value a framework constructor refuses, unless every argument of the call is a literal and the class is one of those built with literal arguments (#602): MetricCondition(cfg.metric, label="m") with an unknown metric, or any other framework class, raises at setup().

docs.title: Checking the framework itself
docs.text:
The scenario check trusts the model: it never compiles the framework's own source. The library check does, a module at a time, as each is made to compile:

uv run scenario-check --library                                   # every checked module
uv run scenario-check --library autoware_carla_scenario.kinematics.vector

from autoware_carla_scenario.typecheck import typecheck_library

result = typecheck_library()  # the modules typecheck/library.py lists as checked
assert result.ok, result.format()

test_typecheck_library.py makes the same check in the test suite.

The checked modules get the None check too (#277), as a scenario's modules do: after the compile, mypy runs over every module the run compiled, with the CARLA stubs, and an Optional used without a test for None fails the check at its line. Codon unwraps an Optional in the framework as it does in a scenario, so the compile alone accepted CollisionCondition reading CollisionEvent.other_actor (None for a collision with map geometry) as a carla.Actor, and the sensor callback raised in Python:

conditions/collision.py:158:32: error: Incompatible types in assignment (expression has type "Actor | None", variable has type "Actor"): Codon unwraps an Optional implicitly, so test the value for None before this use, or Python fails here when it is None (mypy: assignment)

It adds about 11 seconds to a run with mypy's cache cold, and under a second with it warm, to a compile of about a minute. A verdict kept between runs (below) holds the None check's too: the key already covers what it reads. test_typecheck_none_check.py runs the same None check over CHECKED without Codon, so a machine without a Codon compiler catches it as well.

So do the class rules (#587, #588): before the compile, the library check imports each module it compiles and refuses an __init__ that skips a base's (any class of the package counts as the framework here) and an attribute declared at class level that nothing assigns, as the scenario check does (Writing a scenario that type-checks). A module that does not import in Python has its classes left alone. test_typecheck_class_rules.py runs both rules over every module of the package without Codon.

A run that names modules is a slice of the full run. With the named modules, it compiles from their source the CHECKED modules they import, transitively. It does not follow an import that MODELLED_IMPORTS routes through the model, or one inside an UNCALLED function. It also brings the other modules of a REPLACED_MODELS entry once one of them is in, so that the model re-exports the checked definitions, as it does in the full run. scenario_base, for example, imports register_vehicle_entity from the checked entity.registry, which the model does not declare, and entity._spawn holds the checked GroundProjectionConfig, which the model VehicleEntityConfig must share. The modules it imports are checked as fully as the named ones: their functions and methods are called too, and errors are reported for every compiled module, not only the named ones. An error in a module the named one imports is an error the full run reports as well, and it would stop the named module from compiling anyway. Hiding it would only make the run fail without a reason. The result's title gives both counts (1 checked modules, 44 more they import for scenario_base, at the time of writing). Run without names, the check compiles exactly CHECKED, as before. Every checked module passes on its own.

The check's driver imports the model before any checked module, whichever module it names first. The model reaches the checked coordinate.frames through _poses.codon, and a run that started at coordinate.frames would reach the model, and come back to coordinate.frames, before that module defines anything.

docs.title: The manifest: typecheck/library.py
docs.text:
CHECKED lists the modules compiled from their source; EXCLUDED maps every other module to the reason it is not. "not yet checked (#45)" marks a module nobody has made compile yet; any other reason names what keeps a module out ("imports omegaconf, hydra": a package or a standard module Codon cannot compile). numpy is not one: Codon ships its own, and a module's numpy calls compile. Every module of the package except typecheck/ is in exactly one of the two, which the test suite checks, so a new module needs an entry.

UNCALLED names the few functions and methods of a checked module the check leaves out (module.Class.method, or module._helper for a protected one), each with its reason: one whose job Codon cannot express, in a module that otherwise compiles, such as what builds a condition's details (a dict[str, Any] of mixed value types) or reads a config node of any type (What is checked of the framework below lists every entry). Codon compiles a function only when something calls it, so neither its body nor an import made inside it is compiled: a module that needs a package or a standard module Codon lacks for one function imports it inside that function (import yaml in constraints_from_text()) and lists the function here. (json is not one of them: its shim, typecheck/codon/json.codon, writes any one-typed value and reads opaquely; what keeps to_json() out is the mixed-type dict it writes.) A test checks that every entry names a function or method of a checked module.

To check one more module:

  1. Move its entry from EXCLUDED to CHECKED. CHECKED holds one module a line, sorted (a test keeps it so), so the move is one line removed and one added, each where no other pull request's lines are.
  2. Run uv run scenario-check --library and fix what it reports, in the module. Only annotations and Codon-friendly rewrites: the module must behave exactly as it did. A function that cannot compile gets an UNCALLED entry, one line, with its reason.
  3. Run uv run pytest autoware_carla_scenario/test/carla_scenario/test_typecheck_library.py.

This page needs no edit: the counts and the lists of What is checked of the framework are generated from typecheck/library.py when the docs are built (mkdocs_hooks/typecheck_library.py, #789). A checked module is listed with the first paragraph of its docstring, so give it one that says what the module is.

The 121 EXCLUDED modules fall in three groups. Many fit more than one, so each belongs to the first group that fits it; most are in the first:

  • Those that import what Codon cannot compile: a package (pydantic, pickle, grpc, protobuf, omegaconf and hydra, yaml, jinja2, fastapi, cv2, cyclonedds, or openodd and hilspy, Rust extensions) or a standard module Codon lacks (socket, inspect, concurrent.futures, importlib beyond importlib.metadata, or more of os, pathlib, shlex, shutil, signal, subprocess, tempfile, threading, dataclasses, importlib.metadata or urllib.parse than their shims declare), at module level or inside a function the check calls. This is most of the tooling around a run (the editor, the UI, authoring, the sweeper's expansion and Hydra sweeper, the SLURM launcher's submitting side, the recordings and exports of a run, the HILS bridge), the ODD and coverage modules that wrap openodd, and the rest of what reads Lanelet2. A reason names pathlib only where the module uses more of it than the shim declares, and the other shimmed modules likewise; test_typecheck_library.py holds every reason to that.
  • Those that build on an excluded module, and import nothing Codon lacks themselves: they import a module that is neither checked nor modelled, or names that its package's model does not declare. Among them are packages that only re-export such a module. Some of them also hold values Codon has no type for.
  • Those that hold values Codon has no type for, and nothing else keeps them out: Any, or a class as a value.
